One report from Ibn ʿAbbās calls them the branches of the religion, thirty in number, ten named in one surah and ten in another, and he supports it with the verse that praises Abraham as the one who fulfilled his trust. Other reports from him through different students name the practices of bodily cleanliness and grooming, some listing ten, others dividing them between the body and the rites of the pilgrimage. Another group names the words of the prayer preserved in the following verses, in which Abraham and Ishmael ask their Lord to accept them and to show them the rites. A further report from al-Ḥasan lists the trials of the star, the moon, the sun, the fire, the emigration, and the circumcision, with the offering of his son added in one version. The discussion gathers these accounts and declines to fix one of them: the trial could have included all of them or some of them, since Abraham is reported to have passed through each, and no report from the Prophet with a sound chain settles the question. It adds that two reports from the Prophet have been transmitted on the point, one of them explaining the fulfilment as a prayer said morning and evening and the other as four units of prayer in the day, but it says both chains are open to criticism, so neither can bear the weight of the interpretation. The discussion ends by observing that the view identifying the words with the verses that follow would be a defensible position, since those verses give the imamate, the House, the covenant, and the prayer their clearest expression.

### **THE LEADER AND HIS DESCENDANTS**

The word rendered as leader is explained as the one who is followed and imitated: the promise given in the words ***“I will certainly make you into a role model for the people”*** meant that later believers would take their example from him, walking in his path and keeping his practice. The discussion draws out the sense of the term from the language, where the leader is the one who goes in front of the people and whom they follow. Abraham's request that his descendants receive the same is read as a question about the continuance of the honour, and the discussion rejects the view that he was asking about their religion in general, because his question follows directly on the promise of the imamate and must therefore be asking for the same gift. The question's generosity is then met by the answer that follows.

### **THE COVENANT AND THE WRONGDOERS**

The answer excludes the wrongdoers from the covenant, and the discussion records four explanations of what the covenant is. One report from al-Suddī takes it as the prophethood, so that the wrongdoers among Abraham's descendants would have no share in it. Reports from Mujāhid and other early authorities take it as the imamate itself, so that a wrongdoer is never made a leader who is imitated. A report from Ibn ʿAbbās takes it in a different direction: no covenant of obedience binds anyone to a wrongdoer in the wrong he does. A report from Qatādah takes the covenant as the security God grants, so that the wrongdoer will not receive it in the next world though he may share in its benefits here. The discussion settles on the sense that runs through all these: the wrongdoer is not made a leader to be followed, since leadership belongs to God's friends and the obedient, and the honour given to Abraham did not pass to those of his line who chose the other path. The promise to the father thus became a condition for the children, and the passage has already shown the community that claimed him what happens to those who substitute the book he kept.
verses.125:
> And ˹remember˺ when We made the Sacred House a centre and a sanctuary for the people ˹saying˺, “˹You may˺ take the standing-place of Abraham as a site of prayer.” And We entrusted Abraham and Ishmael to purify My House for those who circle it, who meditate in it, and who bow and prostrate themselves ˹in prayer˺

### **MEANING**

The verse recalls the House being made a place of return and a place of safety, the command to treat the standing place of Abraham as a place of prayer, and the charge laid on Abraham with his son Ishmael to keep the House pure for those who walk around it, for those who stay beside it, and for those who pray with bowing and prostration. The three parts move from the House's standing in the world, to the worship performed at it, to the service required to keep it fit for that worship.

### **A CENTRE AND A SANCTUARY**

The word rendered as centre is explained through its root, which carries the sense of returning: the House is a place to which people come back, generation after generation, and from which a visitor departs only to yearn for it again. Several reports state the point in the same way: *“no one leaves it having finished with it,”* and one report adds that the return happens yearly and the attachment never ends. The discussion also takes up the feminine form of the word and records what the two grammatical schools said about it: one explains the ending as marking the multitude of those who return, and the other treats it as the equivalent of the masculine form, like the pair of words for a standing place, with the distinction resting on whether the place itself or the act of standing is meant. A line of poetry describing the sanctuary as a returning place for the tribes is cited for the usage. The safety named alongside the centre is then explained, in keeping with the earlier treatment of the sanctuary, as the security granted to those who dwell around it and come to it, so that the House is both a destination and a protection.

### **THE STANDING PLACE**

The command connected with the standing place of Abraham is read by most as an instruction to the community to make that spot a place of prayer, and the discussion reports the practice that demonstrates what was meant: the Prophet performed the circuit of the House, then came to the standing place, recited the command, and prayed two units with the station between him and the House, as reported from two companions. One report interpreted the standing place as the whole sacred precinct, and another as the pilgrimage stations themselves, on the view that the word for prayer carries the sense of supplication, so that the command would be to make the pilgrimage sites places of invocation. The discussion prefers the first view, resting on the transmitted practice, and it explains the history of the stone as the spot where Abraham stood when he built, one report adding that his footprints remained in it and were worn away at last by the hands of those who sought them.

### **THE PURIFYING CHARGE**

The charge laid on the two of them is explained as a command, and the purification is explained as cleansing the House of idols, of their worship, and of everything contrary to the exclusive service of God; one report adds the speech of falsehood to the things cleansed. The discussion records two ways of taking the command: that the two were to build the House in purity, founding it on the exclusive worship of God, or that they were to cleanse the site before the building and the building after it from the traces of the idolatry that had been practised at the place before their time. The reports describing the purification as removal of idols and of doubt are gathered for both readings, and the discussion notes that the two interpretations agree on the substance, namely that the House was to be kept for the worship God had appointed.

### **THOSE WHO CIRCLE AND THOSE WHO STAY**

The three groups named at the end are explained in order. The first group, the circlers, are those who walk around the House, and the discussion prefers the view that the name belongs to anyone performing the circuit and not only to visitors from abroad, since the name belongs to the act. Those who stay are explained by one early authority as those who remain at the House without circling or praying, and other reports name them as the sojourners, the residents of the sacred city, or those engaged in prayer; the discussion prefers the view of the one who stays as a neighbour at the House, because the verse has already named the circling and the praying separately, so the third group must be those whose devotion is expressed through remaining. The bowing and prostrating are then explained as the people of prayer, and the plural forms of both words are traced in the discussion to the patterns the language uses for a person and a group. The list as a whole describes the House as a place kept for every manner of worship, and the charge to purify it is measured by the variety of worshippers it must accommodate.
verses.126:
> And ˹remember˺ when Abraham said, “My Lord, make this city ˹of Mecca˺ secure and provide fruits to its people—those among them who believe in Allah and the Last Day.” He answered, “As for those who disbelieve, I will let them enjoy themselves for a little while, then I will condemn them to the torment of the Fire. What an evil destination!”

### **MEANING**

The verse carries the founding account into the prayer made over the city. Abraham asks that the place be held safe and that produce from the earth reach the people settled in it, and the answer grants more than was asked while setting a term on part of it: the denier is given his share of the provision and a span of enjoyment, and afterwards he is driven to the punishment, and the destination is named as an evil one. The sentence closes the founding with a warning that the goods of this life are not the reward, and that the blessing of a place is measured by the worship it exists to serve.

### **THE SANCTUARY AND THE TWO ANSWERS**

The safety Abraham asked for is explained as security from tyrants who would overrun the place, and from the punishments that fall on other lands, whether the earth swallowing a settlement, cities overturned, or drowning. The discussion then asks whether the city had been safe only from the hour of the prayer, and the answers divide. One body of opinion holds that it was sacred from the day the heavens and the earth were made, and it argues from the words spoken by the Prophet when Mecca was taken, in which he announced that God had made the city sacred *"on the day when He created the heavens and the earth"*, that its sanctity stands until the resurrection, and that it was opened to him for one hour of a day against the wish of the townspeople and then returned to what it had been. Others hold that the city became sacred through the prayer itself, and they argue from the words the Prophet spoke about the two sanctuaries, in the report of Jābir ibn ʿAbd Allāh: *"Abraham made the House of God sacred and gave it safety, and I have made Medina sacred between its two lava fields."* The same sense is reported from Abū Hurayrah and from Rāfiʿ ibn Khadīj, each of them naming the city of the Prophet as the second sanctuary whose trees and game are protected.

The discussion then reconciles the two bodies of material rather than choosing between them. Before Abraham settled his family at the site, the place was guarded by God against those who meant it harm and shielded from the plagues that fell elsewhere, but no obligation rested on people to treat it as inviolable. After Abraham had settled his wife and son there and asked for its safety, the duty of its sanctity was laid on mankind at his request and proclaimed on his tongue, so that the later claim that he made it sacred describes the obligation imposed through him, while the earlier claim describes the protection that had always been God's. Neither set of reports cancels the other, and the discussion insists that reports from the Prophet, once established, do not contradict one another in substance.

### **PROVISION, ITS TERM, AND ITS END**

The request for provision is answered inside the verse, and the discussion draws out what the answer adds. Abraham asked for the believers, and the answer extends the provision to those who deny, with the difference stated: the denier is granted enjoyment for a limited term before he is impelled to the punishment. A report read to Muhammad ibn Muslim says that at the time Abraham prayed for the sanctuary to be given fruits, God moved al-Ṭāʾif there from Palestine, and the discussion uses that to explain how a valley without crops could feed a settled population. The wording that adds the deniers is then examined, because the reciters read the sentence in two forms: some read it as God's own answer, so that He is the speaker who promises enjoyment and then compulsion; others read it as Abraham's further plea for the deniers as well, asking that they too be provided for before they are driven away. The discussion prefers the reading in which God answers, on the ground that the established transmission supports it and that the alternative is rare, and it explains the sense accordingly: God told Abraham that his request was granted, that believer and denier alike would be given from the fruits of the town, that the denier's share is a loan of enjoyment until his death arrives, and that afterwards he is driven to the fire.

The words of the closing sentence are then unpacked. To be impelled means to be compelled and driven along, and the discussion compares the verb with the verse that describes the guilty being shoved towards the fire of hell, Q 52:13, so that the compulsion is pictured as a driving rather than a leading. The destination is explained as the place a thing ends up in, the final lodging of the one who took the road of denial, and the verdict on it is read as God's own summary of the whole account.
verses.127:
> And ˹remember˺ when Abraham raised the foundation of the House with Ishmael, ˹both praying,˺ “Our Lord! Accept ˹this˺ from us. You are indeed the All-Hearing, All-Knowing

### **MEANING**

The account returns to the building itself, with Abraham raising the House's foundations and Ishmael beside him, the two of them asking their Lord to receive the work from their hands. The prayer is set inside the account so that the reader hears what the builders said while the walls rose, and the two names that close the verse answer the request they had made.

### **THE FOUNDATIONS AND THE EARLIER HOUSE**

The word for the foundations is explained as the bases on which a building rests, and the discussion adds a grammatical note: the singular form keeps its feminine ending when it names a woman past the age of childbearing, but drops it when it names the base of a wall, since the word follows a pattern that has no masculine counterpart in that sense. What the foundations were is then taken up, and the reports fall into two groups. One group holds that a house had stood on the site before Abraham and that he raised its remaining bases. In this group, the first house is said to have been built by Adam on God's command, after he complained that he could no longer hear the voices of the angels, and the answer he received promised him *"a house around which you shall circle as the angels circle about My throne"*. Another report from the same group has the house sent down with Adam and circled by the prophets after him, until the flood lifted it away and left its foundation, which Abraham later found. The second group holds that no building had stood on the site in physical form, and that God spread the ground out from beneath the first sanctuary, so that the place existed as a raised patch of red earth, or as a rock like a dome, before any wall was raised on it. A report from ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib describes how the site was cleared for Abraham: a wind called the sakīnah, with two heads, swept the ground until the first foundation was exposed, and Abraham built on it, while the stones he used were of a size that thirty men could not lift.

The discussion's own position is a refusal to decide. It observes that the reality of the matter is reached only through a report from God or His messenger carrying an uninterrupted transmission, and that no such report exists here, nor can the question be settled by reasoning, so no one of the possibilities is preferable to another. The point the discussion does insist on is the one the accounts share and the verse establishes: the House whose foundations Abraham lifted was not the invention of a new worship, but the raising of foundations already laid for the worship of the One God.

### **THE TWO BUILDERS AT WORK**

The discussion notes the disagreement about how the work was shared, and the reports mostly agree that the father built and the son supplied the material. One has Ishmael carrying the stones on his neck while the elder set them in place; another has the two working together, with Ishmael bringing the stones and Abraham building. A report from Ibn ʿAbbās describes the exchange over the corner stone: Abraham asked his son for a good stone to place there, the son went looking while Gabriel brought the Black Stone, and when the son returned and found it in place he asked where it had come from, and his father answered that it had been brought by one who had not relied on the boy's building. The same report explains the standing place: when the structure rose higher, the elder stood on a stone to work, and that stone is the one honoured in the sanctuary. Another has the two of them saying the prayer of the verse as they worked, so that the words of the verse are the sound of the building site itself.

The discussion draws a conclusion from the request itself. Because the two asked that their work be received rather than merely describing it, the building could not have been raised as a dwelling for themselves; acceptance is asked for acts of nearness, and a house built for one's own use would have had nothing in it to accept. The request shows that the structure was meant for those who would come to worship at it, and that the builders regarded the labour itself as an offering made on behalf of others.
verses.128:
> Our Lord! Make us both ˹fully˺ submit to You and from our descendants a nation that will submit to you. Show us our rituals, and turn to us in grace. You are truly the Accepter of Repentance, Most Merciful

### **MEANING**

The prayer continues with the two builders asking to be made submissive to their Lord, and asking that a community of submitters come from their descendants. They ask to be shown the rites of worship, and they close by asking their Lord to turn back to them, naming Him as the one who accepts the return of the repentant and whose mercy is vast.

### **BEING SHOWN THE RITES**

The request to be shown is read in two ways. The common reading of the people of the Ḥijāz and of Kūfa takes it as a request for sight, so that the two asked God to display the rites before their eyes, and the discussion attaches the reports that describe what they were shown: the circuit of the House, the running between the two hills, the departure from the plain of ʿArafah, the departure from Jamʿ, and the stoning of the pillars, until God completed the religion. In support of the other reading, in which the word means to teach and to guide rather than to make visible, the discussion quotes a line of ancient poetry in which a man asks his mother to *"point me to a generous man who died of wasting, or a miser who lives forever"*, and it explains that the poet asks to be directed to the man, not to see him with the eye. Al-Suddī's account of how the rites were taught then follows: Abraham was commanded to call mankind to the pilgrimage, he stood between the two hills of the city and called, every believer's heart received the call, and then God showed him the stations one by one — the plain that was named for his recognising it, the two places that were named for his stopping and drawing near, and the pass that was named for his passing it by.

The word for the rites is itself explained, and here too the discussion records a difference. Its root sense is the place where a rite is performed and where a person draws near to God by an act that pleases Him, whether by slaughtering, praying, circling the House, or running between the hills; the word came to name the stations of the pilgrimage because people frequent and return to them. A group of the early authorities restricted the word here to the places of sacrifice, so that the request becomes a plea to be taught how to slaughter the offerings. The discussion acknowledges that this sense is possible, but prefers the broader one, since the pilgrimage stations are what the word most commonly names, and it adds a report from ʿAlī: when Abraham finished the building he said that he had done what he was commanded and asked to be shown his rites, and God sent Gabriel, who performed the pilgrimage with him. The reading attributed to the codex of Ibn Masʿūd changes the request into one made for the descendants, which fits the way the two men had already joined the community of their line to themselves in the prayer.

### **SUBMISSION, THE COMMUNITY, AND THE RETURN**

The request to be made submissive is explained through the sense of handing oneself over and bowing to the command, so that the two asked to be obedient to God's order without associating anything else with Him in obedience or worship. The request for a community from their descendants is narrowed deliberately, because God had already informed Abraham that some of his line would not attain His covenant, and the two therefore asked for the portion of their descendants who would answer. One opinion holds that the community meant is the Arabs, and the discussion rejects the restriction, since the descendants of Abraham include others besides the Arabs and the answering of God's command is found among both. The word rendered as community is explained as a group of people, in the manner of the verse that speaks of a group among the people of Moses guiding by the truth, Q 7:159.

The closing request is explained through the meaning of turning back. The root denotes a return from what is disliked to what is loved; the servant's turning is his return from what God dislikes by regret, by ceasing, and by resolving not to go back, while God's turning towards His servant is His return to him with pardon and forgiveness. The discussion asks whether the two builders had sins that required such a plea, and answers that no one is free of the need to turn, that the two may have meant the state of the work they had just completed, and that they may also have intended the wrongdoers among their descendants, so that the apparent request for themselves carries a request for their line. The two names at the close of the verse are then read as the answer already given: the One who returns to His servants with grace, and the Merciful who rescues from ruin whom He wills.
verses.129:
> Our Lord! Raise from among them a messenger who will recite to them Your revelations, teach them the Book and wisdom, and purify them. Indeed, You ˹alone˺ are the Almighty, All-Wise.”

### **MEANING**

The prayer ends by asking that a messenger be raised up from that people, one who would recite the revealed verses before them, convey the Book and its wisdom, and cleanse their lives. The request names the office that the community addressed has already received, and it links the fulfilment of the father's petition to the messenger who now stands in their midst.

### **THE MESSENGER OF THE PRAYER**

The discussion states that this petition of Abraham and Ishmael concerns the Prophet Muhammad in particular, and it is the supplication he himself pointed to when he described who he was. One report has the Prophet telling a group of his companions, when they asked him about himself, *"I am the supplication of my father Abraham and the glad tidings of Jesus."* Another report, from ʿIrbāḍ ibn Sāriyah, has him declaring that he was written with God in the mother of the Book as the seal of the prophets while Adam was still being shaped, and then naming the tokens of it: the supplication of his father Abraham, the announcement of Jesus to his people, and the vision his mother saw. The discussion also records how the answer was understood by the earliest expositors: Qatādah says that God granted the request and raised a messenger from their own number, whose face and lineage they knew, bringing them out of the darkness into the light and guiding them to the path of the Mighty, the Praised; al-Rabīʿ says it was said to Abraham that his prayer had been answered and that the messenger would appear in the last age. The position of the petition inside the passage is treated as evidence of the messenger's standing, since the acceptance of the request is visible in the community that has received him.

### **RECITING, TEACHING, AND PURIFYING**

The tasks named in the prayer are then taken one by one. To recite the verses means to read aloud the Book that is revealed to him, and the discussion treats this as the first way the message enters a community. The Book he teaches is identified with the Qur'an, and the wisdom joined to it is the subject of several explanations: the practice of the Prophet handed down alongside the revelation, in the report from Qatādah; knowledge of the religion and understanding of it and following it, in the answer Mālik gave when he was asked what wisdom is; and the religion that could not be known except through the messenger, which Ibn Zayd described as a light God places in the heart, citing the verse that says whoever is given wisdom has been given much good, Q 2:269. The discussion's own conclusion is that wisdom here is the knowledge of God's rulings that is reached only by the messenger's exposition, derived from the root that means the deciding between truth and falsehood, so that the verse's sense becomes a request that the messenger recite God's verses, teach His Book, and set out the judgements He has taught.

The purifying is explained through the sense of cleansing and of growth together: the messenger clears the community of the worship of anything besides God and of the practices that clung to them from the age of ignorance, and he causes them to increase by obedience. A report from Ibn ʿAbbās glosses the word as obedience to God and sincerity; another from Ibn Jurayj says it means to cleanse them from associating others with God and to free them from it. The discussion connects this cleansing with the purifying of the House that the two builders had been charged with in the verse before, so that the community becomes what the House was built to serve. The verse closes with the two names by which the request is sealed, and they are read as its guarantee: the Almighty is the One whose will nothing frustrates, so He can do for the two men and their line what they asked; the All-Wise is the One whose planning admits no flaw, so He grants what benefits them and their descendants, and the giving costs Him nothing.

### **THE ANSWER IN THE COMMUNITY**

The whole petition is treated in the discussion as answered in the sight of the community that reads it. The messenger Abraham asked for was raised from his line, and the tasks named in the prayer are the tasks that community had seen performed in its own days: the revealed verses recited in its gatherings, the Book taught together with its understanding, and a people cleansed from the worship of anything besides God. The account of the House that began with two men raising its foundations therefore ends with the worship that would be offered in it, and the father's prayer is shown to have been granted long after his death in the community standing before the reader.
verses.130:
> And who would reject the faith of Abraham except a fool! We certainly chose him in this life, and in the Hereafter he will surely be among the righteous

### **MEANING**

The verse asks who would turn away from the religion of Abraham, and answers that no one does so except a person who has fooled himself. It then states the standing given to Abraham in this world and the standing he holds in the world to come, and with that the account of the founding closes and the community that claims him is left with the measure of what claiming him requires.

### **THE RELIGION ABANDONED**

The people addressed are identified as the two communities who chose their own traditions over what Abraham had followed. The religion of Abraham is described as the pure submission to the One God, the way named in the verse that declares Abraham to have been neither Jew nor Christian but a man of pure faith and a submitter, Q 3:67, and the point is put in the same shape by the reports from Qatādah and al-Rabīʿ: the two communities turned aside from his religion, took up *"innovations that were not from God"*, and left the submission that God had sent His prophet with. The question at the head of the verse is therefore read as an indictment rather than an inquiry, since the sentence itself supplies the only possible answer, and the community that appeals to Abraham is reminded that the appeal costs it the very path he walked. The discussion adds that the one who departs from the way Abraham left for those after him has departed from God, since God chose Abraham, made him a leader, and named his religion the submission.

### **THE FOOL, AND THE MAN CHOSEN**

The person who turns away is described as one who has made himself foolish, and the word is explained as ignorance: such a person does not know where his own interest lies, since he has miscalculated what profits and what harms him in his final destination. A report from Ibn Zayd phrases the sense as the one who has missed his share. The discussion then examines the grammatical form of the phrase, noting that the word for the self stands in the accusative as a clarification, because the foolishness belongs to the self rather than to the man, in the way a statement about someone's spaciousness of house locates the space in the house and not in the person; the discussion adds that the construction follows the pattern of verbs of this class which take the self as their object, and records a Basran objection that treats the verb as one that does not normally pass over to an object at all.

The second half of the verse names the honour given to Abraham. Chosen is explained as selected and taken for closeness to his Lord, and the choosing is joined to his being made a leader for those who came after him. The closing words place him in the world to come among the upright, and the upright are explained as those who pay what is due to God. The discussion draws the two sentences together: Abraham is a chosen one in this world and a friend in the next, entering where those who kept God's covenant enter, and the man who abandons his way separates himself both from the one God selected and from the company to which that one belongs. The claim to Abraham is settled by conduct rather than by descent: whoever holds to what he held to follows him, and whoever turns away has nothing from the connection but the foolishness this verse named.
verses.131:
> When his Lord ordered him, “Submit ˹to My Will˺,” he responded, “I submit to the Lord of all worlds.”

### **MEANING**

The verse completes the portrait of Abraham that the preceding verse began. Having declared that only a fool would turn away from his religion, and that God chose him in this world and placed him among the righteous in the next, the passage now names the moment in which that choosing became visible: God called him to surrender, and he answered at once. The command ***“Submit”*** asks for two things together: that worship be given sincerely to God alone, and that the person yield to Him in obedience. Abraham’s reply, ***“I submit to the Lord of all worlds,”*** is the same surrender stated in the first person, with the object of that surrender named as the Owner and Director of every created thing, to the exclusion of anything else.

The verse is short, but it carries the argument of the whole passage. The communities that claimed Abraham as their ancestor are being shown what he actually was. He was not defined by a lineage or a later communal label; he was defined by an act of surrender to God. The next verses will show that this same surrender was what he handed on to his sons, and what Jacob handed on after him.

### **HOW THE VERSE CONNECTS TO THE CHOOSING**

The opening word, rendered ***“When,”*** marks a time, and early grammarians asked what event it is tied to. The explanation given is that it attaches to the statement just before it: *“We certainly chose him in this life.”* The sense of the two verses together is therefore: *“We chose him in this world at the time **his Lord** said to **him, Submit**, and he said, I have submitted to the Lord of the worlds.”* The choosing and the surrender are presented as one event seen from two sides. God’s selection of Abraham is not an arbitrary favour detached from his conduct; it is set at the very moment of his answer.

This reading also explains a change of voice in the passage. The previous verse speaks in the first person plural, ***“We certainly chose him,”*** while this verse speaks of God in the third person, ***“his Lord ordered him.”*** Arabic usage allows a speaker to refer to himself as though he were absent once he has already been mentioned directly, and the point is illustrated by a line of the poet Khufāf ibn Nudbah, who speaks of himself by name in the middle of his own boast: *“Look well at Khufāf — I am that very one.”* The shift does not introduce a new speaker; it lets the sentence name God as ***“his Lord”***, which stresses the bond between the One who commands and the servant who answers.

### **WHEN THE CALL CAME**

A natural question arises: did God actually call Abraham to submission, and if so, when? The explanation offered is that He did, and that the occasion is the one recounted in Surah 6. There, after Abraham had examined the star, the moon, and the sun, and had seen each of them set, he declared to his people: *“O my people, I am free of what you associate with God. I have turned my face to the One who originated the heavens and the earth, inclining to truth, and I am not one of those who associate partners with Him,”* Qur’an 6:78–79. On this reading, the command ***“Submit”*** came after Abraham had been tested by the heavenly bodies, and his declaration to his people was the outward form of the answer recorded here.

This connection gives the verse a concrete setting. Abraham’s surrender was not a formula pronounced in isolation; it was a decision reached in the face of the worship practised around him, and it cost him his standing among his own people. The same Surah 6 passage describes him rejecting every object of worship that rises and sets, which matches the description here of a surrender made to the **Lord of all worlds**, the One who directs every created thing rather than being one of them.

### **WHAT SUBMISSION MEANS HERE**

The word behind ***“Submit”*** and ***“I submit”*** shares its root with the name of the religion that the Prophet was later commanded to proclaim. The explanation given for this verse defines it as sincerity of worship together with humility in obedience, so Abraham’s reply means: *“I have humbled myself in obedience and made my worship sincere to the Owner of all creation and its Director.”* The word is therefore not a label that one group may claim against another. It describes a relationship between a servant and God, and the verse uses it precisely to show that Abraham’s religion was this relationship.

The point prepares for the argument that follows. In the verses ahead, the claims of later communities that Abraham belonged to them are answered by reminding them what he submitted to, what he bequeathed to his descendants, and what his descendants promised at Jacob’s deathbed. The single exchange in this verse, a command and an immediate answer, becomes the standard against which those claims will be measured.
verses.132:
> This was the advice of Abraham—as well as Jacob—to his children, ˹saying˺, “Indeed, Allah has chosen for you this faith; so do not die except in ˹a state of full˺ submission.”

### **MEANING**

Abraham did not keep his surrender to himself. The verse says that he urged it on his sons, and that Jacob, his grandson, did the same with his own sons. What they were urged to hold to is the word Abraham had just spoken, ***“I submit to the Lord of all worlds”***: sincere worship of God alone and the humbling of heart and limbs before Him. The content of the charge is then quoted directly: God has selected this religion for you, so never let death find you in any state but surrender.

The verse turns the personal answer of the previous verse into an inheritance. The faith of Abraham is shown passing from father to son to grandson, not as ancestry but as an instruction to be kept. For the communities addressed by the surah, who appealed to their descent from Abraham and Jacob, the verse identifies exactly what those patriarchs left behind.

### **WHAT WAS BEQUEATHED, AND BY WHOM**

The pronoun in the Arabic, translated by ***“This was the advice,”*** points back to the word of surrender in the preceding verse. The bequest is therefore not a general moral counsel but a specific charge: to worship God sincerely and yield to Him.

Early explanations agree that Jacob is named as a second testator who repeated the same charge. Qatādah, in the report through Saʿīd and Yazīd ibn Zurayʿ, says that Jacob gave the same instruction to his sons after Abraham, and Ibn ʿAbbās, in the report through al-ʿAwfī’s family, says that Abraham charged his sons with submission and *“Jacob charged them with the like of it.”* Some grammarians proposed a different division: the sentence about Abraham ends after ***“his children,”*** and a new statement begins with Jacob, so that only Jacob is the one who says the quoted words. That division is unconvincing, because what Jacob urged on his sons is identical to what Abraham urged on his: obedience to God, humility before Him, and submission. Splitting the sentence would separate two charges that the verse presents as the same.

### **THE GRAMMAR OF THE CHARGE**

The quoted words begin with the address *“O my sons”* without the connecting particle that would normally follow a verb of instructing. The explanation is that an instruction is a kind of speech, so the sentence is constructed according to its meaning rather than its form, as if it read: Abraham and Jacob said to their sons. The same construction appears in Qur’an 4:11, *“God instructs you concerning your children: for the male, the like of the share of two females,”* where the content of the instruction follows directly. An unattributed Arabic line shows the same thing with a verb of declaring: *“I will disclose to you, among what I disclose, that I have two longings: one longing in Najd, and one in the land of Sind.”* A second view held that the vocative itself makes the particle unnecessary, as Arabs say *“I called out: Where is Zayd?”* without inserting a connective.

There are also two readings of the verb. Some reciters read it in a simple form meaning *“he entrusted,”* while the common reading uses an intensive form, which conveys a charge given again and again, one instruction after another. On that reading, the bequest was not a single sentence at the deathbed but a repeated emphasis.

### **REMAINING IN SUBMISSION UNTIL DEATH**

The definite article in ***“this faith”*** has a reason: the sons had already been taught this religion by their fathers, so they are reminded of something they know. The fathers then say, in effect, *“God has selected for you this religion that has been entrusted to you, so fear God lest you die in any state other than it.”*

The command ***“do not die except in ˹a state of full˺ submission”*** raises an obvious objection, since no one controls the moment of death. The answer is that the command concerns the life before death: never part from this religion for any part of your life. Since no one knows whether death will come by night or by day, the only way to be sure of dying in submission is never to leave it. Whoever abandons it risks being overtaken by death in a state other than the religion God chose, and dying while his Lord is displeased with him.

The wording thus makes the end of life the test of the whole of it. The patriarchs did not ask their sons merely to begin in submission, but to remain there at every moment, so that whatever hour death came, it would come to people who had kept the charge.
verses.133:
> Or did you witness when death came to Jacob? He asked his children, “Who will you worship after my passing?” They replied, “We will ˹continue to˺ worship your God, the God of your forefathers—Abraham, Ishmael, and Isaac—the One God. And to Him we ˹all˺ submit.”

### **MEANING**

The verse turns to the people who were claiming the patriarchs for their own communities and asks them a pointed question: were you present when Jacob was dying? The question expects the answer no. They were not there, and so they cannot claim to know that Jacob or his fathers followed the religion they now attribute to them. The verse then recounts what was actually said at that deathbed. Jacob put a question to his sons about what they would worship once he was gone, and they answered that they would worship his God and the God of his fathers, a single God, and that they were submitting to Him.

The scene is the clearest proof the passage offers. The previous verse said that Jacob charged his sons with submission; this verse shows them accepting the charge in words that leave no room for any later sectarian label.

### **THE QUESTION PUT TO THE CLAIMANTS**

The question opens with the Arabic particle usually used for alternatives, but here it begins a new inquiry following on from earlier speech, a usage also found at the start of Surah 32, where the description of the Book is followed by *“Or do they say, He invented it?”* Qur’an 32:1–3. The sense is simply: were you witnesses?

The addressees are identified in the early explanations as the People of the Book; al-Rabīʿ, in the report through Ibn Abī Jaʿfar from his father, says that ***“Or did you witness”*** refers to them. The meaning drawn from this is: you who reject the Prophet and claim the patriarchs for yourselves, were you present at Jacob’s deathbed? You were not, so do not attach falsehoods to God’s prophets and messengers by ascribing your later religions to them. God sent Abraham, his sons Isaac and Ishmael, and their descendants with the pure monotheism of submission, and that is what they enjoined on their children. Had you been present and heard them, you would know that they did not follow the religions you have ascribed to them. These verses are therefore understood as a refutation of the claim, made by both communities, that Abraham and Jacob had belonged to them.

### **THE DEATHBED EXCHANGE**

Jacob’s question, ***“Who will you worship after my passing?”***, is phrased in Arabic with the word for *“what,”* meaning: what thing is it that you shall worship once I am gone? The sons answer: we will worship the one you worship and the one your fathers worshipped. The phrase ***“the One God”*** explains what that worship consists of: devotion given sincerely to Him, His lordship affirmed as unique, no partner associated with Him, and no lord taken besides Him. Grammatically the word for *“God”* in this phrase is a circumstantial description of ***“your God,”*** so the sons are describing the manner of their worship as much as its object.

Their final words, ***“And to Him we ˹all˺ submit,”*** can be read in two ways. They may describe the state in which the worship is offered: we shall ***“worship your God,”*** submitting to Him in obedience. Or they may be a new statement: we shall ***“worship your God”*** after you, and we are submitting to Him now and in every state. The first reading fits the flow of the sentence more naturally, since it presents submission as the manner of their worship rather than an added claim.

### **WHY ISHMAEL IS NAMED AMONG THE FATHERS**

The list of fathers places Ishmael before Isaac. Ibn Zayd, in the report through Ibn Wahb, says it begins with Ishmael *“because he was the elder.”*

Ishmael was Jacob’s uncle, not his father, and one early reciter read *“the God of your father Abraham,”* in the singular, apparently thinking that an uncle could not be counted among the fathers. That reading was rejected as a misunderstanding of Arabic usage, in which uncles are regularly spoken of as fathers and maternal aunts as mothers. All the recognised reciters read ***“your forefathers,”*** in the plural, and the isolated reading carries no weight against their agreement. The plural is significant: Jacob’s sons place Ishmael, the forefather of the Arabs, in the same line of worship as Abraham and Isaac, so the single God worshipped by the whole family stands above the divisions later drawn between their descendants.
verses.134:
> That was a community that had already gone before. For them is what they earned and for you is what you have earned. And you will not be accountable for what they have done

### **MEANING**

After showing what Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and their sons actually believed, the passage closes the argument with a firm separation. These patriarchs and their faithful children were ***“a community that had already gone before”***: their lives are complete and their record is sealed. Whatever good they did belongs to them; whatever the present generation does belongs to it. No one will be questioned about the deeds of another.

The verse is addressed to those who were appealing to the patriarchs while rejecting the message that had come to them. It tells them that a claimed connection with righteous ancestors cannot help them before God. What helps a person is the good he has himself sent ahead, and the patriarchs’ good deeds cannot be transferred to descendants who do not share their submission.

### **WHO THE COMMUNITY IS**

The ***“community”*** referred to is identified as Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and their children. The word used for it here means a group or generation of people. The verse therefore speaks to the Jews and Christians of the Prophet’s time in effect as follows: leave off describing Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and the faithful among their children with what does not belong to them; do not attribute to them the later religions you hold. They were a generation that has passed on its way.

The verb translated ***“had already gone before”*** literally means *“has become empty”* or *“has gone off alone.”* Its root is used of a man who goes to a place where he has no companion and is cut off from people. The same word came to be used of someone who has died, because the dead person is separated from this world and from the company of family and friends he had in it. The image gives the sentence its finality: the patriarchs have left the world in which people argue about them, and nothing said about them now can change the people they were.

### **EACH GENERATION AND ITS OWN EARNINGS**

The pronoun in ***“For them is what they earned”*** can refer either to *“that”* or to the ***“community,”*** with no difference in meaning. The earnings are the good deeds the patriarchs performed. The present generation likewise has what it has done, and the sentence ***“you will not be accountable for what they have done”*** makes clear that neither party is taken to account for the other. The principle is stated in general form elsewhere in the Qur’an: every soul has what it has earned and bears what it has incurred, as the closing verse of this surah, Qur’an 2:286, puts it in the words *“for it is what it has earned, and against it is what it has incurred.”*

The point is drawn out plainly in the explanation of this verse: *“Leave off claiming them and claiming their religions, for claims do not avail you with God; what will avail you with Him is whatever righteous deeds you have already done and sent ahead, if you have done them.”* The patriarchs are not asked about what their descendants did, and their descendants are not credited with what the patriarchs did.

### **THE VERSE IN THE PASSAGE**

The same sentence will be repeated almost word for word a few verses later, at 2:141, after another round of argument about whether the patriarchs were Jews or Christians. Here it closes the account of Abraham’s surrender, his bequest, and Jacob’s deathbed scene. The repetition frames the debate that follows: whatever arguments the communities bring about the patriarchs, the outcome for each person depends on his own response to the truth that has reached him.

Read in this setting, the verse does not deny the honour of the patriarchs; the preceding verses have just affirmed it. It denies only that this honour can be inherited without the faith that produced it. The faith of Abraham is open to whoever submits as he did, and closed to whoever relies on his name while abandoning his way.
verses.135:
> The Jews and Christians each say, “Follow our faith to be ˹rightly˺ guided.” Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “No! We follow the faith of Abraham, the upright—who was not a polytheist.”

### **MEANING**

The verse records the invitation each community extended to the Prophet and his followers. The Jews said, in effect, *“become Jews and you will be guided,”* and the Christians said, *“become Christians and you will be guided.”* Guidance here means arriving at the path of truth. The Prophet is told to answer with a single sentence that sets both invitations aside: rather, we follow the religion of Abraham, who was upright and inclined to the truth and was never one of those who associate partners with God.

The answer is brief but complete. Both communities acknowledged Abraham and honoured him; neither could claim that his religion was something other than the worship of God. By pointing to Abraham, the Prophet offers common ground that all parties already recognised, instead of entering a contest between two later identities. The passage has just shown, through Abraham’s surrender and Jacob’s deathbed scene, what that religion contained.

### **THE INVITATION AND ITS SETTING**

A report from Ibn ʿAbbās, transmitted by Ibn Isḥāq through Muḥammad ibn Abī Muḥammad from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr or ʿIkrimah, gives the occasion. ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ṣūriyā al-Aʿwar said to the Prophet: *“Guidance is nothing but what we are upon. So follow us, Muhammad, and you will be guided!”* The Christians said the same, and the verse was revealed concerning them. The report presents the claim in the same form as the verse: each group equated guidance with membership in itself.

The reply is described as the most concise and complete argument that could be given. Its sense is: come, let us follow the religion of Abraham, which all of us agree in testifying was the religion God approved, chose, and commanded; and let us leave the other religions over which we differ, which some of us reject and others accept. On those disputed identities there is no way for us to agree, while on the religion of Abraham there is.

### **THE MEANING OF UPRIGHT**

The Arabic word translated ***“the upright”*** is *ḥanīf*, and its basic sense is straightness in anything. A man whose feet turn in towards each other was called by a related name, which philologists explained as a hopeful name meant to wish him soundness, as the desert where travellers perish was called by a word meaning *“a place of salvation,”* and a man stung by a snake was called *“the sound one.”* On this basis the sentence means: rather, we follow the religion of Abraham, as one who is straight upon it.

The early interpreters gave several more specific meanings. Some said the *ḥanīf* is the pilgrim. Al-Ḥasan, asked about the term in a report through Kathīr Abī Sahl, answered: *“The pilgrimage to the House.”* ʿAṭiyyah, Mujāhid, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, and Ibn ʿAbbās through ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah gave the same gloss, and ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Qāsim said that the people of Muḍar who made the pilgrimage in the age of ignorance were called by this name, so God revealed Qur’an 22:31, *“inclining to God, not associating partners with Him.”* Others explained the word as one who follows; another view tied it to circumcision, which Abraham was the first to establish; al-Suddī explained it as sincerity, one whose religion is devoted to God alone; and still others said it simply meant submission.

The pilgrimage and circumcision views cannot be the whole meaning. If the word meant performing the pilgrimage, the idolaters who went on pilgrimage in the age of ignorance would have qualified, yet Qur’an 3:67 says of Abraham that he was *“upright, a submitter, and he was not of the polytheists,”* separating uprightness from idolatry. If it meant circumcision, those who practised it while rejecting Abraham’s way would have qualified, yet the same verse says Abraham *“was neither a Jew nor a Christian.”* The more coherent sense is steadfastness on the religion of Abraham and following him in it, including the rites and practices he established.

### **WHY THE TITLE BELONGS TO ABRAHAM**

Earlier prophets and their followers were also upright in obeying God. The term is tied to Abraham because God made him a leader for all who came after him until the Last Hour, in the rites of pilgrimage, circumcision, and other practices of submission, and those practices became a mark separating believers from unbelievers. The one who follows him is called upright, while those who departed from his way became known by the names of the other religions.

The closing clause, ***“who was not a polytheist,”*** denies that Abraham worshipped idols, and in the setting of this verse it also answers the two claims: he was neither of the one community nor of the other, but upright and submitting to God.

Three grammatical explanations are offered for the case of ***“the faith of Abraham”***: it may follow the implied sense of the opponents’ words, as if they had said *“follow Judaism or Christianity”* and the reply were *“rather, the religion of Abraham”*; it may be governed by an unstated verb, *“we follow”*; or it may stand for *“the people of the religion of Abraham,”* with the word for people omitted. Some reciters read it in the nominative, giving the sense: rather, guidance is the religion of Abraham.
verses.136:
> Say, ˹O believers,˺ “We believe in Allah and what has been revealed to us; and what was revealed to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and his descendants; and what was given to Moses, Jesus, and other prophets from their Lord. We make no distinction between any of them. And to Allah we all submit.”

### **MEANING**

After the Prophet was given the reply to the invitation to become Jews or Christians, the believers themselves are now taught what to say. Their statement is a declaration of faith that leaves nothing out: belief in God; in the revelation sent down to them through their Prophet; in what was sent down **to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob,** and the prophets among Jacob’s descendants; in the Torah that Moses received and the Gospel given to Jesus; and in what every prophet received from his Lord. All of it is affirmed as truth, guidance, and light from God, and all the prophets are affirmed as having been on the same path, confirming one another in calling to the oneness of God and obedience to Him.

The decisive clause is ***“We make no distinction between any of them.”*** The believers do not accept some prophets and reject others, nor declare loyalty to some and disown others. The statement closes with ***“And to Allah we all submit,”*** meaning that they humble themselves before Him in obedience and yield to Him in servitude.

### **REVELATION SENT TO US**

The revelation came to the Prophet, yet the believers say ***“what has been revealed to us.”*** The phrase is explained by their relationship to it: they follow it and they are commanded and forbidden by it, so in effect it has been sent down to them. Belief, in this verse, means affirmation: to believe in God and in these revelations is to declare them true.

### **THE OCCASION AND THE REFUSAL OF JESUS**

A report from Ibn ʿAbbās, transmitted by Ibn Isḥāq through Muḥammad ibn Abī Muḥammad from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr or ʿIkrimah, describes a group of Jews coming to the Prophet, among them Abū Yāsir ibn Akhṭab, Rāfiʿ ibn Abī Rāfiʿ, ʿĀzar, Khālid, Zayd, Azār ibn Abī Azār, and Ashyaʿ. They asked him which of the messengers he believed in, and he recited the words of this verse. When he mentioned Jesus, they denied his prophethood and said: *“We do not believe in Jesus, nor in anyone who believes in him.”* Then God revealed Qur’an 5:59: *“Say: People of the Book, do you resent us for anything except that we believe in God, in what has come down to us, and in what came down before?”* Another route of the same report names Nāfiʿ ibn Abī Nāfiʿ in place of Rāfiʿ ibn Abī Rāfiʿ.

The report shows how the clause ***“We make no distinction between any of them”*** functions. The Jews of the time disowned Jesus and Muhammad while accepting the rest, and the Christians disowned Muhammad while accepting the others. The believers, by contrast, testify that all of them were God’s messengers and prophets sent with truth and guidance. Qatādah, in the report through Saʿīd and Yazīd, describes the verse in general terms: *“God commanded the believers to believe and affirm all His prophets and messengers, and not to separate one of them from another.”*

### **WHO THE DESCENDANTS ARE**

The phrase translated ***“his descendants”*** renders a word usually understood as *“the tribes”*: the twelve sons of Jacob, each of whom became the ancestor of a nation of people, which is why they were given this name. Qatādah and al-Rabīʿ both describe them as Joseph and his brothers, the sons of Jacob, twelve men from each of whom a nation descended. Al-Suddī lists several of them by name: Joseph, Benjamin, Reuben, Judah, Simeon, Levi, Dan, and Qahath. Ibn Isḥāq gives a fuller account, naming the mothers of the twelve, and connects their multiplication into separate peoples with Qur’an 7:160, *“We divided them into twelve tribes, as nations.”*

Placing these figures among the recipients of revelation shows the breadth of the declaration. The believers do not restrict their faith to the prophets connected with their own descent. They affirm the whole chain of prophecy, from Abraham down to Jesus and every prophet whose name they know or do not know, and they do so as people who have submitted to the One who sent all of them.
verses.137:
> So if they believe in what you believe, then they will indeed be ˹rightly˺ guided. But if they turn away, they are simply opposed ˹to the truth˺. But Allah will spare you their evil. For He is the All-Hearing, All-Knowing

### **MEANING**

The verse completes the exchange with the communities that invited the believers to join them. Should those communities affirm what the believers have just affirmed, namely God, the revelation to the Prophet, what came to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and the tribes, and what Moses, Jesus, and all the prophets received, they have found the right way, entered the path of truth, and become one community with the believers. Should ***“they turn away”*** instead and continue to separate God’s messengers from one another, accepting some and rejecting others, they are in a state of opposition and hostility towards God, His Messenger, and the believers. The Prophet is then assured that God will be sufficient for him against them, for He hears what they say and knows what they conceal.

The verse gives the believers a measure for the dispute. Guidance is not membership of a group but affirmation of the whole of revelation.

### **BELIEF IN WHAT YOU BELIEVE**

The verse sets out a single condition for guidance: that ***“they believe in what you believe.”*** Ibn ʿAbbās, in the report through ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah, draws the principle out of this and similar verses: *“God informed us that faith is the firmest handhold, that He accepts no deed except with it, and that Paradise is forbidden only to the one who abandons it.”*

The Arabic wording is literally *“in the like of that in which you have believed,”* and a report attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās through Abū Ḥamzah, transmitted by Shuʿbah, records him objecting to it: *“Do not say, in the like of what you have believed in, for God has no like; say rather, in what you have believed in.”* That reading contradicts the copies of the Qur’an used by Muslims and was abandoned by all the reciters. It seems to rest on reading the comparison as one between God and some likeness of Him. The comparison, however, is between two acts of belief, not between the objects believed in: whoever affirms in the way you have affirmed, they are guided. Arabic uses the same structure in a sentence such as *“ʿAmr passed by your brother like I passed by him,”* where the comparison is between two acts of passing, not between ʿAmr and the speaker.

### **OPPOSED — THE MEANING OF THE WORD**

The word translated ***“opposed”*** is *shiqāq*. Qatādah and al-Rabīʿ explain it as separation; Ibn Zayd explains it as separation and warfare, saying: *“When someone sets himself in opposition he has made war, and when he makes war he has set himself in opposition; the two are one in the speech of the Arabs.”* He recites Qur’an 4:115, *“whoever opposes the Messenger,”* which uses the same root.

The root may come from the expression for something being hard on someone, distressing and burdening him; the mutual form then describes two parties each inflicting on the other what distresses him. The same root appears in Qur’an 4:35, *“if you fear a breach between the two of them,”* referring to a breakdown between husband and wife. Read together, these uses show what the verse means by turning away: not merely a difference of view, but a break with the believers that becomes hostility.

### **THE PROMISE OF SUFFICIENCY**

***“But Allah will spare you their evil”*** is addressed to the Prophet. It promises that God will be enough for him against those who said, *“Be Jews or Christians,”* should they persist in rejecting faith like that of his companions. The sufficiency would take the form of punishments such as fighting or expulsion from his neighbourhood. The closing names fit the two sides of their hostility: ***“He is the All-Hearing”*** of what they say aloud, their invitations to unbelief and their mockery, and ***“All-Knowing”*** of the envy and hatred they conceal towards him and his companions.

The promise is understood to have been fulfilled in the Prophet’s lifetime: God gave him authority over his opponents among them, so that some were killed, some expelled, and some humbled under the tribute. The verse therefore closes the argument with reassurance. The believers are not required to win every dispute in words; they are required to hold to what they have declared, while God undertakes to deal with those who reject it.
verses.138:
> This is the ˹natural˺ Way of Allah. And who is better than Allah in ordaining a way? And we worship ˹none but˺ Him

### **MEANING**

The verse continues the believers’ reply to those who invited them to Judaism or Christianity. Instead of the identity those communities offered, the believers declare that they hold to the dye of God, which is the religion of submission and the upright monotheism of Abraham. No one gives a better dye than God, and the believers are His worshippers. In other words, if people are to be marked by a religion, the mark that God Himself gives is the best and purest one.

The translation renders the key word as ***“Way of Allah,”*** and the image behind it is that of colour soaking into cloth. A religion that God gives colours the whole person, as dye colours fabric. The believers say that they have taken that colour and nothing else.

### **THE IMAGE OF DYEING**

The word chosen in this verse is explained against a practice of the Christians of the time: when they wished to make their children Christians, they immersed them in water, which they regarded as a sanctification, comparable to the ritual bath of purification among Muslims, and they considered it a dye marking them as Christians. The verse answers that practice with a different kind of colouring: follow the religion of Abraham, the dye of God, which is the best of dyes, the upright religion of submission; and leave the association of partners with God and straying from His guidance.

Qatādah, in the report through Saʿīd and Yazīd, broadens the point to both communities: *“The Jews dye their children Jewish, and the Christians dye their children Christian, but the dye of God is Islam; there is no dye finer than Islam or purer, and it is the religion of God with which He sent Noah and the prophets after him.”* ʿAṭāʾ, in the report through Ibn Jurayj, says that the Jews dyed their children and thereby went against the natural disposition.

### **RELIGION OR NATURAL DISPOSITION**

The early interpreters explain the word in two closely related ways. Most say it means the religion of God. This is the gloss of Qatādah through Maʿmar; of Abū al-ʿĀliyah through al-Rabīʿ, who adds that ***“who is better than Allah”*** means *“whose religion is finer than God’s?”*; of Mujāhid through several routes; of ʿAṭiyyah; of al-Suddī; of Ibn ʿAbbās through al-ʿAwfī’s family; and of Ibn Zayd.

Others explain it as the natural disposition with which God created people. Mujāhid, in the report through Ibn Abī Najīḥ, says: *“The natural disposition of God with which He created people.”* Another report from him through Jaʿfar ibn Rabīʿah gives the same gloss, and in the report through Ibn Jurayj he joins the two: *“Islam, the natural disposition of God with which He created people.”* ʿAbd Allāh ibn Kathīr, according to Ibn Jurayj, explained it as the religion of God and then added that it is His natural disposition. On this second interpretation, the believers are saying that they follow the natural pattern and religion according to which God created His creatures. The root of the word for natural disposition is the same as in Qur’an 6:14, which calls God *“the Originator of the heavens and the earth.”*

The two explanations do not conflict. The religion God gave is the one that matches the disposition with which He created people, and the dyeing practised by later communities is presented as an attempt to overlay that original colour with another.

### **THE GRAMMAR AND THE CLOSING DECLARATION**

The word ***“Way”*** is in the accusative in the common reading, linking it with ***“the faith of Abraham”*** two verses earlier: rather, we follow the religion of Abraham, the dye of God. Those who read that earlier phrase in the nominative read this one the same way, and it can also be read as the start of a new sentence: it is the dye of God. It may also be linked to the believers’ declaration in 2:136, so that the faith they have just professed is itself the dye of God.

The final clause, ***“And we worship ˹none but˺ Him,”*** is what the Prophet is told to say to those who invited him to their communities. It describes the believers as humble before God in following the religion of Abraham and holding to it, not too proud to follow His command or to acknowledge His messengers. The contrast is with pride: some of those who invited the believers had rejected the Prophet out of arrogance, rivalry, and envy, while the believers present their worship as a mark of humility.
verses.139:
> Say, “Would you dispute with us about Allah, while He is our Lord and your Lord? We are accountable for our deeds and you for yours. And we are devoted to Him ˹alone˺

### **MEANING**

The Prophet is told to put a question to those communities who said, *“Be Jews or Christians and you will be guided,”* and who claimed that their religion and Book were better because they came first, and that they were therefore closer to God. The question is: do you argue with us about God, when He is the Lord of both of us? He holds all good in His hand, and to Him belong reward, punishment, and recompense for good and bad deeds. Each party will be repaid for what it has done, not on the basis of lineage or the antiquity of its religion and scripture. And the believers add that they worship Him sincerely, associating nothing with Him.

The verse dismantles the basis of the claim to precedence. If there is one Lord for all, no community can own Him; and if each is repaid for its own deeds, being earlier gives no advantage.

### **WHAT THE DISPUTE WAS ABOUT**

The question ***“Would you dispute with us about Allah”*** means: do you contend with us and argue with us? In the reports from Mujāhid through Ibn Abī Najīḥ and from Ibn Zayd through Ibn Wahb, both gloss it as *“Do you quarrel with us?”*; Ibn ʿAbbās, through al-ʿAwfī’s family, glosses it as *“Do you argue with us?”*

The words *“about God”* are understood to mean about the religion of God that He has commanded the believers to follow. The claim behind the dispute is spelled out in the explanation of the verse: the opponents held that their religion was better than that of the believers and their Book better than the Qur’an because it had come earlier, and that they were therefore more entitled to God. The verse answers that God is one, just, and does not wrong anyone; He repays servants for what they have earned. Precedence in time therefore decides nothing.

### **ONE LORD AND SEPARATE DEEDS**

The two clauses ***“while He is our Lord and your Lord”*** and ***“We are accountable for our deeds and you for yours”*** together remove the ground of the argument. The first denies that God belongs to one group more than another. The second establishes that each party has what it has done and earned, good or bad, and will be rewarded or punished for it.

The same principle has just been stated in Qur’an 2:134 about the patriarchs, and it will be stated again in Qur’an 2:141: a community has what it earned, and no one is questioned about the deeds of another. In this verse it is applied to the present generation: the believers and their opponents will each answer for their own works. The argument thus moves from the past, where the patriarchs cannot be claimed, to the present, where God cannot be monopolised.

### **DEVOTED TO HIM ALONE**

The final clause, ***“And we are devoted to Him ˹alone˺,”*** means that the believers make their worship and obedience sincere to God, associating nothing with Him and worshipping no one besides Him. The clause is pointed. It contrasts the believers with those who worshipped idols alongside God and with the people of the calf, who worshipped the calf beside Him.

The verse is described as a rebuke to the Jews and an argument placed in the mouths of the believers. Its reasoning runs: you claim to be closer to God than we are because your religion, Book, and prophet came first; yet we are sincere in worshipping Him and have associated nothing with Him, while you associated others with Him in your worship, some of you taking the calf and some the Messiah. How then can you be better than us or closer to God? The claim to precedence collapses against the test that matters, which is sincere worship. In this way the verse prepares for the next, where the claim that the patriarchs themselves belonged to the later communities is taken up directly.
verses.140:
> Do you claim that Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and his descendants were all Jews or Christians?” Say, “Who is more knowledgeable: you or Allah?” Who does more wrong than those who hide the testimony they received from Allah? And Allah is never unaware of what you do

### **MEANING**

The argument now reaches its core claim. The communities who invited the believers to join them asserted that **Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and** the tribes had belonged to their religions. The verse asks whether they really say that, and then answers with a further question: do you know better, or God? Judaism and Christianity came into existence after these prophets, so the claim is plainly untenable. The verse then condemns those who conceal a testimony from God in their possession, and closes with a warning that God is not heedless of what they do.

The whole verse is an argument given to the Prophet. Either produce proof that your religion is better and that you are guided while we are astray, or produce proof that these prophets were of your religion. If neither can be produced, the claim exposes itself.

### **TWO WAYS OF READING THE QUESTION**

The verse opens with ***“Do you claim,”*** and there are two readings of its first word. Most read it in the second person, *“or do you say,”* linking it to the preceding question: which of these two do you do — do you argue with us about God, or ***“do you claim that Abraham”*** and the others were ***“Jews or Christians”***? Others read it in the third person, *“or do they say,”* making it a fresh question, as in Qur’an 32:3, *“Or do they say, He has invented it?”* The second-person reading is the one shared by the reciters generally, and the third-person reading is isolated; it also fits the flow of the address better, since the Prophet is speaking directly to the people he is answering.

Whichever reading is followed, the point is the same. The question ***“Who is more knowledgeable: you or Allah?”*** forces the issue. God has said what the patriarchs were, and the later religions did not yet exist in their time. To insist on the claim is to set one’s own knowledge above God’s.

### **THE TESTIMONY THAT WAS HIDDEN**

The phrase ***“those who hide the testimony they received from Allah”*** is explained in two ways. In the first, the testimony concerns the patriarchs themselves. Mujāhid, in reports through Ibn Abī Najīḥ, says it refers to the Jewish assertion that Abraham, along with Ishmael and those mentioned with them, had been ***“Jews or Christians,”*** and God says to them: *“Do not hide from Me a testimony if you have one concerning them,”* knowing that they were lying. Al-Ḥasan, in a report through Abū al-Ashhab, recited the verse and said: *“By God, the people had a testimony from God that His prophets were free of Judaism and Christianity, just as they had a testimony from God that your property and lives are sacred among you; so on what basis did they make them lawful?”* Al-Rabīʿ adds that the People of the Book found it written in the Torah and the Gospel that these prophets belonged to neither Judaism nor Christianity, and that those religions came long after them.

In the second explanation, the testimony concerns the Prophet. Qatādah, through Saʿīd, says the People of the Book concealed Islam while knowing it was God’s religion, and concealed Muhammad while knowing he was God’s Messenger, finding him written in the Torah and the Gospel; in the report through Maʿmar he says simply: *“The testimony is the Prophet, written with them, and it is what they concealed.”* Ibn Zayd likewise says they were asked about the Prophet and his description in their scripture and concealed it.

The first explanation fits the position of the clause better, since it stands in the middle of the account of the patriarchs and is followed by its conclusion. The testimony was what God had revealed to them in the Torah and the Gospel about following the practice of these prophets, who were upright and submitting to God. They concealed it when the Prophet invited them, saying instead *“None will enter Paradise except one who is a Jew or a Christian,”* Qur’an 2:111.

### **NOT UNAWARE OF WHAT YOU DO**

The verse closes with ***“And Allah is never unaware of what you do.”*** It means that God is not heedless of their concealment of the truth that their Book required them to make clear about Abraham and the others, nor of their punishment for it; He is recording it in order to repay them, in this world and the next. The argument has a further edge: if they claimed the patriarchs for Judaism or Christianity, their falsehood would become clear even to their allies, because those religions arose later; and if they denied it, they would be invited to the religion those prophets actually followed, which all parties acknowledged to be true.
verses.141:
> That was a community that had already gone before. For them is what they earned and for you is what you have earned. And you will not be accountable for what they have done

### **MEANING**

The verse repeats, word for word, the sentence that closed the account of the patriarchs at 2:134, and here it closes the argument about whether they were Jews or Christians. The ***“community”*** is Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and the tribes. They have passed on their way and gone to their Lord, alone with their deeds and hopes. For them before God is the good gained in their lifetimes and against them the evil they incurred; nothing benefits them but their own good deeds, and nothing harms them but their own bad ones.

The address is to those who argued with the Prophet about God, who concealed the knowledge they had about the patriarchs’ submission and claimed them for their own religions. If even these honoured prophets will be helped only by their own works, then those who boast of them while persisting in their own wrongs have even less reason to expect help from the connection.

### **WHO IS MEANT**

Qatādah, in the report through Saʿīd and Yazīd, says that ***“That was a community that had already gone before”*** refers to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and the tribes, and al-Rabīʿ, in the report through ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī Jaʿfar from his father, says the same. The word for community means a group of people, as was explained at 2:134. The verb translated ***“had already gone before”*** describes those who have passed away and are cut off from this world.

The identification matters because the previous verse named exactly these figures as the subjects of the dispute. The repetition of the sentence is therefore not a mere refrain; it gives the verdict on the specific claim that has just been examined.

### **THE ARGUMENT FROM THE GREATER TO THE LESSER**

The explanation of this verse draws out a reasoning that runs from the greater to the lesser. The communities addressed took pride in the patriarchs and claimed that through them they hoped to be saved from their Lord’s punishment, despite their sins and great offences. But if these patriarchs themselves will be benefited before God only by the good they sent ahead and harmed only by the evil they did, then those who claim them are even less likely to be benefited by anything other than their own good works.

On this basis, the verse calls them to look to themselves: to hasten to repentance and return to God from the unbelief, error, and fabrication against God and His prophets in which they persisted, and to stop relying on the merits of fathers and grandfathers. ***“For you is what you have earned”***: what you have is what you earn, and against you is what you incur.

### **WHY THE SENTENCE IS REPEATED**

At 2:134 the sentence followed the scene at Jacob’s deathbed, where his sons promised to worship the One God and submit to Him. Here it follows the challenge ***“Who is more knowledgeable: you or Allah?”*** and the condemnation of those who conceal the testimony they possess. The first occurrence establishes what the patriarchs were; the second rules out the use being made of them.

The final clause, ***“And you will not be accountable for what they have done,”*** completes the point.
