On the Day of Resurrection, every soul that comes before God will be asked only about what it earned and sent ahead, not about what another soul sent ahead. The patriarchs are not asked about their descendants, and their descendants are not asked about the patriarchs; each will meet its own record. With this verdict the long passage on Abraham and his house closes, and the surah turns to the change of the direction of prayer, a matter in which the same question, who truly follows Abraham, takes practical form.
verses.142:
> The foolish among the people will ask, “Why did they turn away from the direction of prayer they used to face?” Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “The east and west belong ˹only˺ to Allah. He guides whoever He wills to the Straight Path.”

### **MEANING**

The surah now turns to the change in the prayer direction. For a period after the emigration to Medina, the Prophet and his companions faced Jerusalem in prayer; then God turned them towards the Sacred Mosque in Mecca. The verse tells the Prophet in advance what certain people would say when that happened: what has turned them ***“away from the direction of prayer they used to face?”*** It also supplies the answer he should give: the east and the west both belong to God, and ***“He guides whoever He wills to the Straight Path.”***

The word translated ***“The foolish”*** describes people who act out of ignorance and make light of the truth. Those meant are identified as some of the Jews and the hypocrites. The verb behind ***“turn away”*** means to turn something so that one’s back is to it, and the word for the prayer direction, *qiblah*, is whatever a person faces, in the way two people facing each other are each the other’s *qiblah*. The question therefore amounts to: what has turned their faces away from the place they had been facing in their prayer?

### **WHO ASKED THE QUESTION**

Most of the early authorities identify the questioners as Jews. Mujāhid, in the report through Ibn Abī Najīḥ, says: *“The Jews say it, when he left Jerusalem.”* Al-Barāʾ ibn ʿĀzib, through Abū Isḥāq, identifies them as the Jews, and in one route as the People of the Book, and Ibn ʿAbbās through ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah says the same. Al-Suddī, by contrast, says the verse was revealed about the hypocrites, who asked: *“What is wrong with them? They kept to one direction for a time, then abandoned it and turned to another.”*

The people are called foolish because they treated the truth with contempt. Their learned men pretended not to know what they knew, and their ignorant members thought it too great a thing to follow a prophet who came from the Arabs rather than from the Children of Israel, while the hypocrites were left confused.

### **THE SETTING OF THE CHANGE**

Several reports describe when the change occurred. Ibn ʿAbbās, in the report transmitted by Ibn Isḥāq through Saʿīd ibn Jubayr or ʿIkrimah, says the direction was changed from Syria to the Kaʿbah in Rajab, seventeen months after the Prophet arrived in Medina. A group of Jewish leaders, including Rifāʿah ibn Qays, Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf, and Kinānah ibn Abī al-Ḥuqayq, came to him and said: *“Muhammad, what has turned you from the direction you once faced, while you claim to follow the religion and way of Abraham? Return to your former direction and we will follow you and believe you.”* The report adds that they only wanted to lure him away from his religion, and the verses were revealed about them.

Al-Barāʾ, in reports through Abū Isḥāq, gives the period as sixteen or seventeen months; Sufyān, transmitting through Yaḥyā, was unsure which, and a version of this report is also recorded in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī and Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim through Yaḥyā from Sufyān. In another route al-Barāʾ adds that the Prophet longed to be turned towards the Kaʿbah, and that a man who had prayed the afternoon prayer with him passed a mosque whose people were bowing and said: *“I bear witness that I have prayed with the Messenger of God facing Mecca,”* and they turned around as they were, towards the House. Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib puts the change two months before Badr, while a report from Anas gives nine or ten months and one from Muʿādh ibn Jabal thirteen.

The reports also differ on why Jerusalem had been faced at first. ʿIkrimah and al-Ḥasan say it was the Prophet’s own choice, to win over the Jews; Abū al-ʿĀliyah says he was given the choice and chose Jerusalem to draw the People of the Book closer. Ibn ʿAbbās, through ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah, says God commanded it when he arrived in Medina, the Jews rejoiced, and the Prophet, who loved the direction of Abraham, kept looking to the sky until Qur’an 2:144 was revealed.

### **THE ANSWER: EAST AND WEST BELONG TO GOD**

Qatādah, in the report through Saʿīd, records one form of the mockery: *“The man has longed for his birthplace!”* The answer given to the Prophet goes beyond the immediate dispute. ***“The east and west belong ˹only˺ to Allah”*** means that He owns everything between the furthest points where the sun rises and sets, and all that lies between them. No direction has value in itself; a direction has value because God appoints it. To object that the believers turned from one direction to another is therefore to object to the One who owns both.

The second sentence, ***“He guides whoever He wills to the Straight Path,”*** applies the principle. God directs those He chooses among His creatures and enables them to follow the right road, which here means the direction of Abraham, whom He made a leader for people; and He leaves those He chooses to go astray. Read in the setting of the passage, the reply says in effect: God has guided us, by facing the Sacred Mosque, to the direction of Abraham, and has left you without what He guided us to. The change that the foolish presented as confusion is presented in the verse as guidance, and the following verses explain its purpose.
verses.143:
> And so We have made you ˹believers˺ an upright community so that you may be witnesses over humanity and that the Messenger may be a witness over you. We assigned your former direction of prayer only to distinguish those who would remain faithful to the Messenger from those who would lose faith. It was certainly a difficult test except for those ˹rightly˺ guided by Allah. And Allah would never discount your ˹previous acts of˺ faith. Surely Allah is Ever Gracious and Most Merciful to humanity

### **MEANING**

The verse explains what the change of the prayer direction reveals about the community that received it. Just as God guided the believers to the direction and religion of Abraham and favoured them with it, so He made them a middle, just community, distinguished above other religious communities. This standing has a purpose: they will testify for the prophets against the nations that they delivered their messages, and the Messenger will testify concerning them.

The verse then explains the change itself. The earlier direction, and the turning away from it, served to make visible who would follow the Messenger and who would turn back on his heels. The change was a heavy matter ***“except for those”*** whom God had guided. Finally, it reassures the believers that their prayers towards Jerusalem were not lost, for God is kind and merciful to people.

### **A MIDDLE AND JUST COMMUNITY**

The word translated ***“upright”*** literally means *“middle.”* In Arabic it also means the best and choicest, as when a man is called *“middle in lineage”* among his people to mean that his lineage is high. Zuhayr ibn Abī Sulmā uses it in this sense: *“They are a middle people; mankind accepts their judgement when one of the nights brings a grave calamity.”* The community may be called middle because it stands between two extremes in religion: it neither exaggerates, as some exaggerated in monasticism and in what they said about Jesus, nor falls short, as those did who altered their scripture and killed their prophets.

The transmitted explanation, however, is that the word means just. This is the gloss in a report from Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī from the Prophet, through al-Aʿmash and Abū Ṣāliḥ: *“Just,”* and the same is given from Abū Hurayrah from the Prophet. Mujāhid, Qatādah, al-Rabīʿ, ʿAṭāʾ, and Ibn ʿAbbās through al-ʿAwfī’s family all say the same. Justice and choiceness meet in the same people, since the best of people are those who are just. Ibn Zayd adds that they are *“a middle between the Prophet and the nations.”*

### **WITNESSES OVER HUMANITY**

The phrase ***“so that you may be witnesses over humanity”*** is explained by a report from Abū Saʿīd through al-Aʿmash, also recorded in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī through al-Aʿmash, in which the Prophet says: *“Noah will be called on the Day of Resurrection and asked, Did you convey what you were sent with? He will say, Yes. His people will be asked, Did he convey it to you? They will say, No warner came to us. He will be asked, Who knows that? He will say, Muhammad and his community.”* One route adds that they are then called and testify that he conveyed the message. Zayd ibn Aslam, through Maʿmar, gives a similar account, adding that Noah’s people object, *“How can you testify against us when you never met us?”* and the believers answer that their Prophet told them and that it was revealed to him.

A related report from Jābir has the Prophet say that he and his community will stand on a raised place on the Day of Resurrection overlooking creation, and *“there is no prophet whom his people denied except that we shall be his witnesses on the Day of Resurrection that he conveyed the messages of his Lord.”* Another report, from Salamah ibn al-Akwaʿ, connects the testimony with this world: a funeral passed and was praised, and the Prophet said, *“It has become due”*; another passed and was spoken of less well, and he said the same. Asked what he meant, he said: *“The angels are God’s witnesses in heaven, and you are God’s witnesses on earth.”*

***“And that the Messenger may be a witness over you”*** means that he testifies to their faith in him and in what he brought. Qatādah puts the two testimonies side by side: the community testifies that the messengers delivered their message, and the Messenger testifies that he delivered his. Ibn Zayd counts this among the witnesses of Qur’an 40:51, *“the Day the witnesses will stand.”*

### **THE PURPOSE OF THE FORMER DIRECTION**

***“We assigned your former direction of prayer”*** refers to Jerusalem, as al-Suddī and ʿAṭāʾ say; the sense is that God did not make the turning away from it except to make visible who would follow. The trial lay in the change itself, as Qur’an 17:60 says of the Prophet’s vision that it was made *“a trial for people”* through his telling of it. When the direction changed, some who had accepted Islam turned back; hypocrites said, *“What is wrong with Muhammad, turning us here one time and there another!”*; idolaters said he had become confused in his religion; and believers asked about the prayers of their brothers who had died. Qatādah calls it *“a trial and a sifting.”*

The words ***“to distinguish”*** render a verb that literally says *“so that We might know.”* God knows all things before they happen, so the phrase is explained as knowledge that becomes manifest in His Messenger and his followers, since Arabic attributes to a leader what his followers do. Ibn ʿAbbās, through ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah, glosses it: *“That We might distinguish the people of certainty from the people of association and doubt.”* Others proposed that *“know”* here means *“see,”* or that the wording is gentle address, as in Qur’an 34:24. To turn *“on their heels”*, the literal image behind ***“lose faith,”*** is to walk back along a road one had already travelled, as Moses and his companion *“retraced their footsteps”* in Qur’an 18:64; Ibn Zayd says it describes the one who, *“when a doubt enters him, turns back from God.”*

### **A HEAVY MATTER, AND FAITH NOT LOST**

What was ***“a difficult test”*** is explained in three ways. Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, and Qatādah say it was the change of direction; Abū al-ʿĀliyah says the Jerusalem direction itself; Ibn Zayd says the prayer towards it. The first fits best, since it was the turning that weighed on people. Ibn ʿAbbās says the exception refers to *“the humble,”* those who affirm what God revealed.

***“Allah would never discount your ˹previous acts of˺ faith”*** is explained in many reports as referring to prayer. Ibn ʿAbbās, through ʿIkrimah, says that when the direction changed people asked, *“What of our brothers who died before this, praying towards Jerusalem?”* and the verse was revealed. Al-Barāʾ says men had died and been killed before the change, and *“we did not know what to say about them.”* Al-Suddī adds that the verse means *“that was obedience and this is obedience.”* Prayer is called faith because it was an act of affirming the Messenger. The address is to the living, yet it includes the dead, since Arabic folds the absent into the addressed.

The closing names give the reason. God is ***“Ever Gracious”***, a word for the highest degree of mercy, and ***“Most Merciful”***; He is too merciful to waste an act of obedience, and too gracious to punish anyone for not doing what He had not yet commanded. The word for gracious has several dialect forms, and the recognised readings use either a short form, read by the Kufans, or a long form, read by the Medinans, which al-Walīd ibn ʿUqbah’s verse also attests.
verses.144:
> Indeed, We see you ˹O Prophet˺ turning your face towards heaven. Now We will make you turn towards a direction ˹of prayer˺ that will please you. So turn your face towards the Sacred Mosque ˹in Mecca˺—wherever you are, turn your faces towards it. Those who were given the Scripture certainly know this to be the truth from their Lord. And Allah is never unaware of what they do

### **MEANING**

This is the verse that actually commands the change of the prayer direction. God tells the Prophet that He has seen him turning his face again and again towards the sky, and promises to turn him to a direction he will be pleased with. The command follows at once: **turn your face towards the Sacred Mosque**; and the believers, wherever they are on earth, receive the same command in their prayer: ***“turn your faces towards it.”*** The verse then notes that the learned among the People of the Scripture know that facing this direction is **the truth from their Lord**, and it closes by assuring the believers that God is not heedless of their deeds.

The words ***“turning your face”*** describe repeated movement, and ***“towards heaven”*** means in the direction of the sky. The Prophet, before the change, used to raise his eyes to the sky waiting for God’s command to face the Kaʿbah. The promise ***“a direction ˹of prayer˺ that will please you”*** means a direction he loved and longed for.

### **THE PROPHET’S LONGING**

Several early reports describe the scene. Qatādah, through Maʿmar, says: *“He used to turn his face to the sky, loving that God would turn him to the Kaʿbah, until God turned him to it.”* In the report through Saʿīd he adds that the Prophet prayed towards Jerusalem while longing for the Sacred House, and God turned him to the direction he longed for. Al-Rabīʿ says that the Prophet would turn his face during prayer while facing Jerusalem, and al-Suddī says that whenever he prayed he raised his head to the sky to see what he would be commanded.

The reports give two reasons for the longing. Mujāhid, through Ibn Jurayj, says the Jews were saying, *“Muhammad opposes us yet follows our direction!”* so the Prophet prayed and asked for the direction to be prescribed; when the verse came, that taunt ended. He adds that the change happened during the noon prayer, and that the men and women changed places in the rows as they turned. Ibn Zayd says the Prophet had faced Jerusalem for sixteen months after reasoning that the Jews faced one of God’s houses, until he heard them say, *“By God, Muhammad and his companions did not know where their direction was until we guided them,”* and he disliked it. Ibn ʿAbbās, through ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah, gives the other reason: the Prophet *“loved the direction of Abraham,”* so he prayed and looked towards the sky.

### **TOWARDS THE SACRED MOSQUE**

The word translated ***“towards”*** is *shaṭr*, which means the direction or side of something, the place one faces. A poet of Hudhayl uses it of a sick camel whose *“gaze towards it is weary,”* and Ibn Aḥmar describes a camel racing *“towards Jamʿ.”* The early authorities agree: Abū al-ʿĀliyah glosses it as *“facing it,”* Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, and Qatādah as *“towards it,”* al-Barāʾ as *“in its direction,”* and Ibn Zayd as its side, adding that its sides are called by the plural of the same word.

There was a difference about which part of **the Sacred Mosque** is meant. ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAmr, in a report through Yaḥyā ibn Qumṭah, sat facing the water spout of the Kaʿbah and recited the verse, saying: *“This is the direction God spoke of to His Prophet.”* Ibn ʿAbbās, through Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, said that the whole House is the direction, and that its door is the direction of the House. Usāmah ibn Zayd, in reports through ʿAṭāʾ, relates that the Prophet prayed in every corner of the House without praying, and when he came out he prayed two units facing it and said: *“This is the direction.”*

The wording of the verse itself settles the practical question. Whoever obeys the command to ***“turn your face towards the Sacred Mosque”*** has faced the direction, provided he intends it and does not turn his back on it, just as a person praying at the end of a long row follows the imam without standing directly behind him. ʿAlī, in a report through ʿUmayrah ibn Ziyād, glosses the word as *“its direction.”*

### **WHEREVER YOU ARE**

The clause ***“wherever you are, turn your faces towards it”*** extends the command from the Prophet to the believers. It makes facing **the Sacred Mosque** an obligation in their prayers in every part of the earth. Grammatically it is conditional: wherever you may be, **turn your faces towards it**.

### **WHAT THE PEOPLE OF THE SCRIPTURE KNOW**

***“Those who were given the Scripture”*** are explained as the learned among the Jews and the Christians; al-Suddī says the clause was revealed about the Jews specifically. Their knowledge is that facing **the Sacred Mosque** is the truth that God prescribed for Abraham, for his descendants, and for His servants after him. ***“From their Lord”*** stresses that it is an obligation laid on God’s servants, not a preference of the Prophet.

The closing words, ***“And Allah is never unaware of what they do,”*** are explained as reassurance to the believers: God is not unaware of their obedience in following His command, their faith in praying towards Jerusalem, and then their prayer facing the Kaʿbah. He records all of it and will reward them for it with the best reward. The verse thus answers both the objectors and the anxious believers of the previous verses.
verses.145:
> Even if you were to bring every proof to the People of the Book, they would not accept your direction ˹of prayer˺, nor would you accept theirs; nor would any of them accept the direction ˹of prayer˺ of another. And if you were to follow their desires after ˹all˺ the knowledge that has come to you, then you would certainly be one of the wrongdoers

### **MEANING**

The previous verse said that the learned among the Scripture-holders know the new direction to be the truth. This verse explains why that knowledge does not lead them to accept it. Were the Prophet to bring them every sign and argument that the truth lies in what he brought, namely the change from Jerusalem to the Sacred Mosque, they still would refuse his direction. Nor is there any way for him to follow theirs, and they do not even follow one another’s directions. The Prophet is then warned that should he go along with their wishes after the knowledge he has received, he would be among the wrongdoers.

The word translated ***“proof”*** is explained as a sign, meaning a demonstration and argument. The point is that their refusal does not come from a lack of evidence; it comes from attachment to their own positions.

### **NO SINGLE DIRECTION TO SATISFY THEM**

The clause ***“nor would you accept theirs”*** is explained by the actual practice of the two communities: the Jews faced Jerusalem in their prayer and the Christians faced the east. Since their directions differed, there was no way for the Prophet to adopt *“their”* direction at all. The verse therefore tells him to hold to the direction he has been commanded to face and to leave aside what the Jews and Christians say and the direction they invite him to.

***“Nor would any of them accept the direction ˹of prayer˺ of another”*** is glossed by al-Suddī: *“The Jews do not follow the direction of the Christians, nor do the Christians follow the direction of the Jews.”* In the report through Asbāṭ, al-Suddī connects the passage with what the Jews said when the direction was changed: *“Muhammad longs for the land of his father and his birthplace! Had he stayed with our direction, we would have hoped that he was the one we are waiting for,”* and he says that God revealed about them the verses from ***“Those who were given the Scripture certainly know”*** down to ***“hides the truth knowingly.”*** Ibn Zayd gives a similar explanation.

The lesson drawn from this is that the Prophet should not trouble himself trying to win the approval of both communities, since that is impossible. If he followed the direction of one, he would anger the other. He should leave what cannot be achieved and invite them to what can: agreement on the upright religion of submission and on the direction of Abraham and the prophets after him.

### **FOLLOWING THEIR DESIRES**

The second sentence, ***“And if you were to follow their desires after ˹all˺ the knowledge that has come to you,”*** means: if you sought the approval of these Jews and Christians, who had said, *“Be Jews or Christians and you will be guided,”* and returned to their direction, after God had informed you that they persist in falsehood out of obstinacy, knowing that the direction you were turned to is the one prescribed for Abraham and the messengers among his descendants, ***“then you would certainly be one of the wrongdoers”***, that is, among those who wrong themselves by opposing God’s command and abandoning obedience to Him.

The grammar of the opening is also noted. The conditional particle here is answered with a past-tense verb, as a condition beginning with *“if”* is sometimes answered in the manner of an oath. The construction strengthens the statement: even with every sign, they will not follow.

The warning addressed to the Prophet has the same function as similar warnings elsewhere in the passage. It sets the believers’ new direction on the basis of revealed knowledge, so that any return to the former direction for the sake of approval would be a departure from that knowledge, not a gesture of reconciliation.
verses.146:
> Those We have given the Scripture recognize this ˹Prophet˺ as they recognize their own children. Yet a group of them hides the truth knowingly

### **MEANING**

The verse states that those who received the Scripture know a certain truth as surely as they know their sons, yet a party of them deliberately conceals it. The translation supplies ***“this ˹Prophet˺”*** as the object of their recognition. The early explanations recorded for this verse mostly take the object to be the new direction of prayer, the Sacred House, which the learned among the People of the Scripture knew to be their proper direction, the direction of Abraham, and the direction of the prophets before Muhammad. The concealment in the second sentence is explained as relating both to that direction and to the Prophet himself, whom they found described in their scriptures.

The comparison ***“as they recognize their own children”*** expresses certainty. A man does not doubt who his son is; their knowledge of this truth was of the same kind.

### **WHAT THEY RECOGNISED**

Qatādah, in the report through Saʿīd and Yazīd ibn Zurayʿ, says: *“They know that the Sacred House is the direction.”* Al-Rabīʿ says the object is the direction of prayer, and in another report: *“They knew that the direction of the Sacred House was the direction they had been commanded to face, as they knew their sons.”* Ibn ʿAbbās, through al-ʿAwfī’s family, says it means *“the Kaʿbah, the Sacred House.”* Al-Suddī says they know the Kaʿbah to be the direction of the prophets as they know their sons, Ibn Zayd says the Jews knew it was the direction, Mecca, and Ibn Jurayj says simply: *“The direction and the House.”*

On this reading the verse continues directly from the two before it. Verse 144 said that the People of the Scripture know the new direction is the truth from their Lord, and verse 145 explained why they would not follow it. This verse returns to their knowledge and describes it as complete.

### **A GROUP WHO HIDE THE TRUTH**

The second sentence restricts the charge: ***“a group of them hides the truth knowingly.”*** Mujāhid, in reports through Ibn Abī Najīḥ and Ibn Jurayj, identifies the group as the People of the Book. The truth they concealed is first of all the direction to which God turned His Prophet, the one the earlier prophets faced. Some of them faced the east and some Jerusalem, rejecting what God had commanded them.

Others explain the concealed truth as the Prophet. Qatādah says: *“They concealed Muhammad.”* Mujāhid says: *“They conceal Muhammad while they find him written with them in the Torah and the Gospel.”* Al-Rabīʿ, on the other hand, says the truth they concealed is the direction of prayer. The two explanations are joined in the account of the verse: they concealed the direction, and with it they concealed the matter of Muhammad, which they found written in their scriptures.

### **CONCEALMENT WITH KNOWLEDGE**

The word ***“knowingly”*** carries the weight of the charge. God informed His Prophet and his community of their betrayal of God and of His servants, and stated that they did what they did knowing that the truth was otherwise and that their duty before God was the opposite. They knew they had no right to conceal it, so their concealment was deliberate disobedience.

The verse thus explains why the argument with them could not be settled by evidence alone. Those who know a truth as they know their sons, and still conceal it, are not waiting for proof. The next verse turns from them to the Prophet and tells him where the truth comes from.
verses.147:
> ˹This is˺ the truth from your Lord, so do not ever be one of those who doubt

### **MEANING**

After describing those who conceal what they know, the passage addresses the Prophet directly: the truth is what your Lord has taught you and given you from Himself, not what the Jews and Christians tell you. In the setting of the change of the prayer direction, the verse confirms that the direction to which God turned him is the true direction, the one that Abraham, the Friend of the Most Merciful, and the prophets after him faced. He is told to act on the truth that has come from his Lord and never to be among ***“those who doubt.”***

The verse is short, but it closes the argument of the preceding verses. Against claims, mockery, and concealment, it places a single source of certainty: what comes ***“from your Lord.”***

### **THE TRUTH THAT CAME TO HIM**

Al-Rabīʿ, in the report through Ibn Abī Jaʿfar from his father, explains the address as follows: God said to His Prophet, ***“the truth from your Lord, so do not ever be one of those who doubt,”*** meaning, *“Be in no doubt, for it is your direction and the direction of the prophets before you.”* Ibn Zayd explains ***“those who doubt”*** as those who are uncertain, and paraphrases the command: *“Have no doubt about that.”*

Both explanations tie the verse to the direction of prayer. The previous verses showed that the People of the Scripture knew the truth about the Sacred House and some of them hid it. This verse tells the Prophet that the same truth has reached him openly from his Lord; he has no reason to waver because others deny it.

### **THE WORD FOR DOUBT**

The word translated ***“those who doubt”*** comes from a root meaning doubt, in a form suggesting someone who is drawn into uncertainty. The poet al-Aʿshā uses the same form in a line about a racing horse, describing *“the legs of those who press it hard, when the mirage sways,”* where the related verb has the sense of drawing something out by repeated effort. The basic idea is the hesitation of a person who keeps turning a matter over without settling it.

### **WHY THE PROPHET IS TOLD NOT TO DOUBT**

A natural question arises: was the Prophet in doubt about whether the truth came from his Lord, or about whether the direction God had turned him to was true, so that he needed to be forbidden from doubting? The answer given is that Arabic often frames a command or prohibition as addressed to one person while those intended are others. The Qur’an does this in Surah 33, which opens: *“O Prophet, be mindful of God and obey not the disbelievers and the hypocrites,”* Qur’an 33:1, and continues: *“Follow what is revealed to you from your Lord; God is aware of what you do,”* Qur’an 33:2, where the closing words address a plural audience. The address is formally to the Prophet, while the intended audience includes his companions who believed in him.

Read in this way, the verse is directed at the believers who had just lived through the change of direction, some of whom were unsettled by the objections they heard. The address to the Prophet gives the instruction its authority, while its practical effect falls on his followers: the direction they now face is the truth from their Lord, and the questions raised by those who mocked or concealed should not shake them. The following verse will turn from the dispute to what matters more than direction itself: competing in good deeds.
verses.148:
> Everyone turns to their own direction ˹of prayer˺. So compete with one another in doing good. Wherever you are, Allah will bring you all together ˹for judgment˺. Surely Allah is Most Capable of everything

### **MEANING**

After the long dispute over the prayer direction, the verse steps back and puts the matter in proportion. Every religious community has a direction it faces in its prayer. The believers are not told to argue endlessly about this; they are told to race each other towards good deeds, because wherever they are, God will gather all of them, and all those who differed from them, on the Day of Resurrection. He is able to do anything, including raising them from wherever they lie.

The verse therefore shifts the attention of the believers from the contest of words to the contest of deeds. God has shown them the truth and guided them to the direction that others missed; what remains is to act on it.

### **EACH COMMUNITY AND ITS DIRECTION**

The opening, ***“Everyone turns to their own direction,”*** literally reads *“for each there is a direction,”* with the word *“community”* or *“people of a religion”* left unstated because the context makes it clear. Mujāhid, in the report through Ibn Abī Najīḥ, glosses it as *“for every adherent of a religion.”* Al-Rabīʿ says: *“The Jew has a direction he turns to, and the Christians have a direction they turn to, and God has guided you, O community, to the direction that is the true direction.”* ʿAṭāʾ, Ibn Zayd, and al-Suddī say the same, Ibn Zayd adding: *“The Jews have a direction, the Christians have a direction, and you have a direction,”* meaning the Muslims. Ibn ʿAbbās, through al-ʿAwfī’s family, says each religion has a direction it is pleased with, *“and the face of God is wherever the believers turn,”* citing Qur’an 2:115, *“Wherever you turn, there is the face of God.”*

Qatādah, in the report through Maʿmar, gives a different explanation: the two directions meant are the believers’ own prayer towards Jerusalem and their prayer towards the Kaʿbah. On this reading, the sense is that every direction to which God turned His Prophet was a direction God Himself assigned to His servants.

The word translated ***“direction”*** is a verbal noun from the root meaning to face. Mujāhid and Ibn Zayd gloss it as *“a qiblah,”* and al-Rabīʿ as *“a facing.”* Manṣūr is reported to have read it in a fuller form: *“For each We have made a direction they are pleased with.”* The phrase ***“turns to”*** renders a participle meaning one who turns his face towards it; Mujāhid glosses it as *“the one who faces it.”* The verb usually means to turn away, but with the preposition *“to”* it means to turn towards something while turning away from something else.

A reading attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās and others gives the passive, *“he is turned towards it,”* with God as the implied agent who turns each community towards its direction. A third reading, joining the words in a construct without the final vowel, was rejected as ungrammatical, since it leaves the sentence incomplete.

### **SO COMPETE WITH ONE ANOTHER IN DOING GOOD**

The verb behind ***“compete”*** means to race and hurry. Al-Rabīʿ glosses the phrase as *“hasten to good deeds.”* The sense drawn out of it is: I have made the truth clear to you and guided you to the direction from which the Jews, the Christians, and others strayed; so hasten to righteous deeds in gratitude to your Lord, and take provision from this world for the next, since the paths of salvation are now clear and there is no excuse for negligence. Hold to your direction and do not lose it as earlier communities lost theirs.

Qatādah, in the report through Saʿīd, glosses it with a pointed warning: *“Do not let yourselves be overcome concerning your direction.”* Ibn Zayd glosses it simply: *“Righteous deeds.”*

### **GATHERED FROM WHEREVER YOU ARE**

***“Wherever you are, Allah will bring you all together”*** means: in whatever place you die, God will gather all of you on the Day of Resurrection. Al-Rabīʿ and al-Suddī both explain it as the gathering on that Day. The verse thus urges the believers to obedience and to provision for the hereafter, because God will gather them together with those who differed from their direction, religion, and law, from every part of the earth, so that the doer of good is repaid for his good and the wrongdoer for his wrong, unless God pardons.

***“Surely Allah is Most Capable of everything”*** is applied directly to that gathering: He is able to assemble them after death from their graves, wherever they were and wherever their graves lie. The implication is drawn plainly: hasten to do good before your souls depart, for the day of your raising and gathering.
verses.149:
> Wherever you are ˹O Prophet˺, turn your face towards the Sacred Mosque. This is certainly the truth from your Lord. And Allah is never unaware of what you ˹all˺ do

### **MEANING**

The command to face **the Sacred Mosque**, first given in 2:144, is repeated here and extended in a new direction. There it was given in the setting of the Prophet’s longing and the change of direction itself. Here it is attached to his movements: from whatever place he sets out, and to whatever place he heads, he is to **turn his face towards the Sacred Mosque** in prayer. The verse then confirms that facing it is the truth from his Lord, beyond any doubt, and closes with the assurance that God is not heedless of anything the believers do.

The translation renders the opening as ***“Wherever you are,”*** and the Arabic literally speaks of the place from which one has gone out. The point is that travel does not suspend the command. Whether at home or on a journey, the believer at prayer faces the same House.

### **FROM WHEREVER YOU GO OUT**

The opening clause is explained as: from any place you go out to any place you head for, **turn your face**, O Muhammad. The verb ***“turn”*** here means to direct the face to something, as was explained at the first occurrence of the command; and the word rendered ***“towards”*** is the same word meaning direction, side, or facing that was discussed there. Its root sense is the place one faces, as the early authorities glossed it: towards it, facing it, in its direction.

The repetition gives the command a wider scope. In 2:144, the command ***“wherever you are, turn your faces towards it”*** spoke to the believers wherever they might be on earth. Here, the address to the Prophet adds the situation of setting out and travelling, so that no circumstance of movement is left outside the obligation. The next verse will repeat the same words again, adding the reason for the command.

### **THE TRUTH FROM YOUR LORD**

***“This is certainly the truth from your Lord”*** is explained as: facing towards it is the truth, beyond doubt, from your Lord, so keep to it and obey God in facing it. The sentence echoes Qur’an 2:144, where the learned among the People of the Scripture were said to know that this direction was ***“the truth from their Lord,”*** and Qur’an 2:147, where the Prophet was told, *“**the truth from your Lord**, so do not ever be one of those who doubt.”* In each case the truth of the direction is grounded in its source, God, rather than in the approval or disapproval of others.

The emphasis matters in the setting of the passage. The believers had just heard the objections of the Jews, the hypocrites, and the idolaters of Mecca, and some among them had worried about the prayers of those who had died before the change. Repeating that the direction is the truth from their Lord answers both kinds of disturbance: the doubt planted by opponents and the anxiety arising within the community.

### **GOD IS NOT UNAWARE**

The closing sentence, ***“And Allah is never unaware of what you ˹all˺ do,”*** means that God is not forgetful of their deeds nor heedless of them; He records them for them in order to repay them on the Day of Resurrection. In 2:144 the same reassurance was explained as God’s noting of the believers’ obedience, both their prayer towards Jerusalem and their prayer facing the Kaʿbah, and His storing up of it for their reward.

In this verse the assurance carries the same encouragement and a warning alongside it. Those who keep to the direction they were commanded to face will find their obedience recorded; those who neglect it will find that, too, before a Lord who **is never unaware**.
verses.150:
> Wherever you are ˹O Prophet˺, turn your face towards the Sacred Mosque. And wherever you ˹believers˺ are, face towards it, so that people will have no argument against you, except the wrongdoers among them. Do not fear them; fear Me, so that I may ˹continue to˺ perfect My favour upon you and so you may be ˹rightly˺ guided

### **MEANING**

The command to face **the Sacred Mosque** is given a third time, now joined to its purpose. From whatever place the Prophet sets out, he is to turn his face to it, and wherever the believers are on God’s earth, they are to turn their faces towards it in prayer. This is **so that people will have no argument against** them, **except the wrongdoers among them**. The believers are told not to fear those wrongdoers but to fear God, so that He may complete His favour on them and so that they may be guided.

The verse closes the section on the direction of prayer by showing what the change achieved. It removed a pretext from those who had used the former direction against the believers, and it completed a favour that God had begun with them.

### **THE ARGUMENT THAT WAS REMOVED**

The ***“people”*** in ***“so that people will have no argument against you”*** are identified by Qatādah and al-Rabīʿ as the People of the Book, who said when the Prophet was turned towards the Kaʿbah: *“The man has longed for his father’s house and his people’s religion!”* The argument they had used while the believers faced Jerusalem was recalled in earlier reports: *“Muhammad and his companions did not know where their direction was until we guided them,”* and *“Muhammad opposes us in our religion and follows our direction!”* That was the argument by which they quarrelled with the Prophet and tried to mislead the ignorant. The word for argument here means dispute and contention, and God cut it off by turning the believers from the direction of the Jews to the direction of His Friend Abraham.

### **EXCEPT THE WRONGDOERS**

***“Except the wrongdoers among them”*** is explained by the early authorities as referring to the idolaters of Quraysh. Mujāhid says, *“the people of Muhammad”*; al-Suddī says, *“the idolaters of Mecca”*; al-Rabīʿ, Qatādah, and ʿAṭāʾ say, *“the idolaters of Quraysh.”*

How could the idolaters have any case to make against the believers? The word here means only a contentious claim. Mujāhid says their argument was: *“You have come back to our direction!”* Qatādah and Mujāhid, in the report through Maʿmar, say that when the direction was turned to the Kaʿbah they said: *“He has returned to your direction; soon he will return to your religion.”* Al-Suddī, in a report through Abū Mālik and Abū Ṣāliḥ from Ibn ʿAbbās and through Murrah from Ibn Masʿūd and other companions, records the Meccans saying: *“Muhammad’s religion has confused him, so he turned his direction to you, knowing that you were better guided than he; soon he will enter your religion.”* ʿAṭāʾ reports Quraysh saying: *“He could not do without us; he has faced our direction!”*

The exception is therefore a true exception: no one has any dispute against the believers over their direction, ***“except the wrongdoers”*** of Quraysh, who make a false claim. Some grammarians proposed that *“except”* here means *“and not,”* or *“but,”* or begins a new sentence. These readings conflict with the explanation of the early authorities, and Arabic does not use *“except”* to mean *“and”* unless an earlier exception precedes it.

Al-Rabīʿ relates that a Jew disputed with Abū al-ʿĀliyah, saying that Moses used to pray towards the Rock in Jerusalem. Abū al-ʿĀliyah replied that he prayed at the Rock facing the Sacred House, and said that he had prayed in the mosque of Ṣāliḥ, carved from the mountain, and its direction was the Sacred House, and that he had passed the mosque of Dhū al-Qarnayn, whose direction was the Kaʿbah.

### **FEAR AND FAVOUR**

***“Do not fear them; fear Me”*** means: have no fear of these wrongdoers in their arguments and claims that Muhammad has returned to their direction and will return to their religion, nor fear that they can harm your religion or turn you from the truth; fear My punishment if you oppose My command. Al-Suddī glosses it: *“Have no fear that I will return you to their religion.”*

***“So that I may ˹continue to˺ perfect My favour upon you”*** connects the command to its fruit. By guiding them to the direction of Abraham, whom He made a leader for people, God completes His favour on them and completes the laws of their upright religion, which He enjoined on Noah, Abraham, Moses, Jesus, and the other prophets. ***“And so you may be ˹rightly˺ guided”*** means: so that you may be directed to the right direction. Grammatically, this clause and the one before it both join on to ***“so that people will have no argument against you,”*** giving three purposes for one command: no case against them, a completed favour, and guidance.
verses.151:
> Since We have sent you a messenger from among yourselves—reciting to you Our revelations, purifying you, teaching you the Book and wisdom, and teaching you what you never knew—

### **MEANING**

The verse links the completion of God’s favour, promised at the end of the previous verse, to a favour already given. God says that He will complete His favour on the believers by showing them the laws of their upright religion and guiding them to the religion of Abraham, just as He has already sent among them a messenger from their own people. That messenger recites God’s verses to them, purifies them, teaches them **the Book and wisdom**, and teaches them what they did not know.

The verse answers the prayer of Abraham and Ishmael recorded earlier in the surah. They had asked God to make them submissive to Him and to make from their descendants a submissive community, and then asked Him to raise from among them a messenger to recite His verses, teach **the Book and wisdom**, and purify them. This verse announces that the request has been granted.

### **THE PRAYER OF ABRAHAM FULFILLED**

The connection with Abraham’s prayer is made explicit in the explanation of the verse. God completes His favour by granting the community the supplication of His Friend Abraham, who prayed in Qur’an 2:128, *“Our Lord, make us submissive to You and from our descendants a community submissive to You,”* and in Qur’an 2:129, *“Our Lord, raise up among them **a messenger from among** them who will recite Your verses to them and teach them **the Book and wisdom** and purify them.”* So God sent among them the messenger whom Abraham and his son Ishmael had asked Him to raise from their descendants.

On this reading, the opening word, translated ***“Since,”*** literally *“just as,”* connects to the preceding clause, ***“so that I may ˹continue to˺ perfect My favour upon you.”*** The meaning is: I will complete My favour on you just as I sent a messenger among you.

Some, including Mujāhid in the report through Ibn Abī Najīḥ, connected it instead to the following verse: *“As I have done, so remember Me.”* That reading is grammatically awkward, because the following command already has its own answer, ***“I will remember you,”*** which shows that it begins a new sentence. A grammarian’s suggestion that the command could carry two answers was considered a possible construction but not the most natural Arabic.

### **A MESSENGER FROM AMONG YOURSELVES**

The phrase ***“a messenger from among yourselves”*** is explained as addressed to the Arabs: hold to obedience to Me, O Arabs, and face the direction I commanded, so that the argument of the Jews against you is cut off and I complete My favour on you, just as I began My favour by sending you a messenger from your own people. Al-Rabīʿ, in the report through Ibn Abī Jaʿfar from his father, identifies the messenger: *“He means Muhammad.”*

The emphasis on his being ***“from among yourselves”*** links the favour to the community’s own history. The direction of Abraham was restored to the descendants of Abraham through a prophet raised from their own number, exactly as their forefather had asked.

### **THE MESSENGER’S WORK**

Each of the tasks named in the verse is explained. ***“Reciting to you Our revelations”*** means the verses of the Qur’an. ***“Purifying you”*** means cleansing you from the stain of sins. ***“Teaching you the Book”*** means teaching the criterion of truth, that is, its rulings. ***“And wisdom”*** means the Prophet’s practice and understanding of the religion. These terms were explained at the corresponding words of Abraham’s prayer in 2:129.

The final clause adds something not present in that prayer: ***“and teaching you what you never knew.”*** This is explained as the reports of the prophets, the stories of past communities, and information about things yet to happen, which the Arabs did not know and learned from the Messenger. The verse thus tells them that all of this reached them only through him, and it prepares them for the command of the next verse: to remember and thank the One who gave it.
verses.152:
> remember Me; I will remember you. And thank Me, and never be ungrateful

### **MEANING**

The verse completes the sentence that began in the previous verse. Having reminded the believers of the messenger sent among them and the direction to which they were guided, God now tells them what response this calls for: **remember Me**, and **I will remember you**; give thanks to Me, and do not deny My favour.

To remember God here means to obey Him in what He commands and forbids; His remembering them means His mercy and forgiveness towards them. To thank Him means to acknowledge the favour of Islam and guidance to the religion He prescribed for His prophets and chosen servants. Ingratitude means to deny His kindness, which would lead Him to withdraw the favour He has given, while gratitude leads Him to increase it, complete His favour, and guide them as He guided those with whom He is pleased.

### **REMEMBRANCE AND ITS RETURN**

The early explanations differ in how they understand the two remembrances. Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, in the report through ʿAṭāʾ ibn Dīnār and Ibn Lahīʿah, says: *“**Remember Me** through your obedience, and **I will remember you** through My forgiveness.”* On this view, remembering God is not only a matter of words; it is the practical response of obeying Him, and His remembrance is His pardon and mercy.

Others took the remembrance to include praise and mention. Al-Rabīʿ, in the report through Ibn Abī Jaʿfar from his father, says: *“God remembers whoever remembers Him, increases whoever thanks Him, and punishes whoever is ungrateful to Him.”* Al-Suddī says: *“There is no servant who remembers God except that God remembers him. No believer remembers Him except that He remembers him with mercy, and no disbeliever remembers Him except that He remembers him with punishment.”* Al-Suddī’s explanation shows that remembrance carries different consequences according to the state of the one who remembers.

The two views are compatible. Obedience is the substance of remembering God, and praise and mention are part of it; God’s remembrance in return takes the form of mercy, forgiveness, and increase for those who obey and thank Him.

### **GRATITUDE AND INGRATITUDE**

The command ***“thank Me”*** is phrased in Arabic with a preposition, literally *“be thankful to Me.”* The Arabs say *“I was thankful to you”* and *“I gave sincere counsel to you”* more often than the forms without the preposition, though both occur. An unattributed Arabic line uses the direct form: *“They gathered upon you both hardship and ease; why did you not thank the people, since you did not fight?”* And al-Nābighah uses the direct form of the parallel verb: *“I counselled Banū ʿAwf, but they did not accept my messenger.”*

Thankfulness is explained elsewhere as praising someone for his good deeds, and ingratitude as covering something over. To be ungrateful to God is therefore to cover over His favour, to deny that it came from Him.

### **THE PROMISE BEHIND THE COMMAND**

The explanation of ***“and never be ungrateful”*** draws on a general promise: God has promised His creation that whoever thanks Him will be given more, and whoever is ungrateful will be deprived and stripped of what was given. Al-Rabīʿ’s words above express the same principle: God increases whoever thanks Him.

In the setting of the passage, the command is concrete. The favours the believers were to thank God for had just been listed: guidance to the direction of Abraham, a messenger raised from among them, the recitation of revelation, purification, the teaching of the Book and wisdom, and knowledge they had never had. The command to remember and thank closes that list, and the next verse turns to the means of bearing the trials that would accompany it: patience and prayer.
verses.153:
> O believers! Seek comfort in patience and prayer. Allah is truly with those who are patient

### **MEANING**

The verse urges the believers to obey God and to bear whatever hardship obedience brings to their bodies and property. They are told to seek help through **patience and prayer** in carrying out God’s commands, in accepting the rulings He replaces with new ones, in submitting to His command when it binds them and turning from it when He turns them, and in striving against their enemies in His cause. The hardship may come from the false accusations of their opponents, from fatigue in carrying out what is required, or from loss of wealth.

Patience in facing hardship earns God’s pleasure, and prayer brings success in what they ask of Him. The verse closes with the assurance that God is **with those who are patient**: He supports them, watches over them, and protects them until they attain what they hoped for from Him.

### **THE SETTING AFTER THE CHANGE OF DIRECTION**

The verse follows directly on the change of the direction of prayer and the command to remember and thank God. That change was itself a ruling replaced by another, and it brought with it mockery from the Jews and the idolaters, doubt among the hypocrites, and anxiety among the believers about their earlier prayers. The call to **patience and prayer** comes at the point where the community has been tested by a change of ruling and is about to be told, in the following verses, about further trials: death in God’s cause, fear, hunger, and loss.

Patience here therefore has a definite object. It is the steadiness to accept God’s command when it changes, to bear the words of opponents without wavering, and to endure the costs of obedience. Prayer is the refuge to which they turn when serious matters befall them.

### **PATIENCE AND PRAYER AS HELP**

A similar command was addressed earlier in the surah to the Children of Israel, Qur’an 2:45, *“And seek help through **patience and prayer**,”* and the meanings of **patience and prayer** were explained there. Abū al-ʿĀliyah, in the report through al-Rabīʿ, explains the command: *“Seek help through **patience and prayer** towards God’s pleasure, and know that they are part of obedience to God.”* Al-Rabīʿ, in another report, says: *“Know that they are a help towards obedience to God.”*

Both explanations make the same point: **patience and prayer** are not only means towards obedience but are themselves acts of obedience. The believer who seeks help through them is already doing what God commands while asking for strength to do more.

### **GOD IS WITH THOSE WHO ARE PATIENT**

***“Allah is truly with those who are patient”*** is explained as meaning that God is their helper and supporter and is pleased with what they do. Arabic uses the same expression when one person says to another, *“Do such and such, and I am with you,”* meaning: I will support you in it and help you with it.

The reassurance is tied to **those who are patient** in carrying out God’s obligations and abandoning disobedience. It does not promise them an easy path; the next verses speak of loss and death. What it promises is God’s support through that path, and it introduces the passage on martyrs and on those who meet calamity by returning to God.
verses.154:
> Never say that those martyred in the cause of Allah are dead—in fact, they are alive! But you do not perceive it

### **MEANING**

The verse continues the address that began with the call to seek help through patience and prayer. The believers, who are to be patient in obeying God, in striving against their enemies, and in abandoning disobedience, are now told not to speak of those killed in God’s cause as dead. The dead, in the sense meant here, are those from whom God has taken life and removed the senses, so that they feel no pleasure and receive no blessing. Those killed in His cause are not like that. **They are alive** with God, in a life of blessing, ease, and generous provision, rejoicing in the favour He has given them and the honour with which He has singled them out.

The final clause, ***“But you do not perceive it,”*** explains why the living might think otherwise: they cannot see the martyrs and so cannot know that **they are alive**. They know it only because God has told them.

### **THE LIFE OF THE MARTYRS**

The early explanations describe the life meant here in concrete terms. Mujāhid, in the report through Ibn Abī Najīḥ, says **they are alive** with their Lord, *“provided with the fruit of Paradise and finding its fragrance, though they are not in it.”* Qatādah, in the report through Saʿīd, says: *“We used to be told that the souls of the martyrs recognise one another in white birds that eat from the fruits of Paradise, and that their dwelling is the Lote Tree of the Boundary.”* He adds that whoever strives in God’s cause has three good outcomes: if he is killed he becomes alive and provided for, if he is overcome God gives him a great reward, and if he dies God provides him with good provision. In the report through Maʿmar, Qatādah says the martyrs’ souls are *“in the forms of white birds,”* while al-Rabīʿ says *“in the forms of green birds that fly in Paradise wherever they wish and eat wherever they wish,”* and ʿIkrimah, through ʿUthmān ibn Ghiyāth, says *“in green birds in Paradise.”*

A report from Ibn ʿAbbās, transmitted by Ibn Isḥāq through al-Ḥārith ibn Fuḍayl and Maḥmūd ibn Labīd, records the Prophet as saying: *“The martyrs are at Bāriq, a river at the gate of Paradise, in a green dome,”* or in another wording *“in a green garden,”* and *“their provision comes out to them from Paradise morning and evening.”* A further report through Ibn Bashshār al-Sulamī, or Abū Bashshār, describes the martyrs’ souls in white domes of Paradise and gives a vivid account of their daily provision.

### **WHAT IS PARTICULAR TO THE MARTYRS**

An objection arises. Many reports from the Prophet describe the state of believers and disbelievers after death: for believers, doors to Paradise are opened from their graves, from which they sense its fragrance, and for disbelievers, doors to the Fire. If all are in some sense alive in the interval before resurrection, what is particular to those killed in God’s cause?

The answer given is that the martyrs are provided with the food and drink of Paradise in their interval before resurrection, enjoying what others will enjoy only after they enter it. That is the distinction God gave them. The fuller statement is found in Qur’an 3:169–170: *“Think not of those killed in the cause of God as dead; rather, **they are alive** with their Lord, receiving provision, rejoicing in what God has given them of His bounty.”* Since that passage had already described their provision, this verse needed only to forbid people from calling them dead. The purpose of mentioning their life is to point to the blessing in which they live.

### **THE GRAMMAR OF THE PROHIBITION**

The words translated ***“are dead”*** and ***“they are alive”*** are both in the nominative, with an unstated pronoun: say not of those killed in God’s cause, *“they are dead”*; rather, *“**they are alive**.”* The accusative is not possible here, because the verb *“say”* introduces quoted speech rather than acting on the words directly.

The verse comes at a point in the surah where the believers are being prepared for hardship. They have been told to seek help through patience and prayer, and the next verse announces that they will be tested with fear, hunger, and loss of life. This verse places the hardest of those losses, death in God’s cause, in its true light: those who are lost to the living have not been lost to God.
verses.155:
> We will certainly test you with a touch of fear and famine and loss of property, life, and crops. Give good news to those who patiently endure—

### **MEANING**

God informs the followers of His Messenger that He will test them with hardships, so that it becomes clear who follows the Messenger and who turns back on his heels, just as He tested them with the change of the prayer direction and just as He tested His chosen servants before them. The tests are named: some fear of enemies, some hunger in years of drought, loss of wealth because livelihoods become difficult, loss of lives in war and through the death of children and families, and loss of crops through barren seasons. All of this is a trial, through which the truthful in faith are distinguished from the false, and those with insight from those with hypocrisy and doubt. Then the Prophet is told to give glad tidings to those who endure patiently.

### **A WORLD OF TESTING**

The word translated ***“test”*** means to try and examine. Ibn ʿAbbās, in the report through ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah, explains the verse: *“God informed the believers that this world is an abode of trial and that He would test them in it. He commanded them to be patient and gave them **good news**, saying, **Give good news to those who patiently endure**.”* He adds that God then told them He had done the same with His prophets and chosen ones, to reassure them, quoting the words *“affliction and hardship touched them, and they were shaken.”*

Those words come from Qur’an 2:214, where God says to the believers: *“Or did you think you would enter Paradise without there having come to you the like of those who passed before you? Affliction and hardship touched them, and they were shaken until the Messenger and those who believed with him said, When is God’s help? Indeed, God’s help is near.”* That later verse states as a general principle what this verse announces in particular terms.

ʿAṭāʾ, in the report through ʿAbd al-Malik, identifies the addressees: *“They are the companions of Muhammad.”*

### **A TOUCH OF EACH TRIAL**

The Arabic says literally *“with something of fear,”* in the singular, rather than *“with things.”* The reason given is that the trials named are of different kinds, and the preposition *“of”* indicates that each kind carries an implied *“something”*: something of fear, something of hunger, something of loss of wealth. Mentioning *“something”* once at the beginning was enough. The translation’s ***“a touch of”*** conveys the same idea: the trials are real but measured.

Al-Rabīʿ, in the report through Ibn Abī Jaʿfar from his father, says of the list: *“That has happened, and what is harsher than that will happen.”* The trials were not hypothetical; the early community experienced them, and al-Rabīʿ expected more severe ones to come.

### **GOOD NEWS FOR THE PATIENT**

The command ***“Give good news to those who patiently endure”*** tells the Prophet to single out for **good news** those who are patient under God’s testing, who restrain themselves from what He has forbidden, and who keep to what He has required despite the trials. They are described in the following verse as those who, when a calamity strikes, say, *“Surely to God we belong and to Him we will all return.”* The **good news** is reserved for them; it is not promised to everyone who suffers, but to those who meet suffering in this way.

The word for giving **good news** originally means telling someone news, pleasing or displeasing, before anyone else has told him. Here it is used of **good news**, and the content of that news will be stated two verses later: blessings from their Lord, mercy, and guidance. The verse thus continues the sequence that began with patience and prayer: the believers have been told what will come, how to meet it, and what awaits those who meet it well.
verses.156:
> who, when faced with a disaster, say, “Surely to Allah we belong and to Him we will ˹all˺ return.”

### **MEANING**

The verse describes the patient people to whom the Prophet was told to give good news. They are those who know that every blessing they have comes from God, who therefore acknowledge that they are His servants, affirm that He alone is Lord, and believe in the return to Him. Because of this, when God tests them with any of the trials He promised, fear, hunger, or loss of wealth, lives, and crops, they surrender to His decree, hope for His reward, and fear His punishment. Their words at such a moment express this: we are owned by our Lord, whom we worship, while we live, and to Him we shall return after we die.

The sentence is therefore not a formula detached from belief. Its first half acknowledges ownership: we belong to God. Its second half acknowledges the return: we are going back to Him. Together they express acceptance of His decree and contentment with His rulings.

### **THE MEANING OF THE TWO HALVES**

***“Surely to Allah we belong”*** means: we are His property and His servants. Whatever was taken from us was His before it was ours, and we ourselves are His. A person who believes this does not regard a loss as an injustice done to him, since the Owner has disposed of what He owns.

***“And to Him we will ˹all˺ return”*** means: we shall come to Him after death. This half gives the first its weight. The one who returns to God will find with Him the reward for patience, and so the loss is not final. The explanation given for the verse joins the two: the patient say these words *“in surrender to My decree and contentment with My rulings.”* The first clause establishes that God has the right to test; the second establishes that the test leads somewhere.

### **SAYING THE WORDS AT THE TIME OF CALAMITY**

The practice of saying these words when calamity strikes is described in reports attached to this passage. Ibn ʿAbbās, in the report through ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah, says that when the believer surrenders the matter to God and returns, saying these words at a calamity, three good things are written for him: blessing from God, mercy, and the realisation of the path of guidance. The same report records the Prophet as saying: *“Whoever says the words of return at a calamity, God will mend his calamity, make his outcome good, and give him a righteous successor with whom he is pleased.”*

The report places the words in their proper setting. They are spoken at the moment of loss, when a person is most likely to complain or despair, and they turn that moment into an act of surrender. The promise attached to them concerns both this world and the next: repair of the loss, a good outcome, and a worthy replacement.

### **A GIFT TO THIS COMMUNITY**

Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, in the report through Sufyān al-ʿUṣfurī, says: *“No one was given what this community was given: those who, when a calamity strikes them, **say, Surely to God we belong and to Him we will return**; upon them are blessings from their Lord and mercy. Had anyone been given it, Jacob would have been given it. Have you not heard his words, O my sorrow over Joseph?”* He refers to Qur’an 12:84, where Jacob, grieving over the loss of his son, cries out in sorrow.

Saʿīd’s remark does not criticise Jacob; it marks these words as a particular gift to the community of the Prophet, a way of meeting grief that had been given to them in this precise form. The verse, coming after the warning of trials in the previous verse, gives the believers the words with which to meet those trials, and the next verse describes what God gives to those who say them.
verses.157:
> They are the ones who will receive Allah’s blessings and mercy. And it is they who are ˹rightly˺ guided

### **MEANING**

The verse states the good news that the Prophet was told to give to the patient. Those who meet calamity by saying that they belong to God and will return to Him receive three things: blessings from their Lord, mercy, and the description of being **rightly guided**. The blessings are explained as forgiveness: God’s blessing on His servants is His pardon of them. Mercy accompanies that forgiveness, so that their sins are not only covered but replaced with God’s kindness and compassion. And they are declared to be those who are guided: the ones who have found the path of truth, who say what wins God’s pleasure and do what earns His great reward.

The verse closes the short passage on trial and patience that began with the command to seek help through patience and prayer. It shows that the patient are not merely enduring loss; they are receiving gifts that only God can give.

### **BLESSINGS AS FORGIVENESS**

The word translated ***“blessings”*** is the plural of the word usually rendered as prayer. When it is used of God towards His servants, it is explained as His forgiveness. A saying of the Prophet is cited to show this usage: *“O God, bless the family of Abū Awfā,”* meaning, forgive them. The word ***“mercy”*** then adds to forgiveness: besides pardoning and covering their sins, God grants them mercy and gentleness.

The distinction is meaningful. Forgiveness removes what would have counted against them; mercy adds what they could not have earned. The patient receive both, and both come ***“from their Lord,”*** the One who tested them in the first place.

### **THE THREE GIFTS**

Ibn ʿAbbās, in the report through ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah, reads the passage as a whole: *“God informed us that when the believer surrenders the matter to God, returns to Him, and says the words of return at a calamity, three good things are written for him: blessing from God, mercy, and the realisation of the path of guidance.”* His explanation shows how the last clause of the verse, ***“it is they who are ˹rightly˺ guided,”*** counts as a gift in its own right: it is God’s testimony that their way of meeting calamity is the right way.

Al-Rabīʿ, in the report through Ibn Abī Jaʿfar from his father, ties the blessings to the conduct described in the previous verse: *“The blessings and the mercy are upon those who were patient and said the words of return.”* Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, in the report through Sufyān al-ʿUṣfurī, cites this verse together with the previous one as something no earlier community was given in this form.

### **THOSE WHO ARE GUIDED**

The final sentence, ***“And it is they who are ˹rightly˺ guided,”*** uses the same word for guidance that has run through the passage on the change of prayer direction. There, God was described as guiding whom He wills to the straight path, the believers were said to have been guided to the direction of Abraham, and the change was described as heavy except for those whom God had guided. Here the same description is given to those who meet loss with patience and surrender. To be guided means to be directed to what is right, and the verse identifies the patient as the people who have reached it.

The placement of the verse is significant. The passage on the prayer direction ended with the command to remember God and thank Him, followed by the call to patience and prayer, the statement about the martyrs, and the warning of trials. The present verse completes that sequence by naming the reward. Those who have kept the direction of Abraham, endured the mockery of opponents, accepted loss, and returned their losses to God are the ones whom God blesses, has mercy on, and calls guided. The surah then turns to another sign connected with Abraham and his household: Ṣafā and Marwah.
verses.158:
> Indeed, ˹the hills of˺ Ṣafa and Marwah are among the symbols of Allah. So whoever performs the pilgrimage or minor pilgrimage, let them walk between ˹the two hills˺. And whoever does good willingly, Allah is truly Appreciative, All-Knowing

### **MEANING**

The verse tells the believers that the passage to and fro between the hills of Ṣafā and Marwah, inside God’s sanctuary at Mecca, is one of the rites of worship He established. These hills are among the landmarks God set up for His servants as places where they worship Him, by supplication, by remembrance, or by performing what He has required of them there. Going between them is among the rites of pilgrimage that God laid down and commanded His Friend Abraham to perform when Abraham asked to be shown the rites. Although the verse is worded as a statement, it carries the force of a command, since the Prophet was told to follow the religion of Abraham.

The Arabic of the middle sentence literally says that anyone making the pilgrimage to the House or the **minor pilgrimage** incurs no sin in going round them both. Some believers had been reluctant to do so because of practices from the time before Islam; the verse removes that hesitation. It closes by assuring those who do good voluntarily that God appreciates it and knows their intentions.

### **ṢAFĀ, MARWAH, AND THE SYMBOLS OF GOD**

The word *ṣafā* is the plural of a word meaning a smooth rock, used by al-Ṭirimmāḥ in the line *“the One of power and bounty refused that any hoof should ever wear down my rock.”* *Marwah* means a small stone; al-Aʿshā uses its plural of hard pebbles, and Abū Dhuʾayb al-Hudhalī says, *“as though I were, against misfortunes, a stone on the rock of al-Musharraq, struck every day.”* The definite article shows that the verse means the two well-known hills in the sanctuary and not rocks in general.

***“Among the symbols of Allah”*** means among the landmarks God made places of worship. Mujāhid, through Ibn Abī Najīḥ, read the word as coming from God’s informing His servants, glossing it as *“part of the news He gave you.”* That explanation is far from the evident sense. Rather, the verse teaches that going between them is a rite of pilgrimage that God laid down for Abraham. Since the Prophet was commanded in Qur’an 16:123 to *“follow the religion of Abraham, the upright,”* and Abraham practised this rite and established it for those after him, the Prophet and his community must practise it as the Prophet showed them.

### **WHY THE VERSE REMOVES BLAME**

How can the verse command the walk and then say there is no sin in doing it? The answer lies in why it was revealed. Al-Shaʿbī reports that before Islam an idol named Isāf stood on Ṣafā and one named Nāʾilah on Marwah, and people touched them when they went round the House. When Islam came and the idols were broken, Muslims said the hills had been visited only for the idols and that going round them was not one of the rites; so God revealed that they are among His symbols. Ibn ʿAbbās, through ʿAmr ibn Ḥubshī, says idols stood at the hills, and when idols were forbidden people held back from going round them until the verse came. Al-Suddī reports from Ibn ʿAbbās that the Muslims said, *“O Messenger of God, we will not go round Ṣafā and Marwah, for it is idolatry we used to do before Islam.”* Anas, asked by ʿĀṣim al-Aḥwal, says: *“Yes, we used to dislike going round them because they were rites of the time of ignorance, until this verse came down.”* Ibn Zayd says the same and recites Qur’an 22:32, *“whoever honours the symbols of God, that is from the piety of hearts.”*

Others gave a different cause. Qatādah says a tribe of Tihāmah used not to go between the hills before Islam, and God told them it was a practice of Abraham and Ishmael. ʿĀʾishah, asked by ʿUrwah, explained that the Anṣār who worshipped the idol Manāt used to avoid walking between Ṣafā and Marwah, and asked the Prophet about it. When ʿUrwah suggested there was no sin in not going round them, she replied: *“How badly you have spoken, my nephew! If it were as you interpret it, it would read: there is no sin on him if he does not go round them.”* She added that the Prophet established the walk, so no one may abandon it. Abū Bakr ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān heard that the verse came down concerning both groups.

The verse may have addressed both groups: those wary because of the idols, and those who had avoided the walk before Islam. In neither case does the phrase mean that the walk had once been forbidden and was then permitted, for all agree that God never forbade it. Al-Suddī glosses the phrase: *“There is no sin on him, but rather he has a reward.”*

### **THE STATUS OF THE WALK**

Scholars differed. Some held it an essential rite that must be made up if missed: ʿĀʾishah said, *“By my life, anyone who has not gone between Ṣafā and Marwah has not performed the pilgrimage,”* and Mālik and al-Shāfiʿī required anyone who omitted it to return. Al-Thawrī and Abū Ḥanīfah held that a sacrifice compensates for it. Others, including ʿAṭāʾ, Anas, Mujāhid, and ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Zubayr, considered it voluntary, some citing a reading attributed to Ibn Masʿūd and Ibn ʿAbbās that adds *“not.”*

The stronger view is that it is obligatory and must be made up whether missed by forgetfulness or deliberately. Jābir reports that when the Prophet approached Ṣafā in his pilgrimage he recited the verse and said, *“Begin with what God began with,”* and climbed it. The Prophet’s teaching explains what the Book requires, and the walk is a circuit like that of the House, for which no compensation suffices. The added reading contradicts the written copies of the Qur’an; and even if it were read, the *“not”* could be redundant after a negation, as in Qur’an 7:12, *“What prevented you from prostrating?”*

### **DOING GOOD WILLINGLY**

The phrase ***“whoever does good willingly”*** is read in two ways, as a past verb or as a future one, with the same meaning. It refers to one who voluntarily **performs the pilgrimage or minor pilgrimage** beyond the obligatory one: God appreciates it, repays it, and knows the intention behind it. Those who held the walk voluntary took it to mean volunteering the walk itself; Mujāhid says the Prophet volunteered it and it became a practice. Ibn Zayd took it as volunteering the **minor pilgrimage**, which he held not to be obligatory.
verses.159:
> Those who hide the clear proofs and guidance that We have revealed—after We made it clear for humanity in the Book—will be condemned by Allah and ˹all˺ those who condemn

### **MEANING**

The verse speaks of the scholars and rabbis of the Jews and the scholars of the Christians, who concealed from people what they knew about Muhammad and refused to follow him, although they found him described in their own scriptures, the Torah and the Gospel. The ***“clear proofs”*** God revealed are what He made plain about Muhammad’s prophethood, his mission, and his description in those two books. The ***“guidance”*** is what He made clear to them about him in the books revealed to their prophets.

Those who conceal this after God made it plain in the scripture are driven away by God from Himself and His mercy, and **those who condemn** ask God to curse them. Although the verse came down about particular people, it applies to everyone who conceals knowledge that God has made it obligatory to make clear to people.

### **WHO CONCEALED AND WHAT THEY CONCEALED**

Ibn ʿAbbās, in the report through Ibn Isḥāq, relates that Muʿādh ibn Jabal, Saʿd ibn Muʿādh, and Khārijah ibn Zayd asked a group of Jewish rabbis about something in the Torah, and they concealed it and refused to tell them, so God revealed this verse about them. Mujāhid, through Ibn Abī Najīḥ, says simply: *“They are the People of the Scripture.”* Al-Rabīʿ says: *“They concealed Muhammad, while they found him written in their possession; they concealed him out of envy and transgression.”* Qatādah says: *“They are the People of the Scripture; they concealed Islam, which is the religion of God, and they concealed Muhammad, while they found him written in their possession in the Torah and the Gospel.”*

Al-Suddī relates that a Jew had a friend among the Anṣār named Thaʿlabah ibn Ghanamah, who asked him, *“Do you find Muhammad in your books?”* and he answered, *“No.”* Al-Suddī explains that Muhammad himself is the clear proof.

### **AFTER WE MADE IT CLEAR FOR HUMANITY IN THE BOOK**

The word ***“humanity”*** here refers to some people only, because knowledge of Muhammad’s prophethood, description, and mission was held by the People of the Scripture and not by others. It is they who are meant, and ***“the Book”*** here means the Torah and the Gospel. The concealment was therefore not ignorance; it was the hiding of something God had already made clear to them in their own scripture.

Yet the verse applies beyond them. A saying of the Prophet is cited in the same sense: *“Whoever is asked about knowledge he has and conceals it will be bridled on the Day of Resurrection with a bridle of fire.”* Abū Hurayrah used to say, *“Were it not for a verse in the Book of God, I would not have narrated anything to you,”* and he recited this verse.
