In another report through Ibn al-Musayyab he speaks of two verses, this one and Qur’an 3:187, *“And when God took the covenant of those who were given the Scripture: You must make it clear to people.”*

### **THE CURSE AND THOSE WHO CURSE**

***“Will be condemned by Allah”*** uses the verb meaning to curse. Its root sense is to drive away and banish. Al-Shammākh ibn Ḍirār, describing a watering place, speaks of *“the standing place of the wolf, like the banished man,”* meaning the outcast wolf. God’s curse is therefore His removing them far from Himself and His mercy, and the curse of others is their saying, *“O God, curse him.”*

The early authorities differed over ***“those who condemn.”*** Mujāhid, in several reports, says they are the animals and creeping things of the earth, *“the beetles and scorpions,”* who say when rain is withheld, *“we have been denied rain because of the sins of the children of Adam.”* ʿIkrimah says: *“Everything curses them, even beetles and scorpions.”* The masculine plural, normally used for humans, can describe animals when they are given human actions, as in Qur’an 27:18, *“O ants, enter your dwellings.”* Qatādah and al-Rabīʿ say they are *“the angels of God and the believers.”* Al-Suddī, through a report from al-Barāʾ ibn ʿĀzib, and al-Ḍaḥḥāk say they are all creatures except jinn and humans, who hear the cry of the disbeliever struck in his grave and curse him.

The most sound view is that they are the angels and the believers, because God describes the curse falling on disbelievers in Qur’an 2:161 as *“the curse of God and the angels and all people.”* Those who conceal what God revealed are likewise disbelievers, and the same cursers are meant. The view that the cursers are beetles and scorpions cannot be confirmed without a report from God or His Prophet establishing it, and the evident sense of the Book points elsewhere.
verses.160:
> As for those who repent, mend their ways, and let the truth be known, they are the ones to whom I will turn ˹in forgiveness˺, for I am the Accepter of Repentance, Most Merciful

### **MEANING**

The verse makes an exception to the curse announced in the previous verse. God and those who curse condemn those who hid from people what they knew of Muhammad’s prophethood and description in the scripture, except those who turn back from that concealment. They turn in repentance by believing in Muhammad, acknowledging his prophethood, and accepting what he brought from God. They set right their own condition by drawing near to God through righteous deeds that please Him. And they make clear what they knew of God’s revelation to His prophets, including the command to follow Muhammad, showing it instead of hiding it.

It is to those who do this that God turns in forgiveness, making them people who return to obedience to Him and to what pleases Him. He is the One who turns the hearts of His servants back to Him after they have turned away, and who is merciful to those who come to Him, covering them with pardon and overlooking the great wrongs they committed.

### **THREE CONDITIONS**

The verse names three things: repentance, reform, and making clear. Qatādah, in the report through Saʿīd, explains: *“They reformed what is between them and God, and they made clear what had come to them from God; they did not conceal it and did not deny it.”* Ibn Zayd says: *“They made clear what is in the Book of God to the believers, and what the believers asked them about concerning the Prophet. All of this concerns the Jews.”*

Each condition answers part of the wrong. The wrong was concealment of the truth about Muhammad and denial of him; repentance means turning from that denial to faith, reform means setting right their relationship with God through good deeds, and making clear means undoing the concealment itself by showing what they had hidden. The repentance of a concealer is incomplete unless he reveals what he concealed.

Some have claimed that ***“let the truth be known”*** means making their repentance evident through sincere deeds. The evident sense of the passage contradicts this. The people addressed were rebuked in the previous verse for concealing what God had revealed about Muhammad and his religion; the exception therefore concerns those who make that matter clear, and so leave the ranks of those whom God and the cursers condemn. They were not rebuked for failing to show their repentance.

### **GOD WHO TURNS IN FORGIVENESS**

How can God turn to someone who has already repented? Is anyone a penitent without God having turned to him, or one to whom God has turned without being a penitent? The answer is that neither occurs without the other. It is the same whether one says, *“except those to whom God turned, so they repented,”* or ***“those who repent… are the ones to whom I will turn.”*** The repentance of the servant and God’s turning to him go together.

***“For I am the Accepter of Repentance, Most Merciful”*** explains both names. God is the One who brings back to Himself the hearts of His servants that had turned from Him, restoring them after they turned their backs on His obedience to seeking His love. He is the **Most Merciful** to those who come back, covering them with pardon and overlooking what they committed, out of the abundance of His mercy.

### **WHO WAS EXCEPTED**

The exception is not hypothetical. Those whom God excepted from the concealers of the clear proofs and guidance are identified as ʿAbd Allāh ibn Salām and those like him among the People of the Scripture who accepted Islam, became good Muslims, and followed the Messenger of God. They knew what was written in their books about Muhammad, and instead of hiding it they made it known.

The verse thus holds open the door that the previous verse seemed to close. The curse falls on those who persist in concealment; **those who repent**, reform, and reveal are received by a Lord whose names are **Accepter of Repentance** and **Most Merciful**. The following verse turns to those who do not take that path: those who disbelieve and die as disbelievers, on whom falls the curse of God, the angels, and all people.
verses.161:
> Surely those who disbelieve and die as disbelievers are condemned by Allah, the angels, and all of humanity

### **MEANING**

After the exception made for those who repent, the verse describes those who do not. They are the people who reject the prophethood of Muhammad and deny him, whether Jews, Christians, followers of other religions, or idolaters, and who then die while still in that rejection. On them falls the curse of God, which means that He removes them far from His mercy, and the curse of the angels and of all people, which means their saying, *“The curse of God be upon them.”*

The condition that they ***“die as disbelievers”*** is decisive. The previous verse kept the door open for anyone who turned back before death; this verse speaks of those for whom that door has closed, because they reached death without passing through it.

### **WHO IS MEANT**

The phrase ***“those who disbelieve”*** is explained broadly: those who denied Muhammad’s prophethood and called him a liar, from among the Jews, the Christians, the people of other religions, and the idol-worshippers. The previous verses concerned in particular the scholars of the People of the Scripture who concealed what they knew; this verse widens the description to every disbeliever who dies in that state.

The meaning of the curse was explained at the verse before: its root is banishment, so God’s curse is His driving them away from His mercy, and the curse of creatures is their prayer that God curse them.

### **HOW CAN ALL PEOPLE CURSE THEM?**

A question arises. How can the curse of ***“all of humanity”*** fall on one who dies rejecting Muhammad, when most people in the world do not believe in him either? The early authorities answered in three ways.

Qatādah and al-Rabīʿ said that ***“all of humanity”*** here means the believers in particular. Qatādah, in the report through Saʿīd, says: *“By all people, He means the believers.”* Al-Rabīʿ says the same.

Abū al-ʿĀliyah, in the report through al-Rabīʿ, placed the curse on the Day of Resurrection: *“The disbeliever will be made to stand on the Day of Resurrection, and God will curse him, then the angels will curse him, then all people will curse him.”*

Al-Suddī, in the report through Asbāṭ, gave a third explanation: *“No two people curse one another, whether two believers or two disbelievers, so that one of them says, May God curse the wrongdoer, except that the curse falls due upon the disbeliever, because he is a wrongdoer; so every one of creation curses him.”*

### **THE STRONGER VIEW**

The most correct of these views is that the verse means all people, in the sense that they curse disbelievers when they say, *“May God curse the wrongdoer,”* or *“the wrongdoers.”* No human being, of whatever religion, refrains from saying this, and every disbeliever falls within it. This also agrees with what Abū al-ʿĀliyah said, for God has told us that the witnesses will curse such people on the Day of Resurrection, as in Qur’an 11:18: *“Who is more unjust than one who invents a lie about God? Those will be presented before their Lord, and the witnesses will say, These are the ones who lied about their Lord. Indeed, the curse of God is upon the wrongdoers.”*

The view that only the believers are meant goes against the evident wording, and there is no proof for it from report or reasoning. If it was based on the thought that disbelievers do not curse themselves or their allies, God has told us that they will curse one another in the hereafter; and it is known that they curse wrongdoers, among whom every disbeliever is included, since he has wronged himself, denied the favour of his Lord, and opposed His command.

The verse thus presents the end of those who persist: a curse that comes from God, from the angels, and even from the mouths of people who share their disbelief but condemn the very wrongdoing of which they are guilty. The next verse states how long this lasts and what it brings.
verses.162:
> They will be in Hell forever. Their punishment will not be lightened, nor will they be delayed ˹from it˺

### **MEANING**

The verse continues the description of those who disbelieve and die as disbelievers. The Arabic literally says that they abide in it forever, and the pronoun refers to the curse. But what is meant by abiding in the curse is abiding in what the curse leads to, which is the fire of Hell. The translation therefore renders it directly as ***“They will be in Hell forever.”***

The torment is never eased: it continues for ever, without any fixed term and without any easing. Nor is respite granted to them; no time is allowed them to make an excuse.

The verse completes the picture begun in the previous one. The curse of God, the angels, and all people is not a passing word; it is the cause of a lasting state from which there is no relief and no postponement.

### **THE GRAMMAR OF ABIDING**

The word meaning ***“forever”***, literally *“abiding,”* is in the accusative as a circumstantial description of the pronoun in *“upon them”* in the previous verse. The sense is: those are the ones whom God, the angels, and all people curse, while they abide in it. Some read the previous verse with the angels and people in the nominative, as though it said, *“God, the angels, and all people curse them,”* to bring out this meaning. That reading is possible in Arabic but may not be recited, because it differs from the written copies of the Qur’an and from the widely transmitted reading of the Muslims; a rare reading cannot be set against what has been established by widespread transmission.

The pronoun in *“in it”* returns to the curse, while what is meant is what the disbeliever comes to through the curse, which is Hell. Speech is attached to the cause while meaning its result, a usage explained at similar passages before. Abū al-ʿĀliyah, in the report through al-Rabīʿ, says: *“Abiding in Hell, in the curse.”*

### **NO LIGHTENING**

The clause ***“Their punishment will not be lightened”*** is God’s statement that the punishment continues forever, with no set term and no easing. Two other verses describe the same permanence. Qur’an 35:36 says: *“As for those who disbelieve, for them is the fire of Hell; death is not decreed for them so that they might die, and its torment is not eased for them.”* Qur’an 4:56 says: *“Every time their skins are roasted through, We will replace them with other skins.”*

These parallels show that the absence of lightening means two things: the punishment does not end through death, and it does not weaken through time. The one who suffers it neither escapes by dying nor grows accustomed to it.

### **NO RESPITE**

The final clause, ***“nor will they be delayed,”*** is explained as meaning that no respite is granted them to offer an excuse. Abū al-ʿĀliyah, in the report through al-Rabīʿ, says: *“No respite is given them so that they might excuse themselves,”* and compares it to Qur’an 77:35–36: *“This is a Day on which they do not speak, and no permission is given them to offer excuses.”*

The meaning connects with the previous verse. Those described there died as disbelievers; the time for repentance and excuse was their life in this world, and it has passed. The verse that follows turns from the fate of those who reject God’s oneness to the declaration of that oneness itself.
verses.163:
> Your God is ˹only˺ One God. There is no god ˹worthy of worship˺ except Him—the Most Compassionate, Most Merciful

### **MEANING**

Divinity, as explained before, means being the one whom creation worships. The verse therefore tells all people that the One who has the right to their obedience and deserves their worship is a single object of worship and a single Lord. They should worship no one else and associate no one with Him, because whatever they associate with Him in worship is itself a created thing, created by their God just as they are. Their God is a single God, with no like and no equal.

No lord of the worlds exists besides Him, and no one besides Him has the right to the worship of His servants. Everything other than Him is His creation, and all creatures are obliged to obey Him, submit to His command, and abandon the worship of rivals, gods, idols, and images. Every blessing they enjoy in this world comes from Him, not from what they worship besides Him, and every blessing they will reach in the hereafter comes from Him; what they associate with Him can neither harm nor benefit them, now or later. The verse is God’s warning to the idolaters about their error and His invitation to them to turn back from disbelief and from associating partners with Him.

### **WHAT ONE MEANS**

There were two views about the meaning of God’s oneness. Some said it means the negation of any likeness or equal, as one says of a man that he is *“the one of his people,”* meaning that no one among them is like him. They argued that the word *“one”* can be understood in four senses: one member of a kind, as one human being among humans; something undivided, like a part that cannot be split; sameness, as when two things are said to be *“one”* because they resemble each other closely; and the denial of any equal or likeness. Since the first three senses cannot apply to God, they said, the fourth is the meaning.

Others said that God’s oneness means His being distinct from all things and all things being distinct from Him: He is alone because He is not within anything and nothing is within Him. They held that this is the only true sense in which anything can be called one, and they rejected the four senses listed by the first group.

### **THERE IS NO GOD EXCEPT HIM**

The clause ***“There is no god ˹worthy of worship˺ except Him”*** is God’s statement that no lord of the worlds exists besides Him and that no one else deserves the worship of His servants. The reasoning behind it is set out plainly: all besides Him are His creation, so all are obliged to acknowledge Him alone as God. Divinity is fitting only for Him, because every blessing comes from Him, while partners neither harm nor benefit.

The two names that close the verse, ***“the Most Compassionate, Most Merciful,”*** both come from mercy. Their placement here ties God’s oneness to His mercy: the One who alone deserves worship is also the One from whom every blessing comes, which is the very reason given for worshipping Him alone.

### **THE IDOLATERS’ REACTION**

Reports attached to the following verse describe how this declaration was received. ʿAṭāʾ, in the report through Ibn Abī Najīḥ, says that when this verse came down to the Prophet in Medina, the disbelievers of Quraysh in Mecca said: *“How can a single God be enough for all people?”* Abū al-Ḍuḥā, in the report through Saʿīd ibn Masrūq, says that when it came down the idolaters began to marvel and said: *“You say your God is a single God; then bring us a sign, if you are truthful!”*

God answered them in the next verse by pointing to the creation of the heavens and the earth, the alternation of night and day, the ships, the rain, the creatures, the winds, and the clouds. The declaration of oneness in this verse is therefore followed immediately by the evidence for it, inviting those who doubted to reflect on what they could see.
verses.164:
> Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth; the alternation of the day and the night; the ships that sail the sea for the benefit of humanity; the rain sent down by Allah from the skies, reviving the earth after its death; the scattering of all kinds of creatures throughout; the shifting of the winds; and the clouds drifting between the heavens and the earth—˹in all of this˺ are surely signs for people of understanding

### **MEANING**

Having declared that their God is one God, God now shows the idolaters where **people of understanding** find the proof of that declaration. If you are ignorant or in doubt about what I have told you, He says in effect, that your God is one, apart from the rivals and idols you claim as gods, then reflect on My proofs. Among them are **the heavens and the earth** that I brought into being; night and day following one another; the ships that run on the sea carrying what benefits people; the rain I send down, by which I bring the barren earth back to life; the creatures of every kind I have spread over it; the winds I turn as I will; and the clouds I have made subservient between sky and earth. If the idols, gods, and rivals you worship, all together or any one of them alone, could create the like of any of these, you would have an excuse for worshipping them. If not, you have no excuse for taking a god besides Me.

All these are marks and indications that the Creator and Originator of everything is one God. They are set out as lessons for those who have understanding and discernment, since it is they who are addressed by command and prohibition, charged with obedience and worship, and destined for reward or punishment.

### **WHY THE VERSE WAS REVEALED**

The early authorities gave two accounts. ʿAṭāʾ, in the report through Ibn Abī Najīḥ, says that when the previous verse was revealed to the Prophet in Medina, the disbelievers of Quraysh in Mecca said, *“How can a single God be enough for all people?”* So God revealed this verse, *“and by this you know that He is one God, the God of everything and the Creator of everything.”*

Abū al-Ḍuḥā, in several reports, and ʿAṭāʾ ibn Abī Rabāḥ, in the report through Ibn Jurayj, say instead that the idolaters demanded a sign. Abū al-Ḍuḥā relates: *“When this was revealed, the idolaters said: If it is so, let him bring us a sign!”* Saʿīd ibn Jubayr relates that Quraysh asked the Jews about the signs of Moses and the Christians about the signs of Jesus, then asked the Prophet to pray that God turn Ṣafā into gold. God told him He would grant it, but if they then disbelieved He would punish them as He had punished no one in the worlds. The Prophet said, *“Leave me and my people, and I will call them day by day.”* So this verse came down: **the creation of the heavens and the earth** and the alternation of night and day are greater than turning Ṣafā into gold.

Either account may be correct, and no report settles the question. Whichever it was, the purpose of the verse is the same: to direct God’s servants to the evidence of His oneness and His sole right to divinity.

### **THE HEAVENS, THE EARTH, NIGHT AND DAY**

***“The creation of the heavens and the earth”*** means bringing them into being when they did not exist.

***“The alternation of the day and the night”*** means their succession upon you, each taking the place of the other: when night departs, day comes after it, and when day departs, night follows. The word is from the root meaning to come after, as in Qur’an 25:62: *“It is He who made the night and the day in succession for whoever wishes to remember or wishes to be grateful.”*

### **THE SHIPS AND THE RAIN**

***“The ships that sail the sea”*** translates a word for ships that is the same in singular and plural and may be masculine or feminine, as in Qur’an 36:41, *“the laden ship.”* The ships are said to *“run,”* though they are made to run, because the description belongs to them once they are moving. ***“For the benefit of humanity”*** means what benefits people at sea.

***“The rain sent down by Allah from the skies”*** is the water God sends from the sky. ***“Reviving the earth after its death”*** means making it flourish and bringing forth its plants; the death of the earth is its barrenness, the decay of its cultivation, and the cessation of the plants that are food for people and provision for creatures.

### **THE CREATURES, THE WINDS, AND THE CLOUDS**

***“The scattering of all kinds of creatures throughout”*** means God has dispersed them over the earth, as one says that a commander *“dispersed”* his troops. The word for creature comes from the verb meaning to creep or move along, and it names every living being that does not fly with wings, because it moves on the earth.

***“The shifting of the winds”*** means God’s turning of them, sending them at one time to fertilise and at another making them barren, or sending them as a punishment that destroys everything by its Lord’s command. Qatādah, in the report through Saʿīd, says: *“Our Lord, by God, is able to do that: if He wishes He makes it a mercy, fertilising the clouds and spreading before His mercy, and if He wishes He makes it a punishment, a barren wind that does not fertilise.”* It may also mean His varying the directions from which they blow.

***“The clouds drifting between the heavens and the earth”*** are the clouds made subservient. The word for clouds is a collective, as Qur’an 13:12 shows: *“He raises the heavy clouds.”* They may be so called because they drag one another along.

### **SIGNS FOR PEOPLE OF UNDERSTANDING**

How could this be an argument against disbelievers when some deny that **the heavens and the earth** were created at all? Their denial does not stop these things from pointing to a Creator and Maker unlike anything else. But God was addressing people who acknowledged that He created them and yet worshipped idols alongside Him. When they rejected His oneness and claimed He had partners, He reminded them: your God created the heavens and set the sun and moon running, alternating night and day; He made the ships run for your benefit; He sent rain on your barren land and revived you after despair; He gave you livestock for food, riding, and clothing; He sent winds to fertilise your trees and drove the clouds whose rain gives life to you and your herds.

Then He asks: can any of your partners do any of this, that you should make them My rivals in worship? If none can, then in the favours I have counted out, which I alone gave you, there are ***“signs for people of understanding,”*** for those who can tell truth from falsehood and justice from injustice. That is the meaning of the verse, and the next verse turns to those who nevertheless set up rivals to God.
verses.165:
> Still there are some who take others as Allah’s equal—they love them as they should love Allah—but the ˹true˺ believers love Allah even more. If only the wrongdoers could see the ˹horrible˺ punishment ˹awaiting them˺, they would certainly realize that all power belongs to Allah and that Allah is indeed severe in punishment

### **MEANING**

After the signs of God’s oneness have been laid out, the verse turns to those who ignore them. Among people there are those who take rivals besides God, equals they set up alongside Him, and love those rivals as the **believers love** God. Then God tells them that the **believers love** God more intensely than those people love their rivals.

The second half of the verse shows the end of that love. If those who wronged themselves by taking rivals **could see the** punishment God has prepared for them on the Day of Resurrection, it would become clear to them **that all power belongs to** God, not to the rivals and gods, that those rivals cannot help them or ward off any punishment, and that God is severe in punishing whoever disbelieves in Him and claims another god beside Him.

### **WHO ARE THE RIVALS?**

The word rendered ***“equal”*** means a rival or counterpart, as explained earlier in the surah. The early authorities differed over who these rivals were. Qatādah, Mujāhid, al-Rabīʿ, and Ibn Zayd said they were the idols and gods the idolaters worshipped besides God. Al-Rabīʿ says: *“They are the gods worshipped besides God; **they love** their idols as **they love** God.”* Ibn Zayd says: *“These are the idolaters; their rivals are their gods whom they worshipped along with God.”* Mujāhid explains the love as *“a boastful rivalry, matching the truth with rivals.”*

Al-Suddī, in the report through Asbāṭ, said they were men: *“Rivals from among men, whom they obey as they obey God; whenever such men command, their followers obey and disobey God.”*

The following verse decides between these views. It describes the followed disowning their followers when they see the punishment, which shows that the rivals meant here are those who are obeyed, men who commanded their followers and led them into disobedience. Al-Suddī’s explanation is therefore the correct one, since the passage that follows continues the account of those who take rivals.

### **AS THEY SHOULD LOVE ALLAH**

How can the verse say **they love** their rivals *“like the love of God”*? Do the rivals love God, or did those who took rivals love God? The answer is that the phrase is an Arabic comparison in which the subject of the second love is left unstated, as one says, *“I sold my slave like the selling of your slave,”* meaning as you sold yours. A poet says, *“I will not greet Zayd, as long as I live, with the greeting of the commander,”* meaning as the commander is greeted. So the meaning is: some people take rivals besides God and **love them as** you who believe love God.

The translation renders this as ***“they love them as they should love Allah,”*** and the following clause supplies the contrast: ***“but the ˹true˺ believers love Allah even more.”*** Mujāhid, al-Rabīʿ, and Qatādah all explain the comparison as more than the love of the disbelievers for their idols. Ibn Zayd says the **believers love** God more than these people love their gods.

### **IF THEY COULD SEE THE PUNISHMENT**

The reciters differed over the second half of the verse. The people of Medina and Syria read it, *“If you **could see** those who did wrong,”* addressed to the Prophet, with *“that”* in the accusative. The Kufans, Basrans, and Meccans read, as in the translation, ***“If only the wrongdoers could see,”*** with *“that”* in the accusative, meaning: if they **could see the** punishment prepared for them in Hell, it would become clear to them at the moment they see it **that all power belongs to** God. Others read *“you **could see**”* with the following words beginning a new sentence: *“Indeed, **all power belongs to** God.”*

The preferred reading is the one addressed to the Prophet, with the answer left unstated: if you **could see the** wrongdoers when they see the punishment, you would see **that all power belongs to** God. Although the address is to the Prophet, others are meant by it, since the Prophet certainly knew **that all power belongs to** God, as in Qur’an 2:107, *“Do you not know that to God belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth?”* That reading was preferred because the wrongdoers, once they see the punishment, are already certain **that all power belongs to** God; one says *“if you **could see**”* only to someone who has not seen.

### **WHAT THEY WILL REALIZE**

***“When they see the punishment”*** means when they face it directly. Al-Rabīʿ glosses it: *“If they could face the punishment.”*

The whole sentence is explained in this way: if you **could see**, O Muhammad, those who wronged themselves by taking rivals besides Me, loving them as you love Me, at the moment they face My punishment on the Day of Resurrection, you would know that ***“all power belongs to Allah,”*** not to the rivals and gods, which will be of no use to them there and cannot repel the punishment I bring on them, and you would be certain ***“that Allah is indeed severe in punishment”*** towards those who disbelieve in Me. The next two verses describe that scene.
verses.166:
> ˹Consider the Day˺ when those who misled others will disown their followers—when they face the torment—and the bonds that united them will be cut off

### **MEANING**

The verse describes the moment when the punishment mentioned in the previous verse is seen. Those who were followed in associating partners with God disown those who followed them, when both see God’s punishment, and all the ties that joined them are cut. The verse does not limit this to one kind of leader: everyone who was followed in disbelief and error **will disown** his **followers when they face** God’s punishment in the hereafter.

It also shows who the rivals of the previous verse were. They are the leaders whom people obeyed in disobedience to God, and here those same leaders turn their backs on the people who loved and obeyed them.

### **THE LEADERS AND THE FOLLOWERS**

The phrase ***“those who misled others”*** translates an Arabic expression meaning *“those who were followed.”* Qatādah, in the report through Saʿīd, identifies them as *“the tyrants, the leaders, and the heads in idolatry,”* and **their followers** as *“the weak followers.”* Al-Rabīʿ says: *“The leaders disowned the followers on the Day of Resurrection.”* ʿAṭāʾ, asked by Ibn Jurayj, says: *“Their chiefs, their leaders, and their masters disowned those who followed them.”*

Al-Suddī, in the report through Asbāṭ, gives another view: *“As for those who were followed, they are the devils, who disowned the humans.”*

The verse makes the statement general, so it includes every leader followed in disbelief. But the context shows that those disowning **their followers** are the rivals of the previous verse. Since this verse continues the account of those who take rivals, the view that the followed here are the devils is not correct, and al-Suddī’s other explanation, that the rivals are men obeyed in disobedience, is confirmed.

### **THE BONDS THAT WERE CUT**

***“And the bonds that united them will be cut off”*** connects to the previous verse: God is severe in punishment when the followed disown the followers and when the bonds are cut. The early authorities differed over the bonds. Mujāhid, in several reports, says they are *“the bond of connection that was between them in this world,”* or *“affection.”* Ibn ʿAbbās, through ʿAṭāʾ, also says *“affection.”* Qatādah says they are the bonds of friendship by which they loved one another in this world, which become enmity on the Day of Resurrection, and cites Qur’an 43:67: *“Close friends, on that Day, will be enemies to one another, except the righteous.”* Al-Rabīʿ, in one report, says the bonds are regret.

Ibn ʿAbbās, in the report through al-ʿAwfī’s family, and al-Rabīʿ in another report, say they are *“the positions”* they had in this world. Ibn Jurayj reports from Ibn ʿAbbās that they are *“ties of kinship.”* Al-Suddī says *“the deeds,”* and Ibn Zayd explains that the righteous are given firm ropes of deeds that save them, while the others are given ropes of evil deeds that snap and drop them into the Fire.

### **EVERY BOND**

The word translated ***“bonds”*** means anything one holds on to; its singular is used for a rope, and for anything through which one reaches what one seeks. A road is so called because travelling it reaches a goal, a marriage tie because it creates sanctity, and a means because it brings one to one’s need.

The correct view is that all their bonds are cut. God has told us that disbelievers will curse one another; that Satan will say in Qur’an 14:22, *“I cannot help you, nor can you help me”*; that close friends will be enemies; that they will not help one another; and that kinship will not benefit them, as Abraham disowned his father once it became clear he was an enemy of God. Their deeds will become regrets. Each of these was a means to some aim in this world, and because each was contrary to God’s obedience, God severed its benefit in the hereafter. Friendship, worship of rivals, obedience to devils, kinship, and deeds: none will help them. Whoever claims that only one kind of bond is meant must prove it.
verses.167:
> The ˹misled˺ followers will cry, “If only we could have a second chance, we would disown them as they disowned us.” And so Allah will make them remorseful of their misdeeds. And they will never ˹be able to˺ leave the Fire

### **MEANING**

The followers of the men they had taken as rivals besides God, whom they obeyed in disobedience to their Lord, speak when they see God’s punishment in the hereafter. They wish they could return to the world, so that they might disown their former leaders as those leaders disowned them. As God showed them the punishment they used to deny, He also shows them their evil deeds, which earned them that punishment, as bitter regrets. Yet however intense their remorse, and however much they wish to return and repent, there is no coming out of the Fire into which their disbelief has brought them. Their remorse does not save them; they remain in it forever.

### **THE WISH TO RETURN**

The ***“second chance”*** translates a word meaning a return, from the verb used when a rider turns back and charges again after withdrawing. Al-Akhṭal uses it of horses that *“wheeled back upon Fazārah, returning like a winning arrow.”* Qatādah, in the report through Saʿīd, says it means *“a return to this world for us.”* Al-Rabīʿ says: *“The followers said: **If only we** had a return to the world, **we would disown them as they disowned us**.”*

The verb ***“we would disown”*** is in the subjunctive because it answers the wish. They wish to go back so as to disown those they obeyed in disobedience to God, as their leaders disowned them on seeing the punishment. It is the same wish voiced in Qur’an 6:27: *“**If only we could** be sent back, and not deny the signs of our Lord, and be among the believers.”*

### **DEEDS SHOWN AS REGRETS**

***“And so Allah will make them remorseful of their misdeeds”*** literally says that God shows them their deeds as regrets upon them. Just as He showed them the punishment they denied, He shows them their deeds. The word for regrets is the plural of a word meaning the most intense remorse.

But how can deeds become regrets, when one regrets only the good one failed to do, and disbelievers had no good deeds? Al-Suddī says Paradise will be raised before them, so that they see the homes they would have had there had they obeyed God. It is said to them, *“Those are your homes, had you obeyed God,”* and the homes will then be divided among the believers. Abū al-Zaʿrāʾ reports from ʿAbd Allāh a similar description: every soul will look at a house in Paradise and a house in the Fire, *“and that is the Day of Regret.”* On this view, the deeds they were required to do are called *“their deeds,”* as one calls a meal *“your lunch”* before it is eaten.

Al-Rabīʿ says instead: *“Their evil deeds became regrets for them on the Day of Resurrection.”* Ibn Zayd says these are the evil deeds by which God brought them into the Fire, and cites Qur’an 69:24 for the deeds of the people of Paradise.

The stronger view is the second: God shows the disbelievers their evil deeds as regrets, so that they ask why they did them and did not do otherwise, once they see their recompense. That is what the evident wording indicates. Al-Suddī’s view is possible but far-fetched, and no report establishes it.

### **NO EXIT FROM THE FIRE**

***“And they will never ˹be able to˺ leave the Fire”*** means that, despite their remorse and their wish to return, there is no exit for them from the Fire; they remain in it forever. The verse refutes those who claim that God’s punishment of the disbelievers in the Fire will end and come to nothing. God closes the account of these people by denying that they ever come out of it, without excepting any time, so their punishment has no limit and no end.
verses.168:
> O humanity! Eat from what is lawful and good on the earth and do not follow Satan’s footsteps. He is truly your sworn enemy

### **MEANING**

God addresses all people: eat from the foods He has made lawful for you through His Messenger Muhammad and made good for you. This includes the animals that the idolaters had declared forbidden for themselves, such as the camels they dedicated and set free by custom, which God never forbade, but it excludes what He did forbid and declare impure: carrion, blood, the flesh of swine, and what is dedicated to other than Him.

They are to leave the footsteps of Satan, who ruins them, leads them to destruction, and forbids them their own property; they must neither walk in his ways nor act on them. Satan is an open enemy to them. He made his hostility plain by refusing to prostrate to their father Adam and by deceiving him until he was brought out of the Garden, led into error, and ate from the tree. So they should not take his advice, given his open enmity, but leave what he commands and keep to obedience to God in what He has made lawful and unlawful, rather than what they themselves have forbidden or permitted in obedience to Satan.

### **LAWFUL AND GOOD**

The word ***“lawful”*** means freely permitted. It is a verbal noun from the expression *“this thing has become lawful for you,”* meaning it has become open to you without restriction; the Arabs also say *“it is a release for you,”* meaning unrestricted. The word ***“good”*** means pure, neither impure nor forbidden.

The pairing shows that the verse is not only giving permission; it is also correcting a distortion. The idolaters had made rules of their own about which animals could be eaten and by whom. God declares lawful what He has made lawful and identifies what He has forbidden, so that the line between permitted and forbidden is drawn by Him, not by custom.

### **SATAN’S FOOTSTEPS**

The word translated ***“footsteps”*** is the plural of a word meaning the distance between a walker’s two feet. With a different vowel it means a single step taken. To follow someone’s footsteps means to follow his path and his trace, and the prohibition here is a prohibition against following Satan’s path in whatever he calls to that is contrary to obedience to God.

The early authorities explained the phrase in several ways. Ibn ʿAbbās, in the report through ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah, says: *“His work.”* Mujāhid, through Ibn Abī Najīḥ, says *“his sin”* or *“his sins,”* and Qatādah, through Maʿmar, also says *“his sins.”* Al-Ḍaḥḥāk says: *“The sins of Satan which he commands.”* Al-Suddī, in the report through Asbāṭ, says: *“Obedience to him.”* Abū Mijlaz says: *“They are vows made in disobedience.”*

These explanations are close to one another in meaning, since each points to the prohibition against following Satan in his traces and deeds. But the literal sense of the word is the distance between his feet, and it is then used for all his traces and paths. Abū Mijlaz’s example of vows made in disobedience is one such path; obedience to Satan, his deeds, and his sins are all included.

### **AN OPEN ENEMY**

***“He is truly your sworn enemy”*** uses an Arabic word meaning that his enmity is manifest. The pronoun refers to Satan. His hostility was shown openly at the beginning of human history, when he refused to prostrate to Adam, deceived him, and caused him to be expelled from the Garden after eating from the tree.

The reasoning is simple: someone who has openly declared his enmity is not to be trusted as an adviser. When Satan tells people that something God has permitted is forbidden, or that something God has forbidden is allowed, he is acting as an enemy. The next verse describes exactly what he commands.
verses.169:
> He only incites you to commit evil and indecency, and to claim against Allah what you do not know

### **MEANING**

The verse continues the warning about Satan, the open enemy of the previous verse. All he commands people to do is ***“evil and indecency, and to claim against Allah what you do not know.”*** Evil is sin, so called because it harms the one who commits it; indecency is anything whose mention is shameful and ugly to hear. And the false claim about God refers to what the idolaters forbade of their dedicated and freed livestock, alleging that God had forbidden it.

God tells them that their saying, *“God has forbidden this,”* is a lie that Satan commands them to tell. God has in fact made those animals lawful and good for them and has not forbidden them to eat them. They speak about God without knowing the truth of it, in obedience to Satan, following his footsteps and the traces of their misguided forebears and ignorant fathers, who were ignorant of God and of what He revealed to His Messenger and who had strayed from the truth and its way.

### **EVIL AND INDECENCY**

The word translated ***“evil”*** means sin, like the word for harm. It comes from the verb meaning to grieve or distress: it is what brings grief upon the one who does it. It has been said that the evil mentioned here is disobedience to God in general; if so, God calls it by this name because it brings grief upon the one who does it through its bad outcome for him with God.

The word ***“indecency”*** is a verbal noun of the same pattern as the words for prosperity and adversity. It refers to anything whose mention is felt to be obscene and whose sound is ugly. It has also been said that indecency here means fornication; if so, it is so named because of the ugliness of hearing it and the shame attached to whoever is known to have done it.

Al-Suddī, in the report through Asbāṭ, combines both explanations: *“As for evil, it is disobedience, and as for indecency, it is fornication.”*

### **SPEAKING ABOUT GOD WITHOUT KNOWLEDGE**

The last part of the verse, ***“to claim against Allah what you do not know,”*** is tied directly to the setting. The idolaters forbade certain categories of camels and sheep, dedicating some to their idols and letting others roam free, and claimed that God had forbidden them. God answers this in Qur’an 5:103: *“God has not instituted the dedicated she-camel, nor the freed camel, nor the she-camel that bears in succession, nor the stallion released from work. But those who disbelieve invent lies about God, and most of them are without reason.”*

That verse states plainly what this verse implies: the claim that God forbade these animals was an invention, and it was Satan who commanded it. The idolaters attributed to God something they had no knowledge of, simply because they had inherited it.

### **THE ROOT OF THE ERROR**

The explanation ties this false speech to two sources: obedience to Satan, and imitation of forebears who were themselves misguided. The verse therefore leads directly into the next one, where God describes how these people respond when called to follow what He has revealed: they say they will follow what they found their fathers doing.

The sequence of the passage is coherent. People are told to eat what is lawful and good and not to follow Satan; they are told that Satan commands evil, indecency, and false speech about God; and they are then shown that their attachment to ancestral custom is the channel through which Satan’s commands have reached them.
verses.170:
> When it is said to them, “Follow what Allah has revealed,” they reply, “No! We ˹only˺ follow what we found our forefathers practicing.” ˹Would they still do so,˺ even if their forefathers had ˹absolutely˺ no understanding or guidance

### **MEANING**

When these disbelievers are told to eat what God has made lawful for them, to leave the footsteps and the path of Satan, and to act on what God revealed to His Prophet in His Book, they arrogantly refuse to submit to the truth. They say that they will follow their fathers and keep to what they found them doing, permitting what their fathers permitted and forbidding what they forbade.

God answers with a question: does this hold when their fathers, who died in disbelief, understood nothing of God’s religion, His obligations, His commands, and His prohibitions, so that there was no reason to follow the path they took, and were not guided to anything right, so that no one seeking religion and truth could take them as a model? One follows someone who knows a matter and practises it himself; no one follows an ignorant person in what he is ignorant of, except someone without understanding or discernment.

### **TO WHOM DOES THEM REFER?**

There are two possible readings of the pronoun in ***“When it is said to them.”*** It may refer back to those described in 2:165 as taking rivals besides God: some people take rivals, and when they are told to act on God’s revelation, they refuse. Or it may refer to the ***“humanity”*** addressed in 2:168, *“O humanity, eat from what is lawful and good,”* with the speech turning from direct address to speaking about them in the third person, as in Qur’an 10:22: *“Until, when you are in the ships and they sail with them by a good wind.”*

The second reading is more likely, because this verse follows directly after the address to humanity. It is more natural for it to speak about those just addressed than about the people of 2:165, with other verses and a new subject intervening.

### **THE OCCASION**

It is also reported that the verse came down about certain Jews who said this when invited to Islam. Ibn ʿAbbās, in the report through Ibn Isḥāq from ʿIkrimah or Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, says that the Prophet invited the Jews among the People of the Scripture to Islam, encouraged them towards it, and warned them of God’s punishment. Rāfiʿ ibn Khārijah and Mālik ibn ʿAwf replied: *“Rather, **we will follow what we found our** fathers upon, for they were more knowledgeable and better than us.”* So God revealed this verse about what they said. In another version of the same report the first man is named Abū Rāfiʿ ibn Khārijah.

### **WHAT THEY WERE TOLD AND WHAT THEY ANSWERED**

***“Follow what Allah has revealed”*** means: act on what God revealed in His Book to His Messenger, treating as lawful what it makes lawful and as forbidden what it forbids, and taking it as a guide to follow and a leader whose rulings you obey.

The words ***“what we found”*** translate a verb meaning *“we found.”* A poet uses it in the line, *“I found him unwilling to make amends, and remembering God only a little.”* Qatādah, in the report through Saʿīd, glosses it the same way: *“That is, **what we found our** fathers upon.”* Al-Rabīʿ says the same.

### **THE QUESTION THAT EXPOSES THEM**

The closing question, ***“even if their forefathers had ˹absolutely˺ no understanding or guidance,”*** speaks about the fathers of these disbelievers who had died in disbelief. They understood nothing of God’s religion, so they could not be followed in the path they took, and they were not guided to what is right, so that others could be guided by them.

God’s argument is put to these disbelievers directly: how can you keep to what you found your fathers doing and abandon what your Lord commands, when your fathers knew nothing of God’s command, were not right about anything, and reached no sound guidance? The one who follows should follow someone who knows. To follow the ignorant in their ignorance is the conduct of people without reason, which leads into the next verse’s comparison of the disbelievers to animals that hear a call without understanding it.
verses.171:
> The example of the disbelievers ˹not responding to the Messenger’s warning˺ is like a flock not comprehending the calls and cries of the shepherd. ˹They are wilfully˺ deaf, dumb and blind so they have no understanding

### **MEANING**

The verse gives a likeness for the disbelievers described in the previous verses, who refused to follow what God revealed and clung to the customs of their fathers. When they are admonished, called to the oneness of God, and recited what is in His Book, they take in as little of it as an animal takes in from the shepherd who shouts at it. The animal hears the sound when it is called, but it does not understand what is said to it. In the same way, the disbeliever hears the voice of the one who admonishes him but does not grasp what he is being told, because he does not reflect on it or think about it.

They are therefore deaf to the truth and do not hear it; mute, never speaking the truth, acknowledge what God commanded them to acknowledge, or make clear what He commanded them to make clear about Muhammad; and blind to guidance and the way of truth, never seeing it. Having closed every channel through which understanding could reach them, they do not understand.

### **THE ANIMAL THAT HEARS ONLY A SOUND**

Most of the early authorities explained the likeness in this way. ʿIkrimah, in the report through Simāk, says: *“Like the camel or the donkey: you call it, and it hears the sound but does not understand what you say.”* Ibn ʿAbbās, in the report through al-ʿAwfī’s family, says: *“Like the camel, the donkey, and the sheep: if you say to one of them, Eat, it does not know what you are saying, except that it hears your voice. So too the disbeliever: if you command him to good, forbid him evil, or admonish him, he does not understand what you say, except that he hears your voice.”* Mujāhid says it is *“a likeness God struck for the disbeliever, who hears what is said to him and does not understand, like the animal that hears the shout and does not understand.”* Qatādah says the disbeliever *“does not benefit from what is said to him.”* Al-Rabīʿ and ʿAṭāʾ say the same. Mujāhid adds that the one who shouts is the shepherd, which is how the translation renders it.

Al-Suddī, in the report through Asbāṭ, applies it directly: *“So Muhammad calls one who hears nothing but the murmur of speech,”* and links it to the description of the hypocrites in Qur’an 2:18 as deprived of hearing, speech, and sight.

On this explanation, the sentence is shortened. The full sense is that the likeness of admonishing the disbelievers is like the shepherd’s shouting at his flock; the likeness is attached to the disbelievers and the mention of the admonition is left implied. Or the comparison is with the animal shouted at, with the words grammatically attached to the shepherd, as Arabic often reverses the order when the meaning is clear: al-Nābighah of Dhubyān says, *“I feared until the fear of a mountain goat on the peaks would not exceed my fear,”* meaning the reverse of his literal words.

### **THE ECHO AND THE IDOLS**

Ibn Zayd gave a different explanation: *“The man who shouts in the hollow of the mountains, and a sound answers him there, called the echo. The likeness of these people’s gods for them is like the one who answers him with this sound: it does not benefit him, and he hears nothing but a call and a cry.”* On this view the verse compares the disbelievers calling on their gods, which neither hear nor understand, to a man shouting and hearing only his own echo; or to a shepherd shouting at his flock from where they cannot hear, so that he gains nothing but the effort of calling.

The first explanation, that of Ibn ʿAbbās and those who agreed with him, is the stronger. The verse was revealed about the Jews, who were not idol-worshippers placing hope in images, so it cannot mean the disbelievers calling on their gods. The verses before and after it concern the Jews, and the previous verse is reported to have come down about them. ʿAṭāʾ, in the report through Ibn Jurayj, says: *“They are the Jews about whom God revealed, Those who conceal what God has revealed of the Book and sell it for a small price,”* referring to Qur’an 2:174–175.

The verb for the shepherd’s shouting means to call out to sheep. Al-Akhṭal uses it when he taunts Jarīr: *“Shout at your sheep, O Jarīr, for your soul has only deluded you in solitude.”*

### **DEAF, DUMB, AND BLIND**

***“Deaf, dumb and blind”*** describes these disbelievers. Qatādah, in the report through Saʿīd, explains: *“Deaf to the truth, they neither hear it, benefit from it, nor understand it; blind to the truth and guidance, they do not see it; dumb to the truth, they do not speak it.”* Al-Suddī says simply, *“to the truth.”* Ibn ʿAbbās, in the report through ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah, says: *“They do not hear guidance, do not see it, and do not understand it.”*

The three words are in the nominative because they begin a new sentence, as shown by the clause that follows, ***“so they have no understanding.”*** It is like saying, *“He is deaf, he does not hear; he is dumb, he does not speak.”* The final clause gathers the three into one result: having refused to hear, speak, or see the truth, they cannot understand it.
verses.172:
> O believers! Eat from the good things We have provided for you. And give thanks to Allah if you ˹truly˺ worship Him ˹alone˺

### **MEANING**

The address turns from the disbelievers to the believers: those who have accepted God and His Messenger as true, acknowledged that they are God’s servants, and submitted to Him in obedience.

They are told to eat from the lawful provision that God has made permissible for them, which has become good for them through His permitting it. This includes foods and drinks that they used to forbid themselves although God had not forbidden them. They are also told to thank God, praising Him as He deserves for the blessings He has provided and made good for them. And they are told that if they truly submit to His command, listening and obeying, they should eat what He has permitted and made good, and leave Satan’s footsteps in forbidding it.

### **THE GOOD THINGS THEY HAD FORBIDDEN**

The opening call, ***“O believers,”*** is glossed by al-Ḍaḥḥāk, in the report through Juwaybir, as *“those who have affirmed the truth.”* ***“The good things We have provided for you”*** refers to the lawful provision God made permissible. The word *“good”* here is explained by what precedes it: a thing is good because God has made it lawful. Earlier in the passage, the idolaters were described as forbidding themselves certain livestock, such as the camels they dedicated and set free, and claiming that God had forbidden them. This verse urges the believers to eat what God permitted and warns them against believing such things to be forbidden.

The reason is the same as in Qur’an 2:168. Their forbidding of these foods before Islam was obedience to Satan and imitation of those among their fathers and forebears who disbelieved in God. To eat what God has made lawful is therefore not only a matter of diet; it is a rejection of rules that Satan had introduced through ancestral custom, and an acknowledgment that only God decides what is lawful.

The address now goes to the believers rather than to humanity in general. In 2:168, all people were told to eat what is lawful and good; here, those who believe are told the same, with a further command attached: be thankful.

### **GIVING THANKS**

***“And give thanks to Allah”*** means to praise God as He deserves for the blessings He has given and made good. Thankfulness, as explained in 2:152, is praise for a good done, and its opposite is the covering over of a favour. The verse attaches thanks to provision: the believer who eats from what God has provided acknowledges its source by thanking Him.

The command also draws a contrast with the disbelievers described in the previous verses. They followed their fathers in forbidding what God had permitted, which was a form of ingratitude, rejecting His provision. The believers are told to accept His provision and thank Him for it.

### **IF YOU TRULY WORSHIP HIM ALONE**

The condition ***“if you ˹truly˺ worship Him ˹alone˺”*** is explained as: if you are obedient to His command, listening and obeying, then eat what He has permitted and made good for you and leave the footsteps of Satan in forbidding it. Worship here means obedience, and the proof of obedience is to accept what God has permitted without adding prohibitions of one’s own.

The verse thus links three things: eating the lawful, thanking God for it, and worshipping none but Him. To forbid oneself what God has permitted, in obedience to custom, is to give that custom a share of the authority that belongs to God. The next verse sets out exactly what God has forbidden, so that the believers know where the limits lie: carrion, blood, swine, and what is dedicated to other than God.
verses.173:
> He has only forbidden you ˹to eat˺ carrion, blood, swine, and what is slaughtered in the name of any other than Allah. But if someone is compelled by necessity—neither driven by desire nor exceeding immediate need—they will not be sinful. Surely Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful

### **MEANING**

Having told the believers to eat from the good things He provided, God now defines the limits. Do not forbid yourselves what I have not forbidden you, such as the dedicated and freed livestock; eat them, for I have forbidden you nothing except ***“carrion, blood, swine, and what is slaughtered in the name of any other than Allah.”*** The restrictive opening means: He has forbidden you only these.

Then comes an exception for necessity. Whoever is driven by the extremity of hunger to eat any of these forbidden things, provided he is neither seeking the forbidden nor going beyond what he needs, while he has no lawful alternative, bears no sin in eating it. God is forgiving towards the believers if they obey Him in their Islam by avoiding what He forbade and abandoning Satan’s footsteps in what they used to forbid before Islam. He pardons the errors and sins of their past in this matter and does not punish them for it, and He is merciful to them if they obey Him.

### **WHAT IS FORBIDDEN**

The word ***“only”*** renders a single particle that restricts the sentence, which is why the forbidden things stand in the accusative. Someone read them in the nominative, taking the particle as two words, *“what God has forbidden you is carrion…”*; that has a sense in Arabic, but it is not acceptable to recite it, since the authoritative reciters agree on the other reading.

The word for ***“carrion”*** is read with the middle letter either lightened or doubled. Both are well-known usages with the same meaning, as a poet joins them in one line: *“The one who died and found rest is not dead; the dead one is only the dead among the living.”*

***“What is slaughtered in the name of any other than Allah”*** literally reads *“what has been raised in voice for one besides God.”* It refers to what was slaughtered for gods and idols with a name besides God’s pronounced over it, or intended for idols. When people slaughtered offerings to their gods, they named those gods aloud, and the expression came to be used of every slaughterer, whether or not he named aloud. From the same root comes the pilgrim’s raised voice in the talbiyah, the cry of a newborn, and the sound of falling rain.

Qatādah, Mujāhid, and ʿAṭāʾ explain it as *“what was slaughtered for one besides God.”* Ibn ʿAbbās says *“what was dedicated to the false gods,”* meaning what disbelievers, apart from Jews and Christians, slaughtered for someone besides God. Al-Rabīʿ says it is *“what had a name besides God’s mentioned over it,”* and Ibn Zayd explains that people would say over the animal *“in the name of so-and-so,”* as you say *“in the name of God.”* ʿUqbah ibn Muslim and Qays ibn Rāfiʿ held lawful what the People of the Scripture slaughtered for church feasts, since it is the food of the People of the Scripture, and said the phrase refers to the Magians, idol-worshippers, and polytheists.

### **COMPELLED BY NECESSITY**

***“If someone is compelled by necessity”*** refers to anyone afflicted by a hunger that forces him towards these forbidden things. Mujāhid, in one report through Sālim al-Afṭas, adds the case of compulsion: *“The man whom the enemy captures and calls to disobedience to God.”* Such a person, eating with the conditions stated, bears no consequence for eating it and no blame.

### **NEITHER SEEKING NOR EXCEEDING**

The early authorities differed over ***“neither driven by desire nor exceeding immediate need.”*** Mujāhid, in several reports, and Saʿīd ibn Jubayr explained the two words as rebellion and aggression: *“not one who cuts off the road, nor one who leaves the community, nor one who goes out in disobedience to God; such a one has the concession.”* Saʿīd says the highway robber *“has no concession, if he is hungry, to eat dead meat.”*

Others explained them as seeking the forbidden and exceeding the permitted. Qatādah says: *“Not seeking it in his eating, and not transgressing by passing from the lawful to the forbidden while he has an alternative.”* Al-Ḥasan says: *“Not seeking it, and not transgressing by eating it while he can do without it.”* Al-Rabīʿ cites Qur’an 23:7: *“whoever seeks beyond that, they are the transgressors.”* Ibn Zayd says both words mean the same thing: eating the forbidden while leaving the lawful that one has. Al-Suddī says the first means satisfying one’s appetite and the second eating to one’s fill, and that one should eat only enough to keep oneself alive.

The strongest view is that the one compelled may eat if he is not seeking the forbidden and not exceeding in eating, while he has no lawful alternative. God has never permitted anyone to kill himself. The rebel and highway robber have done wrong, but that does not permit them to add the further sin of starving themselves to death; what is required of them is to repent and return to obedience. The view that limits exceeding to eating one’s fill names only one form of exceeding, while God did not specify any, so every forbidden form is included.

### **FORGIVING AND MERCIFUL**

***“Surely Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful”*** looks back over the whole passage. The believers had been forbidding themselves things God never forbade, in obedience to Satan. God forgives what they did in this before Islam, if they now avoid what He has forbidden and stop following Satan’s footsteps, and He is merciful to them in their obedience.
verses.174:
> Indeed, those who hide Allah’s revelations, trading them for a fleeting gain consume nothing but fire into their bellies. Allah will neither speak to them on the Day of Judgment, nor will He purify them. And they will suffer a painful punishment

### **MEANING**

The verse speaks of the rabbis of the Jews who concealed from people the matter of Muhammad and his prophethood, although they found him written in their Torah, in return for bribes given to them for doing so. They took a small price, a little of the goods of this world, for distorting God’s Book, interpreting it wrongly, and hiding the truth in it.

What they consume through those bribes and payments is in reality nothing but what brings them into the Fire and makes them burn in it. On the Day of Resurrection God will not address them with what they love and desire, though He will address them with what they dislike. He will not cleanse them from the filth of their sins and disbelief, and a punishment that causes pain awaits them.

### **WHO CONCEALED WHAT**

The early authorities identify these people clearly. Qatādah, in the report through Saʿīd, says: *“They are the People of the Scripture; they concealed what God revealed to them and made clear to them of the truth and guidance about the sending of Muhammad and his affair.”* Al-Rabīʿ says they concealed *“the truth, Islam, and the matter of Muhammad.”* Al-Suddī says: *“These are the Jews; they concealed the name of Muhammad.”* ʿIkrimah, in the report through Ibn Jurayj, says that this verse and Qur’an 3:77, *“Those who sell the covenant of God and their oaths for a small price,”* both came down about the Jews.

### **A SMALL PRICE**

The phrase rendered ***“trading them for a fleeting gain”*** literally reads *“and they buy with it a small price,”* meaning they acquire it. The pronoun refers to the concealment: they gained through their concealment of Muhammad’s prophethood a small price. What they were given for distorting God’s Book and hiding the truth was a trifle of worldly goods. Al-Suddī explains: *“They concealed the name of Muhammad and took a small gain for it; that is the small price.”* The meaning of such buying was explained earlier in the surah.

### **EATING FIRE**

***“Consume nothing but fire into their bellies”*** means that by eating the bribes and payments they took, they eat nothing but what will bring them into the Fire and burn them in it. The same expression appears in Qur’an 4:10: *“Those who consume the wealth of orphans unjustly are only consuming **fire into their bellies**, and soon they burn in a blaze.”* In both places, the Fire stands for what leads to it, and the listener understands the meaning without its being stated. Al-Rabīʿ glosses it: *“What they took as payment for it.”*

Why mention the belly, when eating takes place nowhere else? The Arabs say, *“I was hungry in other than my belly”* and *“I was full in other than my belly,”* so the phrase specifies, much as one says, *“So-and-so did this himself.”*

### **NO SPEECH, NO PURIFICATION**

***“Allah will neither speak to them on the Day of Judgment”*** means He will not address them with what they love and desire. He will address them with what grieves them, for He has told us that when they say, *“Our Lord, bring us out of it, and if we return we will indeed be wrongdoers,”* He will answer, *“Remain despised in it, and do not speak to Me,”* as in Qur’an 23:107–108.

***“Nor will He purify them”*** means He will not cleanse them from the filth of their sins and disbelief. ***“And they will suffer a painful punishment”*** means a punishment that causes pain. Each of these is the reverse of what they hoped to gain: they sold God’s revelation for a little worldly profit and lost God’s speech, His purification, and His mercy.
verses.175:
> They are the ones who trade guidance for misguidance and forgiveness for punishment. How persistent are they in pursuit of the Fire

### **MEANING**

The verse continues the description of those who concealed what God revealed about Muhammad for a small price. It is they who took error and left guidance, and who took what brings God’s punishment upon them on the Day of Resurrection and left what would have brought them His forgiveness and good pleasure. The verse names the punishment and the forgiveness themselves, rather than the deeds that lead to each, because the listener understands what is meant.

The verse then expresses astonishment at them: how daring they are in doing the deeds that bring them close to the Fire, and how fully they act as the people of the Fire act. God makes His creation marvel at these people, who knowingly concealed the truth about Muhammad and took a little unlawful gain and bribes for it, although they knew that this would bring on them God’s anger and His painful punishment.

### **AN EXCHANGE OF GUIDANCE FOR ERROR**

The phrase ***“trade guidance for misguidance”*** uses the language of buying and selling that the surah applied earlier to the hypocrites, and its meaning was explained there with the differing views on it. Here it is applied to the concealers among the People of the Scripture: they had guidance in their hands, the description of Muhammad in their own Book, and gave it up in exchange for error.

The second pair, ***“forgiveness for punishment,”*** carries the same exchange into the hereafter. By concealing the truth, they exchanged the forgiveness they could have earned by making it known for the punishment that their concealment earns. The punishment and forgiveness stand for their causes, as Arabic often names a result in place of the deed that produces it.

### **HOW PERSISTENT ARE THEY**

The closing words literally say, *“How patient they are upon the Fire!”* The early authorities differed over their meaning. Qatādah, in the report through Saʿīd, says: *“How daring they are in the deeds that bring them close to the Fire.”* Al-Ḥasan says: *“By God, they have no patience for it, but how daring they are towards the Fire!”* Mujāhid or Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, in a report through Ḥammād, says simply: *“How daring they are.”* Al-Rabīʿ says: *“How daring and how patient they are upon the Fire.”* Mujāhid, through Ibn Abī Najīḥ, gives another explanation: *“How much they work falsehood,”* and in the report through Ibn ʿUyaynah, *“How much they do the deeds of the people of the Fire!”*

The translation’s ***“How persistent are they in pursuit of the Fire”*** conveys this sense of a people pressing on towards the Fire with their deeds.

### **QUESTION OR EXCLAMATION?**

The authorities also differed over whether the word *“how”* is a question or an exclamation. Al-Suddī says: *“This is in the form of a question: what has made them so patient upon the Fire?”* ʿAṭāʾ says: *“What makes them patient upon the Fire, when they left the truth and followed falsehood?”* Abū Bakr ibn ʿAyyāsh says it is a question, arguing that if it meant patience the vowel would be different, and that one says to a man, *“What has made you patient?”* meaning, what has done this to you? Ibn Zayd says: *“This is a question: what is it that has made them patient upon the Fire, so that it emboldened them and they did this?”* On this reading, the sense is: what has made them so patient with the Fire, when no one can endure the Fire, that they exchanged God’s forgiveness for it?

Others, including Mujāhid in one report, al-Ḥasan, and Qatādah, took it as an exclamation: how great is their daring towards the Fire, through doing the deeds of its people! This is like Qur’an 80:17, *“Perish man! How ungrateful he is!”*, which expresses astonishment at his disbelief in the One who created and formed him.

The strongest view is that it means: how daring they are towards the punishment of the Fire, and how much they do the deeds of its people. The Arabs are heard to say, *“How patient so-and-so is against God!”* meaning how daring he is against God. The verse mentions the Fire while meaning its punishment, as one says, *“How like Ḥātim your generosity is,”* meaning like Ḥātim’s generosity.
verses.176:
> That is because Allah has revealed the Book in truth. And surely those who differ regarding it are totally engrossed in opposition

### **MEANING**

The verse gives the reason behind everything described in the preceding passage. The concealment practised by the rabbis of the Jews, their hiding of what they knew about Muhammad and his prophethood for a worthless worldly gain, and their opposition to God’s command, together with God’s withholding of His speech and purification from them and the painful punishment He has prepared for them, are all because He sent down His Book with the truth, while they disbelieved in it and differed about it.

The verse then describes those who differed over the Book, the Jews and the Christians, as being in a dispute and a separation from the truth that is far from right guidance and correctness.

### **WHAT THAT REFERS TO**

The early authorities differed over what ***“That”*** points to. Some said it refers to the daring of these people in facing the punishment of the Fire by opposing God’s command and concealing what He commanded them to make clear. This is because God sent down the Book with the truth, and part of that truth is His statement about such people in Qur’an 2:6–7: *“As for those who disbelieve, it is the same to them whether you warn them or do not warn them; they will not believe. God has set a seal on their hearts and on their hearing, and over their eyes is a covering.”* Since God has told us they will not believe, nothing comes from them but exchanging guidance for error.

Others said the meaning is that this punishment is known to be theirs because God sent down the Book with the truth, and He has stated in many places that the Fire is for the disbelievers; the predicate of *“that”* is understood. A third view takes *“that”* as referring to the punishment: We did that to them because God sent down the Book with the truth, yet they disbelieved in it.

The most fitting view is that *“that”* points to everything contained in the passage from Qur’an 2:174 onwards: the account of what the rabbis did, and the punishment God prepared for them. God says in effect: what these rabbis did, concealing what they knew of Muhammad for worldly gain and opposing My command, and what I do to them, leaving them unpurified and unaddressed and preparing a painful punishment for them, is because I sent down My Book with the truth, yet they disbelieved in it and differed about it. The words *“and they disbelieved in it and differed about it”* are left unstated because the rest of the sentence points to them.

### **THOSE WHO DIFFERED**

***“Those who differ regarding it”*** are the Jews and the Christians. They differed over God’s Book: the Jews disbelieved in what God related in it about Jesus son of Mary and his mother, while the Christians accepted some of it and rejected some, and both disbelieved in what God revealed in it commanding them to believe in Muhammad.

Al-Suddī, in the report through Asbāṭ, says: *“They are the Jews and the Christians,”* and adds: *“They are in a far-reaching enmity.”*

### **TOTALLY ENGROSSED IN OPPOSITION**

The phrase ***“totally engrossed in opposition”*** translates an Arabic expression meaning *“in a far-reaching dispute.”* God tells His Prophet that those who differed over what He revealed to him are in contention with and separation from the truth, far from right guidance and correctness. The word for opposition was explained earlier in the surah, where it describes the People of the Scripture who turn away from faith, as in Qur’an 2:137: *“If they believe as you believe, they are guided; but if they turn away, they are only in opposition.”*

The verse thus closes the long passage on concealment that began at 2:159. Those who hid the clear proofs, exchanged guidance for error, and ate fire for a small price did so in the face of a Book revealed in truth; their dispute over it has carried them far from the truth. The next verse turns from this contention to a definition of what true righteousness is.
verses.177:
> Righteousness is not in turning your faces towards the east or the west. Rather, the righteous are those who believe in Allah, the Last Day, the angels, the Books, and the prophets; who give charity out of their cherished wealth to relatives, orphans, the poor, ˹needy˺ travellers, beggars, and for freeing captives; who establish prayer, pay alms-tax, and keep the pledges they make; and who are patient in times of suffering, adversity, and in ˹the heat of˺ battle. It is they who are true ˹in faith˺, and it is they who are mindful ˹of Allah˺

### **MEANING**

The verse follows the long rebuke of the Jews and Christians and turns to a claim they made about righteousness. Righteousness, O Jews and Christians, does not consist in some of you facing the east and others the west. True righteousness, instead, is the righteousness of one who believes in God, ***“the Last Day, the angels, the Books, and the prophets.”*** It belongs to one who gives his wealth while he loves it, is eager to keep it, and holds it tightly, to his relatives, joining the ties of kinship, and to **orphans, the poor**, the traveller, those who ask, and the freeing of slaves. It belongs to one who keeps up the prayer with its proper limits and pays the obligatory alms as God prescribed, to those who fulfil their covenants and do not break them, and to those who restrain themselves from what God dislikes in poverty, illness, and **the heat of battle**, holding themselves to His obedience.

Those who do these things are the ones who were true to God in their faith, confirming their words by their deeds, not those who turn their faces east or west while opposing God, breaking His covenant, concealing what He commanded them to make clear, and denying His messengers. And they are the ones who guard themselves against God’s punishment, avoiding disobedience, staying within His limits, and fulfilling His obligations.

### **TO WHOM THE VERSE SPEAKS**

The early authorities offered two explanations. Ibn ʿAbbās, in the report through al-ʿAwfī’s family, says the verse refers to prayer: *“**Righteousness is not** that you pray and do no deeds.”* He says this was after the Prophet moved from Mecca to Medina, when the obligations were revealed and the limits set. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk says the same. Mujāhid says: *“Righteousness is what is established in the hearts of obedience to God.”*

Qatādah and al-Rabīʿ say: *“The Jews used to pray towards the west and the Christians facing the east, so this came down.”* Qatādah adds that a man asked the Prophet about righteousness, and this verse was revealed and recited to him; and that before the obligations were revealed, a man who testified that there is no god but God and that Muhammad is His servant and messenger and died on that was hoped for good.

The second explanation is preferable, because the preceding verses rebuke the Jews and Christians and describe the punishment prepared for them, and this verse continues that context.

How can righteousness, which is an act, be identified with ***“those who believe,”*** which refers to persons? The sense is *“the righteousness of one who believes,”* with the person standing in place of his act, as the Arabs say, *“Generosity is Ḥātim,”* meaning Ḥātim’s generosity, or as in Qur’an 12:82, *“Ask the town,”* meaning its people. It may also mean *“the righteous person is one who believes,”* with the verbal noun standing for the adjective, which is how the translation renders it.

### **WEALTH GIVEN WHILE LOVED**

***“Out of their cherished wealth”*** means giving it while loving it and being reluctant to part with it. ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd, in several reports through Murrah, explains: *“He gives it while he is healthy and tight-fisted, hoping to live and fearing poverty.”*

Al-Shaʿbī, asked whether a man owes anything from his wealth besides the alms-tax, said yes and recited this verse.
