He related from Fāṭimah bint Qays that she told the Prophet she had seventy mithqāls of gold, and he said, *“Put it among your relatives.”* ʿAṭāʾ told a Bedouin that besides the alms on his camels he owed *“lending the bucket, lending the stallion, and the milking.”* Al-Suddī says this is a duty on wealth apart from the alms-tax.

***“Relatives”*** means the giver’s own kin, as shown by the instruction to Fāṭimah and by the Prophet’s answer when asked which charity is best: *“The effort of one with little, given to a relative who bears hostility.”* ***“Travellers”*** translates *“the son of the road,”* one who passes by. Qatādah says it is the guest, citing the Prophet’s saying that hospitality is three nights and anything after is charity. Abū Jaʿfar, Mujāhid, and Qatādah in another report say it is *“the one who passes you while travelling.”* He is called the son of the road because he keeps to it, as a water bird is called the son of water. ***“Beggars”*** are those who ask for food; ʿIkrimah says, *“the one who asks you.”* ***“Freeing captives”*** refers to slaves working to buy their freedom by paying the agreed sum to their masters.

### **PRAYER, ALMS, AND COVENANTS**

***“Who establish prayer”*** means keep up its practice with its limits, and ***“pay alms-tax”*** means pay it as God prescribed. Some held that because the alms-tax is mentioned after the giving of wealth, the first giving must be a separate duty, for repetition without meaning cannot be ascribed to God. Others held the first giving is the alms-tax itself, named first to show where it should go and then named directly.

***“Keep the pledges they make”*** means they do not break God’s covenant after making it. Al-Rabīʿ says: *“Whoever gives the covenant of God and then breaks it, God takes vengeance on him; and whoever is given the protection of the Prophet and betrays it, the Prophet will be his opponent on the Day of Resurrection.”*

### **PATIENT IN HARDSHIP AND BATTLE**

***“Patient in times of suffering, adversity”*** means restraining themselves from what God dislikes in hardship. Ibn Masʿūd, in reports through Murrah, says: *“As for suffering, it is poverty, and adversity is sickness.”* Qatādah, al-Rabīʿ, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, and Ibn Jurayj explain them similarly, Qatādah citing Job’s words in Qur’an 21:83, *“Harm has touched me.”* ***“In ˹the heat of˺ battle”*** means the time of fighting; Ibn Masʿūd, Mujāhid, Qatādah, al-Rabīʿ, and al-Ḍaḥḥāk all say *“fighting”* or *“meeting the enemy.”*

The word for *“the patient”* stands in the accusative although it describes the same believer, as praise: Arabic sometimes shifts case to single out a quality in a long description. One view joined it to *“those who ask,”* as recipients of wealth, but that would repeat the poor already mentioned, which cannot be meant.

### **TRUE AND MINDFUL**

***“It is they who are true ˹in faith˺”*** means they were truthful to God and proved their words by deeds. Al-Rabīʿ says: *“They spoke the words of faith, and its reality was action.”* He adds that al-Ḥasan used to say: *“This is the speech of faith, and its reality is action; if there is no action with the speech, it is nothing.”* ***“It is they who are mindful ˹of Allah˺”*** describes those who fear His punishment, avoid disobeying Him, and carry out what He has required.
verses.178:
> O believers! ˹The law of˺ retaliation is set for you in cases of murder—a free man for a free man, a slave for a slave, and a female for a female. But if the offender is pardoned by the victim’s guardian, then blood-money should be decided fairly and payment should be made courteously. This is a concession and a mercy from your Lord. But whoever transgresses after that will suffer a painful punishment

### **MEANING**

God tells the believers that retaliation in cases of killing has been prescribed for them. This does not mean that the guardian of a murdered person is obliged to exact retaliation; he may do so, or pardon, or accept blood-money. What is binding is the limit: when **a free man** kills **a free man**, the killer’s life answers for the victim’s, and retaliation is taken from him alone. It is forbidden to go beyond the killer to anyone else who did not kill.

If the guardian forgoes his right to retaliation in return for blood-money, then he should pursue his claim fairly, without demanding more than God has given him, and the killer should pay what he owes in good manner, without reducing it or forcing the guardian to chase him for it. This permission, to pardon a killer in return for blood-money that becomes the guardian’s property, is a lightening from God of what He had made heavy on earlier communities, and a mercy to this community. Whoever goes beyond it after accepting the blood-money, by killing the killer, will have **a painful punishment**.

### **WHAT PRESCRIBED MEANS**

The word translated ***“is set for you”*** means *“is prescribed for you.”* Some ask how that can be, since the word normally means *“written.”* The Arabs use it for obligation, as a poet says, *“Killing and fighting are prescribed for us, and for the chaste women the trailing of skirts.”* Al-Nābighah of Banū Jaʿdah says, *“O my cousin, God’s decree has taken me from you.”* Yet the sense of writing remains, for God has written everything He has prescribed in the Preserved Tablet, as in Qur’an 85:21–22, *“It is a glorious Qur’an, in a Preserved Tablet.”*

***“Retaliation”*** comes from settling one claim against another: killing a killer is retaliation because the same is done to him as he did, even though one act was aggression and the other a right.

If retaliation were an obligation like prayer that could not be left, the following words, ***“But if the offender is pardoned,”*** would have no meaning, since there is no pardon after retaliation. What is prescribed, then, is the limit: that no one but the killer be killed for the victim.

### **FREE FOR FREE, FEMALE FOR FEMALE**

Must **a free man** be avenged only on **a free man**, and a woman only on a woman? No: **a free man** may be killed for a slave and a man for a woman, by Qur’an 17:33, *“Whoever is killed unjustly, We have given his heir authority,”* and by the widely transmitted saying of the Prophet, *“The lives of the Muslims are equal.”*

The early authorities explained the verse in several ways. Al-Shaʿbī and Qatādah said it came down about tribes who, when a slave of theirs was killed, insisted on killing **a free man for** him, and when a woman of theirs was killed by a woman, insisted on killing a man, out of pride. Qatādah says: *“The people of the time of ignorance had transgression and obedience to Satan in them.”* God told them the slave answers for the slave and the female for the female, forbidding them to go beyond the killer. Mujāhid and ʿAṭāʾ held that a man and a woman are equal in this.

Al-Suddī and Abū Mālik said it came down about two groups who fought in the Prophet’s time, and the Prophet reconciled them by setting the blood-money of their slain free men, slaves, and women against one another. A report from ʿAlī, through al-Rabīʿ, said that if a man is killed for a woman, her guardians pay half the blood-money to his heirs. Ibn ʿAbbās, through ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah, said men were not killed for women until God revealed Qur’an 5:45, *“a life for a life,”* making free men and women equal in retaliation.

The sound view is that the verse forbids exceeding the killer. Widely transmitted reports establish that **a free man** is killed for a free woman, and since all agree that no one may sell a limb of his body for compensation, a whole life cannot be taken in return for paying the difference in blood-money. The view that the verse prescribes offsetting one group’s blood-money against another’s also fails, because all agree that such offsetting is optional, while the verse speaks of something prescribed.

### **PARDON, FAIRNESS, AND COURTESY**

The clause rendered ***“if the offender is pardoned by the victim’s guardian”*** literally says, *“whoever is pardoned something by his brother.”* Ibn ʿAbbās, in the report through Mujāhid, says: *“The pardon is that he accepts blood-money in a case of deliberate killing,”* and adds that the claimant must pursue it fairly and the other must pay in good manner. Mujāhid, al-Shaʿbī, Qatādah, al-Rabīʿ, ʿAṭāʾ, and al-Ḥasan say the same; al-Ḥasan says, *“Taking the blood-money is a fine pardon.”* Al-Suddī, consistent with his earlier view, says it means that something remains due to him from his brother’s blood-money or from a wound’s compensation.

***“Decided fairly”*** means pursuing only what God has made due, without adding to it. Qatādah reports the Prophet as saying that whoever demands or takes an extra camel in blood-money follows the ways of the time of ignorance. ***“Payment should be made courteously”*** means paying it in full without delay or reduction. The phrase is in the nominative, which is the more eloquent form for a general ruling, like Qur’an 2:229, *“then keeping on fair terms or releasing with kindness.”*

### **A LIGHTENING AND A MERCY**

***“This is a concession and a mercy from your Lord”*** means that permitting pardon in return for blood-money is a lightening of what was heavy on earlier nations. Ibn ʿAbbās says: *“Among the Children of Israel there was retaliation but no blood-money,”* and God lightened this for the community of Muhammad. Qatādah says: *“The people of the Torah had only retaliation or pardon, and the people of the Gospel only pardon; God gave this community retaliation, pardon, and blood-money if they wish.”*

### **TRANSGRESSING AFTER THAT**

***“Whoever transgresses after that”*** means killing the killer after accepting blood-money. Mujāhid, Qatādah, al-Rabīʿ, al-Suddī, Ibn ʿAbbās, and Ibn Zayd all explain it so. Qatādah reports the Prophet as saying, *“I will not spare a man who kills after taking blood-money.”* Al-Ḍaḥḥāk, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, and ʿIkrimah say the ***“painful punishment”*** is that he is killed. Ibn Jurayj held that the ruler punishes him as he sees fit, and al-Ḥasan that the blood-money is taken back. The stronger view is that he is killed: the heir of anyone killed unjustly has authority over the killer, and whoever is punished in this world for a sin is not pursued for it in the next. Ibn Jurayj’s view contradicts the Book and the consensus of scholars.
verses.179:
> There is ˹security of˺ life for you in ˹the law of˺ retaliation, O people of reason, so that you may become mindful ˹of Allah˺

### **MEANING**

The verse explains the wisdom of the law set out in the previous verse. In what God has prescribed for the believers, and made due from some of them to others, of retaliation for lives, wounds, and injuries, there is something that restrains them from killing one another and holds them back from one another. Because of it they live, and so God’s ruling among them by retaliation is, in effect, life for them.

The address is to those who possess understanding, because it is they who grasp God’s command and prohibition and reflect on His signs and proofs. The purpose is that they may guard themselves: fearing retaliation, they refrain from killing.

The verse therefore presents a law that might seem to be only about death as a law that preserves life. The one who knows that he will be killed if he kills is deterred from killing, and so both the intended victim and the would-be killer remain alive.

### **RETALIATION AS A DETERRENT**

Most of the early authorities explained it in this way. Mujāhid, in several reports through Ibn Abī Najīḥ, glosses it with two words: *“an exemplary punishment, a restraining.”* Qatādah, in the report through Saʿīd, says: *“God made this retaliation life, and an exemplary punishment and admonition for the foolish and ignorant among people. How many a man has intended a calamity, and but for fear of retaliation would have fallen into it; but God has held them back from one another by retaliation.”* He adds a general principle: *“God never commanded anything except that it is a matter of benefit in this world and the next, and never forbade anything except that it is a matter of corruption in this world and in religion, and God knows best what sets His creation right.”*

Qatādah, in the report through Maʿmar, says: *“God has put life in retaliation: when the unjust aggressor remembers it, he refrains from killing.”* Al-Rabīʿ says almost the same: *“How many a man has intended a calamity and was prevented by fear of retaliation from falling into it!”* Ibn Jurayj glosses ***“life”*** as *“protection,”* and Abū Ṣāliḥ as *“survival.”*

Ibn Zayd describes the reasoning from the side of the potential victim: *“Life means survival. If this man fears that he will be killed for me, he refrains from me. Perhaps he is an enemy of mine who wants to kill me; then he remembers that he will be killed in retaliation, and fears to be killed for me, so he refrains because of the retaliation he feared. But for that, he would have killed this man.”*

### **ONLY THE KILLER IS KILLED**

Al-Suddī, in the report through Asbāṭ, gave a different emphasis: *“Survival: no one is killed except the killer, for his crime.”* On this view, the life in retaliation is the survival of others, since under God’s ruling no one is killed for a murdered person except his killer. Before Islam, people would kill a man for a woman and a free man for a slave, and the killing would spread beyond the one who had done it.

This explanation links the verse directly to the previous one, where the law forbade going beyond the killer. Both views see life in retaliation: in the first, because the threat of retaliation deters killing; in the second, because the restriction of retaliation to the killer prevents the cycle of revenge from consuming the innocent.

### **PEOPLE OF REASON**

***“O people of reason”*** addresses those with intellects; the word is the plural of a word meaning the core or kernel of a thing, and so the mind. God singles them out because they understand His command and prohibition and reflect on His signs. A person without understanding sees only the death in retaliation; a person of understanding sees the lives it saves.

***“So that you may become mindful ˹of Allah˺”*** is explained as: that you may guard yourselves against retaliation and so refrain from killing. Ibn Zayd says: *“Perhaps you will guard yourself against killing him, lest you be killed for him.”* The fear that the law produces is thus itself the means by which it gives life.
verses.180:
> It is prescribed that when death approaches any of you—if they leave something of value—a will should be made in favour of parents and immediate family with fairness. ˹This is˺ an obligation on those who are mindful ˹of Allah˺

### **MEANING**

The verse prescribes a bequest for the believers. **When death approaches** one of them and he leaves wealth, he is to make a bequest for his parents and close relatives who do not inherit from him, with fairness, meaning within what God has permitted in bequests: not exceeding a third of the estate and not intending to wrong the heirs. This is made an obligation, a binding right upon whoever fears God and obeys Him.

The verse follows the law of retaliation with another law concerning life and death: having spoken of the protection of life, it now speaks of what a believer owes his family when his own life is ending.

### **IS THE BEQUEST OBLIGATORY?**

Is it obligatory for a man with wealth to make a bequest for parents and relatives who do not inherit from him, so that he commits a fault if he neglects it? The answer given is yes, because the verse says ***“It is prescribed,”*** just as Qur’an 2:183 says, *“Fasting is prescribed for you,”* and all agree that one who is able to fast and abandons it has neglected an obligation.

Al-Ḍaḥḥāk says: *“Whoever dies without making a bequest for his relatives has sealed his deeds with disobedience.”* Masrūq told a dying man who was making improper bequests: *“God has divided among you and divided well; whoever turns from God’s judgment to his own opinion, God leads him astray. Make a bequest for your relative who does not inherit from you, then leave the wealth as God divided it.”* Abū Mijlaz and Lāḥiq ibn Ḥumayd, asked whether a bequest is due from every Muslim, said it is due from whoever leaves wealth. Al-Ḥasan, Jābir ibn Zayd, and Ṭāwūs held that if a man bequeaths to strangers while his needy relatives are left out, part or all of the bequest is redirected to the relatives.

### **ABROGATED OR STILL IN FORCE?**

Scholars differed over whether the verse is abrogated. Some held that none of it is abrogated: its wording is general, but it means only the parents and relatives who do not inherit.

Others held that it was once in force for all of them and that the verses of inheritance abrogated it for parents and relatives who inherit, while the obligation remained for relatives who do not. Qatādah says the bequest was for parents and relatives, then each parent was given a fixed share, *“so the bequest became for relatives who do not inherit, and there is no bequest for an heir.”* Ibn ʿAbbās, in the report through ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah, says God then revealed Qur’an 4:11, *“For each of his parents a sixth of what he leaves,”* and confirmed the bequest for relatives within a third of the estate. Al-Rabīʿ, Ṭāwūs, and al-Ḥasan say the same.

Others held that it is entirely abrogated by the shares of inheritance. Ibn Zayd says: *“God abrogated all of that and prescribed the shares.”* Ibn ʿUmar, ʿIkrimah, al-Ḥasan in another report, Mujāhid, and al-Suddī also said the inheritance verses abrogated it; al-Suddī says that when it came down people had no fixed shares, and a man would bequeath to his father and family until the verse of Sūrat al-Nisāʾ replaced it. Ibn ʿUmar himself made no bequest, and Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī said the Prophet died without making one while Abū Bakr made one, *“and whichever you do is good.”*

Since scholars dispute the abrogation, it cannot be declared abrogated without decisive proof. Abrogation applies only where two rulings cannot both stand at once, and this verse and the inheritance verses can both be applied: the heirs take their shares, and relatives who do not inherit receive the bequest.

### **SOMETHING OF VALUE**

The phrase ***“if they leave something of value”*** literally reads *“if he leaves good.”* The early authorities agree that the good here is wealth. Mujāhid says: *“Good throughout the Qur’an means wealth,”* citing Qur’an 100:8, *“Indeed he is intense in love of good.”* Al-Ḍaḥḥāk cites Shuʿayb’s words in Qur’an 11:84, *“I see you in prosperity.”* Ibn ʿAbbās, Qatādah, al-Suddī, al-Rabīʿ, ʿIkrimah, and ʿAṭāʾ also say it means wealth.

They differed over the amount. Qatādah said a thousand dirhams or more; ʿAlī told a dying man with seven hundred dirhams not to make a bequest, since he had not left good. ʿĀʾishah saw no surplus in four hundred dinars for a man with many children. Abān ibn Ibrāhīm said five hundred to a thousand. Al-Zuhrī said: *“God made the bequest a right, whether from little or much.”*

The strongest view is al-Zuhrī’s: the word covers both little and much, and God set no limit. Whoever is dying and has wealth, little or much, must bequeath part of it, ***“with fairness,”*** to parents and relatives who do not inherit from him, as God has commanded.
